sections.heading: The Year 6 to Year 7 transfer, and the gap that opens there
paragraphs: The move from a Dubai primary into a secondary school is where progress records usually break. The child changes building, often changes operator, meets subject specialists in place of a class teacher, and arrives with a file that may or may not be read. Nobody at the new school knows what was secure in June, and nobody at the old school will be asked. For a family, this is the single most valuable moment to hold their own record.

Two gaps open predictably. The first is written volume: secondary subjects expect more extended writing, faster, in more subjects, and a child who was comfortable producing a paragraph can struggle to produce five in a lesson. The second is mathematical fluency under new content. Secondary schemes assume automatic arithmetic and move straight into algebraic thinking, so a child still counting on from known facts spends their attention on the arithmetic and has none left for the new idea.

Both are easier to close in the summer before Year 7 than in the autumn after it. A short block of work on writing stamina and number fluency, with a measured baseline and a repeat at the end, is a defined piece of work rather than an open commitment. It also hands the new school something concrete. Dubai's sector is growing quickly, with seven new private schools in the 2026-27 intake creating 16,846 new places and enrolment up 6 per cent in the preceding year, so transfers between schools are common and records travel badly.

The third thing to establish at transfer is which boards the new school uses, because that decides what the examined years will look like. Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE differ in tiering, component structure and how practical skills are assessed, and schools in Dubai mix them by subject. Asking in Year 7 is early, but it costs nothing and it prevents a Year 10 surprise about Core and Extended entry.
bullets: Written volume and speed rise sharply in Year 7

sections.heading: Marked work as the unit of evidence, not the hour
paragraphs: Buying tuition by the hour measures the wrong thing. An hour is an input; marked work is an output. Two providers at the same hourly rate can produce very different amounts of readable evidence per month, and the difference is almost entirely whether anything gets marked properly between sessions. A family comparing quotes should be asking how much marked work a month contains, not only what an hour costs.

For an examined student the unit is a marked question or a marked paper section, with lost marks listed by cause rather than by topic. 'Described where explanation was required' is a cause. 'Lost two marks on osmosis' is a topic and leads to the wrong teaching. Causes are always fewer than topics, which is why a list of causes shortens the work while a list of topics lengthens it.

For a primary child the unit is a completed and corrected piece: a timed sheet with the errors classified, a comprehension exercise with question types noted, a piece of writing with the same criteria marked. Corrections matter more than scores at this age, because the pattern of error tells you what to teach next week and the score tells you only how today went.

For an IB student the unit is a draft. A draft read against the lettered criteria, returned with the criterion and the shortfall named, produces evidence a parent can read without understanding the subject. Movement from one draft to the next is visible in a way that no conversation about effort ever is, and it keeps the boundary clean: the student writes, the tutor assesses against published criteria and explains.

sections.heading: Grade movement: what is realistic, and over what period
paragraphs: No honest provider can promise a grade, and this page makes no promise about one. What can be described is how movement tends to behave, because the shape is consistent enough to plan around. Technique gains arrive fastest. Answering to the mark allocation, reading command terms correctly, laying out working so method marks survive a wrong final answer: these are learnable in a handful of sessions and they show up in the next marked paper because the knowledge was already there.

Content gains are slower and they are not linear. A missing foundation, such as algebraic fluency under a maths course or moles under Chemistry, takes a term or more of weekly work, and the marked evidence often stays flat for several weeks before it moves at all. Families who stop at week four because nothing has changed are frequently stopping just before the point where it would have. That is exactly why the record exists: it shows whether the work is landing even when the score has not shifted yet.

Pace gains sit in between. A student who knows the material and runs out of time needs distributed timed practice with marking between attempts, which is weeks rather than months, and the measure is simply how far through the paper they get. It is the easiest thing on this page to evidence and one of the least often measured, because measuring it requires sitting a paper under real conditions rather than a shortened version.

What this means for a decision is modest and useful. Set a review four sessions ahead, agree in advance which measure will be compared, and read the record rather than the feeling. If the measure moved, continue. If the same error is still returning after six weeks of teaching, change the method or change the tutor, because more of a method that is not working is not a plan.
bullets: Technique gains show in the next marked paper

sections.heading: Reports, inspection bands and tutor notes: three different things
paragraphs: Families in Dubai have three sources of information about a child's education and routinely treat them as interchangeable. They are not. A school report describes a child against that school's expectations. An inspection band describes the school, not the child. A tutor note describes what happened in one hour of teaching. Reading any of the three as if it were one of the others is a common and expensive mistake.

Dubai's school inspections produce a band for the school: Outstanding, Very Good, Good, Acceptable, Weak or Very Weak. A high band tells you about provision across hundreds of pupils, and it says nothing about whether your child's maths fluency is secure. Current ratings should be read on the authority's own published listing rather than taken from a tutoring page, and this page does not attach a rating to any school for that reason.

A school report is the most important of the three and the least specific. Ask for component or strand detail rather than an overall grade, because two identical grades can be made of completely different parts. At IGCSE, a 6 built from a strong theory paper and a weak practical paper needs different teaching from a 6 built from two middling papers, and the overall figure hides that entirely.

A tutor note is the most specific and the narrowest. It is evidence about one hour, and it only becomes evidence about learning when several notes are read together against a repeated measure. Used that way it is the fastest feedback a family has, arriving weekly rather than termly, and it is the only one of the three that a parent can act on the same evening.
bullets: An inspection band describes the school, never the child
Ask the school for strand or component detail, not the headline grade
A tutor note is evidence about one hour until several are read together
Check any current inspection rating on the authority's own listing

sections.heading: The exam calendar as a clock for the record
paragraphs: An evidence record needs a clock, and for an examined student the exam calendar provides it. Cambridge International runs IGCSE and O Level exams in a June series and a November series, and UAE centres use those two; the February/March series is offered to India only, so a Dubai candidate never sits it. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs May/June and November. Those are the fixed points everything else counts back from.

Past dates give the rhythm without pretending to predict future ones. The Pearson International GCSE November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Final entries close months ahead of the first paper, which means a resit decision is effectively made before results arrive, and that is worth knowing in advance rather than in August.

Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and states that it is essential to use the correct timetable version for your zone, adding that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. Ask the school's exams officer which zone it sits in and work from the school's own copy. For a primary family none of this applies yet, which is precisely why it is worth reading once now rather than in a hurry later.

For the IB, UAE schools sit the May session. No IB session or results date appears anywhere on this page: the IB's own site blocks automated checking, so nothing here has been confirmed from the source, and an unverified date on a page a parent plans around is worse than no date at all. Confirm IB dates with the school's IB coordinator or the IB directly.

sections.heading: What evidence-led tuition costs, and what a parent can verify
paragraphs: Price is easiest to judge when you know what you are comparing. In Dubai, published market figures read in October 2026 put a qualified online subject tutor at roughly AED 150 to AED 300 an hour, with Unitors publishing IGCSE tuition from AED 150 and IB tuition from AED 200. A budget or university-student tutor runs from about AED 33 to AED 150, with Tutopiya from AED 33 to AED 52 and EdFlik from AED 45 to AED 65. A specialist sits at AED 200 to AED 450 and above, with TutorChase quoting AED 270, and BartyED publishes AED 650 at the premium end. Those are other providers' figures, not an IB Gram price list.

What a parent can actually verify is narrower than price and more useful. You can verify that a written note exists after every session. You can verify that a baseline measure was recorded before teaching started and repeated afterwards. You can verify that the first piece of writing was kept. You can verify that lost marks are listed by cause. None of that requires subject expertise, and a provider who cannot produce it is asking to be judged on feel.

You can also verify the permit. Private tutoring in the UAE requires a private tuition work permit from the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, granted free of charge for two years, with eligible applicants including registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, students aged 15 to 18 and university students. Those tutoring without one face fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no official fine schedule is published, so any specific amount quoted to you is unverified.

In-home tuition sits outside the online band because the tutor's travel is inside the fee, with published in-home figures running from AED 180 to AED 500 an hour. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; that service exists only in India, and no tutor is sent to an Al Safa address. For an evidence-led arrangement the online format also helps mechanically: the annotated work, the baseline and the notes live in one place rather than in a school bag.

sections.heading: Coursework and Internal Assessment: where feedback stops
paragraphs: An evidence-led approach makes the academic-honesty boundary easier to hold rather than harder, because the evidence is the student's own draft. If a tutor's feedback has to name a criterion and a shortfall, there is nothing for the tutor to write. The student writes, the tutor assesses against the published criteria and explains what the criterion rewards, and the next draft shows whether the explanation landed.

Part of this market sells the opposite. One Dubai operator advertises completed IB Internal Assessments at AED 3,750. Submitting purchased work is malpractice under IB rules, the consequence falls on the student, and the exposure extends to the Diploma itself. Families comparing prices are sometimes unknowingly comparing two different products, which is why the boundary belongs on the page rather than in a terms document.

The permitted work is substantial. A tutor may teach what each criterion letter rewards and how marks are allocated across them, discuss a research question the student has proposed, read a draft the student wrote and identify where it falls short, and coach the process of collecting, presenting and referencing evidence. A tutor may not write any part of the submitted text, edit a draft into its final state, or supply a topic, data set or conclusion.

The same boundary applies to IGCSE coursework components, the Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge, and it extends to the boards' own material. Syllabuses, past papers, mark schemes and grade-boundary tables are copyright documents, so a tutor cites and links the official source instead of distributing copies. A provider who removes the student's work is not offering a shortcut; they are offering a risk the student carries alone.

process.title: Agree the measure before the first lesson
process.description: We decide together what will count as evidence: which reading assessment, which timed sheet, which writing criteria, or for an older student which component marks. Agreeing it first means the comparison exists later, and it takes one short conversation.

process.title: Record a baseline in the trial
process.description: The free trial session captures the starting point as well as introducing the tutor. You get the baseline in writing afterwards along with the tutor's read of the main gap, whether or not you continue. That document is useful to the school on its own.

process.title: Collect four-line notes weekly
process.description: After each session you receive a note naming what was worked on, what the student produced, what changed and what is set. It is short deliberately, because a note a parent does not read is not evidence of anything.

process.title: Review against the baseline every fourth session
process.description: The agreed measure is repeated and compared, not replaced with a new one. The review says plainly whether it moved, whether the same error is recurring, and what should change. Continuing is a decision made at that point rather than a default.

process.title: Hand the record over at a transfer
process.description: At a change of school or year group, the baseline, the kept first piece of work and the notes go to you as one file. The new teacher starts with history instead of guessing, which is the whole practical argument for keeping a record in the first place.

whyPoints.title: A record, not an impression
whyPoints.description: Four-line notes weekly and a review every fourth session, comparing a measure that was agreed before teaching began. The record includes what did not work, because a document that only holds successes is marketing rather than evidence.

whyPoints.title: Repeated measures over elaborate ones
whyPoints.description: The same reading assessment twice beats two different clever assessments. A repeat isolates the child as the only variable, which is the only way a parent without subject expertise can read a result with confidence.

whyPoints.title: Primary and examined years in one file
whyPoints.description: A household with a Year 4 and a Year 11 keeps one record in the same format. The measures differ by stage, the shape of the note does not, which makes two children's progress comparable in a way two providers never are.

whyPoints.title: Lost marks listed by cause
whyPoints.description: For examined students, feedback names the cause rather than the topic: explanation marks lost to description, method marks lost to unshown working, marks lost to graph presentation. Causes are fewer than topics, so the work gets shorter.

whyPoints.title: Stated boundary on assessed work
whyPoints.description: Feedback on the student's own drafts, naming the criterion and the shortfall. No writing, editing to completion or supplying of topics and data. The boundary is published because part of this market sells finished Internal Assessments.

whyPoints.title: Online, with the evidence saved
whyPoints.description: Sessions run one-to-one over live video with the child's work annotated on screen and kept. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; that service exists only in India, and the comparison on this page states the trade rather than hiding it.

faqs.question: How will I know whether tuition is working for my Horizon English School child?
faqs.answer: By agreeing a measure before the first session and repeating it, rather than judging the arrangement on how the child feels about the subject. For a primary pupil that usually means a standardised reading assessment, a timed arithmetic sheet, or a piece of writing marked against fixed criteria with the first piece kept. After four sessions the same measure is run again and compared. You also receive a four-line note each week naming what the child produced. Those two things together are readable without any subject expertise on your part.

faqs.question: What should be secure before my child moves from Year 6 into Year 7?
faqs.answer: Two things matter more than the rest: automatic arithmetic and writing stamina. Secondary schemes assume number facts are retrieved rather than calculated, and a child still counting on spends their attention on arithmetic with none left for the new idea. Secondary subjects also expect more extended writing, faster, across more subjects. A short summer block with a measured baseline and a repeat at the end addresses both as a defined piece of work, and it hands the new school something concrete about what was secure in June.

faqs.question: Why does my child's primary progress feel impossible to track?
faqs.answer: Because there is no external grade, year-group expectations are deliberately broad, and classroom performance varies day to day. The fix is not a more elaborate assessment but a small number of narrow measures used repeatedly. Timed number fluency, a standardised reading measure applied the same way twice, and the same writing criteria on two pieces months apart will tell you more than a long report. Track reading comprehension by question type as well, because retrieval and inference questions fail for different reasons and need different teaching.

faqs.question: Does a KHDA inspection rating tell me anything about my own child's progress?
faqs.answer: No. An inspection band describes provision across a whole school, using the scale from Outstanding through Very Good, Good and Acceptable to Weak and Very Weak. It is useful when choosing a school and almost useless as a measure of one pupil. Your child's progress lives in their own marked work and in strand-level detail from the report. Current ratings should be read on the authority's own published listing rather than taken from any tutoring page, which is why no rating is attached to a named school here.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a tutor's note and a school report?
faqs.answer: A school report describes your child against that school's expectations, usually once or twice a year, and it is the more important document. A tutor note describes one hour of teaching and arrives weekly. The note is specific enough to act on the same evening; the report is broad enough to set direction. Neither replaces the other. The useful request to the school is strand or component detail rather than an overall grade, because two identical grades can be built from completely different parts.

faqs.question: How many sessions before there is anything worth reading in the record?
faqs.answer: Four, which is why the first review sits there. One session establishes a baseline and a first impression. Two or three produce notes that show what the child can do when the task is set clearly. By the fourth there is enough to repeat the agreed measure and compare honestly. Earlier than that and you are reading noise; much later and a family has spent money before anyone checked whether the approach fits. If the measure has not moved by the second review, the method should change.

faqs.question: Can one provider keep a record for a Year 4 and a Year 11 in the same family?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is one of the more practical reasons families consolidate. The measures differ completely by stage, since a primary child is tracked on fluency and marked writing while a Year 11 is tracked on component marks and lost marks by cause. The shape of the weekly note stays identical, so a parent reads both in the same format and can see which child needs attention this month. It also means one review conversation rather than two, which matters more than it sounds in a busy term.

faqs.question: Is my child's grade likely to move quickly or slowly?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on the cause, and nobody honest promises a grade. Technique gains, such as answering to the mark allocation or laying out working so method marks survive, show up in the next marked paper because the knowledge was already there. Content gaps, like missing algebraic fluency or an unlearned moles foundation, take a term or more and the marked evidence often stays flat for weeks before it moves. Pace sits in between and needs distributed timed practice. The record tells you which one you are paying to fix.

faqs.question: What does the tutor actually write down after each session?
faqs.answer: Four lines: what was worked on, what the student produced, what changed, and what is set before next time. The second line names an artefact rather than an activity, so 'completed eight equivalent-fraction questions, six correct, two errors both in simplifying' rather than 'worked on fractions'. Notes also record what was tried and abandoned, and when a session found a skill already secure. Keeping the failures in is what separates a record from a sales document, and it is usually where the real gap gets located.

faqs.question: How does an online session work for a seven-year-old in Al Safa?
faqs.answer: Short, structured and with a second surface showing handwriting. A document camera or tablet lets the tutor see the child's working as it is produced rather than after the fact, and the child's own worksheet is shared and annotated on screen. Sessions for younger children are usually shorter than an hour and tightly segmented, because attention rather than ability is the limit. A quiet room and headphones matter more than bandwidth. The free trial exists to test whether the format suits the child before any money moves.

faqs.question: Should I ask the school for component marks or just the overall grade?
faqs.answer: Always ask for the breakdown. At IGCSE a single grade can be built from a strong theory paper and a weak practical paper, or from two middling papers, and those two situations need entirely different teaching. The practical or alternative-to-practical component is the one most often left unpractised, and its marks go on axes, scales, units, significant figures and anomalous points rather than on subject knowledge. Without the breakdown a family can spend a term revising content that was never the problem.

faqs.question: What evidence does an IB Internal Assessment produce along the way?
faqs.answer: Drafts, and they are the best evidence available in the Diploma. Each draft the student has written is read against the lettered criteria and returned with the criterion and the shortfall named, so movement between drafts is visible to a parent who does not know the subject. Three to five sessions across the drafting window works better than one long sitting, because the student needs time to write in between. The student writes every submitted word; the tutor assesses against published criteria and explains what each one rewards.

faqs.question: Which exam series will my child eventually sit from Dubai?
faqs.answer: For Cambridge, the June series or the November series. The February/March series is offered to India only, so no UAE candidate sits it, and a page quoting a February window to a Gulf family is giving a date that does not apply. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs May/June and November. intro.heading: Maths marks disappear in five specific ways
paragraphs: A mathematics grade is the most diagnosable thing on an IGCSE report, and it is almost never diagnosed. Parents are told their child is working at a grade 5 and should aim for a 6, which is a position rather than an explanation. The useful information sits in the script: which questions were attempted, which were abandoned, whether the working was shown, whether the right method was used with the wrong arithmetic, and whether the final answer was rounded into a lost mark.

Those distinctions are not pedantry. They cost completely different amounts to fix. A pupil losing marks because the method was never learned needs teaching, which takes a term. A pupil losing marks because the method is right and the working is not written down needs a habit changed, which takes four sessions. A pupil who ran out of time on the last page needs timed practice, which takes five. On a report these three pupils all look identical, and families routinely buy a term of teaching for a problem that was a habit.

Mathematics also behaves differently from every other IGCSE subject in one important respect: it is cumulative in a way biology is not. A pupil who never secured negative indices does not merely lose the indices marks; they lose the standard-form marks, the algebraic fraction marks, and the parts of physics and chemistry that assume both. That is why a maths gap found in Year 9 is cheap and the same gap found in the spring term of Year 11 is expensive. It has had two years to spread.

Then there is the calculator question, which is more consequential than it looks. Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 sets papers at each tier with different calculator permissions, and the Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics A route handles this differently again. A pupil who has revised exclusively with a calculator to hand has not practised the paper they will sit, and the marks lost are concentrated in exactly the places a confident pupil assumes they are safe: fractions, surds, standard form and multi-step arithmetic under pressure.

So this page is a map rather than a pitch. It sets out what each 0580 paper asks for, which topics carry the most marks at Extended tier, the five error types and what each one costs to repair, how the Cambridge route compares with Pearson's, and where an IGCSE maths grade leads next - into AS and A Level mathematics, or into the IB Diploma's two distinct maths routes, Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation. Tuition for Dubai families is one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time; IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai, and home visits are a service offered only in India.

sections.heading: What the Cambridge 0580 papers actually ask for
paragraphs: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 is examined by two written papers at each tier, with no coursework component. A Core candidate sits the Core pair; an Extended candidate sits the Extended pair. The syllabus is examined across both papers, which means there is no topic a pupil can decide not to revise and no component that can be dropped to protect a weak area.

The tier is a grade ceiling rather than a difficulty setting. A Core entry gives access to the lower part of the grade scale and cannot reach the top grades, however well the papers are answered on the day. An Extended entry opens the whole scale and includes questions that assume content a Core candidate never meets. Because the entry is made by the centre months before the paper, the ceiling is effectively set in the autumn term of Year 11 at the latest.

Calculator permissions differ between the papers, and this is the detail that most reliably surprises families. Confirm the current arrangement for your child's series on the live Cambridge syllabus, because specifications are revised and no tutoring page is the authority on an exam entry. What matters practically is that one of the papers will test arithmetic the pupil cannot delegate to a machine, and that revision done entirely with a calculator to hand does not prepare for it.

The consequence for tutoring is a specific one. Ask which papers your child is entered for, obtain a past paper of each from the official Cambridge site, and have the pupil sit one under timing. That single hour tells you more about where the grade is than a term of lessons will, and it costs a fraction of what the term costs. The table sets out the shape of the two routes side by side.

sections.heading: The calculator question, and why it costs more marks than it should
paragraphs: Almost every pupil revises mathematics with a calculator within arm's reach, because that is how homework is done. The result is a systematic blind spot. Arithmetic that a pupil genuinely could do becomes arithmetic they have not done for eighteen months, and it reappears under timed conditions in a paper where the machine is unavailable. The marks lost are not conceptual and they are not small.

The specific casualties are predictable. Fraction arithmetic with unlike denominators. Surd manipulation and rationalising. Standard form multiplication and division. Percentage reverse problems. Long multiplication and division inside a multi-step question where the pupil is concentrating on the method and the arithmetic quietly fails. Each of these is a few marks, and a paper contains enough of them to move a grade on their own.

There is a second, subtler cost. A pupil who cannot do the arithmetic quickly spends time on it, and time spent on arithmetic is time not spent on the last page of the paper. So a non-calculator weakness presents as a timing problem, and families buy timed practice for what is actually an arithmetic fluency problem. The diagnostic distinguishes them easily: look at whether the abandoned questions were hard or simply late.

The good news is that this is the fastest-moving work in mathematics. The content is already known, so nothing has to be taught, only re-fluent. Six to eight sessions of deliberate non-calculator practice, with the errors re-worked rather than merely corrected, typically recovers marks faster than any other intervention available at Extended tier. sections.heading: The five ways a maths mark disappears
paragraphs: There are only five, and sorting a script into them is the whole of maths diagnosis. Content: the pupil did not know the method, so the question was wrong or blank from the start. Method: the right approach was used but not written down, so the mark scheme could not award the working marks. Arithmetic: the method was right and a number went wrong. Precision: the value was right and the rounding, the units or the exact form was not. Timing: the question was never reached.

Each one has a different price. Content gaps need teaching, which is the expensive option and takes a term for a substantial topic. Method gaps need insisting on, which takes four or five sessions and never recurs once the habit forms. Arithmetic gaps need fluency practice. Precision gaps need a checklist and a few weeks of nagging. Timing gaps need full papers under the clock. A family that knows which one it has is buying a repair; a family that does not is buying reassurance.

The sorting is also the only honest basis for a conversation about what tutoring can and cannot do. A script with sixteen marks lost to method, arithmetic and precision is a script where a grade is genuinely available in a handful of weeks. A script where thirty marks are lost to content across half the syllabus is a different situation, and no amount of weekly tutoring in the final term resolves it. A provider who takes that money without saying so is selling comfort.

Counting is easy and almost nobody does it. Ask the school for the last marked mock paper, go through it question by question, and put each lost mark in one of five columns. The pattern is usually visible within twenty minutes, it is free, and it changes what you should buy. The table gives the recognition signs and the realistic cost of each repair.

sections.heading: Which topics carry the most Extended-tier marks
paragraphs: Not every topic is worth the same. Algebra runs through the whole Extended paper, appearing inside geometry, trigonometry, probability and functions questions, so algebraic fluency pays repeatedly rather than once. A pupil who cannot rearrange confidently loses marks in places that are not labelled algebra at all, which is why algebra repair is the highest-leverage purchase in the subject.

Trigonometry and Pythagoras are the next most profitable, partly because they recur and partly because pupils routinely lose the exact-form marks. Probability and statistics reward careful reading more than technique, and the commonest loss there is answering a different question from the one asked. Transformations and vectors are self-contained, which makes them cheap to repair and easy to abandon in revision because they feel unfamiliar.

Functions, sequences and graph work sit at the top end of the Extended paper and are where the difference between a good grade and a top grade is usually decided. A pupil aiming for the highest grades needs these secure; a pupil trying to lift a 4 to a 6 should probably leave them alone and spend the time on algebra and arithmetic, because that is where their missing marks actually are.

This is the argument against revising a syllabus in order. Revision that starts at chapter one and runs out of term in the middle is revision that spent its best weeks on number work the pupil already had. Revision built from a marked script starts where the marks are, and for most Extended-tier candidates in Dubai that means algebra, non-calculator arithmetic and written method, in that order, before anything else is considered.

sections.heading: Cambridge 0580 against Pearson Edexcel 4MA1
paragraphs: Dubai families move schools, and schools do not all use the same board. A pupil who has spent a year on Cambridge 0580 and transfers into a school entering Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics A has not lost their mathematics, but they have changed examination. Paper structures, calculator permissions and question styles all differ, and revision built on the wrong board's past papers is partly misdirected effort.

The naming differs too, which causes avoidable confusion. Cambridge runs Core and Extended tiers; Pearson Mathematics A runs Foundation and Higher. They are not synonyms, the content boundaries are not identical, and a parent comparing two schools' maths provision needs the board and tier together to make any sense of it. Ask the examinations officer for the specification code on the entry, because a prospectus that says 'IGCSE Mathematics' has told you almost nothing.

The practical remedy for a transfer is short and specific rather than open-ended. Confirm the code. Download the specification and past papers from the official board site, never from a third party. Work through the differences topic by topic, noting what is additional, what is absent and what is examined differently. Three or four sessions usually covers it, and it prevents a whole term of revision aimed at the wrong paper.

Both boards offer a November route, which matters for maths more than for most subjects. A single-subject mathematics retake is a contained plan rather than a crisis: the content is already covered, the diagnosis already exists, and the work is technique under timing. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and November, with the November 2026 timetable having run from late October to 19 November 2026 and results reaching students in January.

sections.heading: Where an IGCSE maths grade leads next
paragraphs: An IGCSE mathematics grade is a gate, and families often meet the gate after it has closed. Sixth-form mathematics departments publish entry grades and apply them, and the two post-16 destinations available in Dubai make different demands. A Level Mathematics assumes fluent Extended-tier algebra from the first week. The IB Diploma splits mathematics into two courses that are genuinely different subjects rather than two difficulty levels.

Analysis and Approaches is the algebraic, proof-oriented route, available at Higher and Standard Level, and it is the one competitive engineering, physics, mathematics and economics courses generally expect. Applications and Interpretation is modelling and data-oriented, also at both levels, and is well suited to pupils heading for business, social sciences, design or medicine-adjacent routes where statistics matter more than proof. Choosing between them on the basis of which looks easier is the commonest mistake.

The bridge between Extended-tier IGCSE and either destination is algebraic fluency, and Cambridge Additional Mathematics 0606 exists precisely to build it. A pupil who takes it alongside 0580 arrives in Year 12 having already met calculus and harder trigonometry, and the first term of A Level or Higher Level work stops being a cliff. Where a school does not offer it, a short block of pre-sixth-form algebra in the summer does much of the same job.

The practical instruction for a Year 10 parent is to look up the thresholds now rather than later. Find out what grade the sixth forms you are considering require in mathematics for the course your child wants, and compare it with where the marked script says they are. That converts an anxiety into a number, a gap and a number of sessions, which is the only form in which the problem can be solved.

sections.heading: When maths practice actually happens in a Dubai school year
paragraphs: Mathematics rewards frequency more than duration, which puts it at odds with how families buy tutoring. Three twenty-minute sessions of non-calculator arithmetic in a week does more for fluency than one ninety-minute lesson, because fluency is built by repetition and not by explanation. The weekly hour is for diagnosis, marking and teaching; the fluency work is homework, and a tutoring arrangement that does not set it is only doing half the job.

The Dubai calendar then imposes its own shape. The heaviest useful revision window for a June series sits in the eight to twelve weeks beforehand, which falls in the spring term. In some years that window overlaps Ramadan, when school days shorten and evenings restructure around Iftar. A family that moves sessions to a post-Iftar slot keeps the most valuable quarter of the two-year course intact. A family that pauses loses six weeks it cannot recover.

The long summer is the other underused asset. A pupil going into Year 11 with a known content gap is far better served by four sessions in August, when the topic can still be taught properly, than by twelve in February, when there is only time to revise what is already there. Diagnosing in June and working in August is the cheapest version of this entire plan, and it is also the version nobody books.

Mock season is the third fixed point, and it is worth planning round rather than merely surviving. A mock paper is a free diagnostic the school has already administered, and it is the single most valuable document in the process. Ask for the script rather than the grade, and ask for it soon enough that the information can still be acted on, which in practice means the autumn term rather than the spring.

sections.heading: What a maths tutor may not do, and how to test one
paragraphs: The honesty line in mathematics is narrower than in essay subjects but it exists. A tutor teaches, questions, models a method and marks the pupil's own attempts. A tutor does not complete a piece of assessed work for a pupil, and does not hand over Cambridge or Pearson past papers, mark schemes, grade-boundary tables or syllabus documents as files. Those belong to the boards, and the right behaviour is to link the official page.

One page ranking in this market sells completed Internal Assessments at a published price. That is a malpractice trigger rather than a service, and the risk sits with the candidate whose certificate is at stake. It is also a useful sorting device for parents: ask a prospective tutor plainly what they would do if asked to write a paragraph or supply a solution for submission. The answer is more informative than anything on a profile.

Testing mathematical competence is easier than parents expect, and does not require any mathematics from the parent. Ask three questions. Which specification code and tier is my child entered for, and what are the calculator permissions on each paper? Having read this marked script, how many marks were lost to method as against arithmetic? And what is the end point of the work you are proposing, stated as a number of sessions and a target? A tutor who cannot answer all three concretely is not worth a specialist rate.

On claims: IB Gram holds no KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, MoE, MoHRE, Cambridge, Pearson or IB approval, accreditation, licensing or partnership, and makes no such claim. It has no office or centre in the UAE. Anyone advertising regulator-approved tutors in Dubai is describing a KHDA Educational Services Permit, which is issued to training institutes with premises, and no online matching platform holds one.

sections.heading: Coverage, permits and getting started
paragraphs: Mathematics at both Cambridge and Pearson tiers is the best-covered subject in this set, and a match is usually quick. Additional Mathematics 0606 is thinner, and so is the combination of Extended-tier maths with a specific sixth-form bridging brief. In a given week the honest answer may be that nobody suitable is free, and that is better said than papered over with a generalist who will cost the same and deliver less.

Three outcomes are possible. The subject is covered and a trial lesson is scheduled within days. The subject is covered by a specialist working into Gulf Standard Time from outside the UAE, which is disclosed rather than hidden behind a local-looking telephone number. Or the brief is not currently covered, in which case saying so is the only decent answer. Rates do not change because a tutor is based outside the UAE.

On the legal position, which parents are entitled to check: private tutoring in the UAE is regulated by permit. The private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is issued through MoHRE, and is granted free of charge for two years. MoHRE's service page, Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Individuals tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no schedule of amounts has been published, so any figure circulating online is unverified.

Starting is deliberately low-commitment. A free trial lesson is one session, with no card details required, and the useful thing to bring to it is your child's last marked mathematics paper rather than a list of worries. Within that hour it should be possible to say how many marks were lost to each of the five error types and what the first four weeks of work would be. If it is not, the match is wrong and the next step is a different tutor.

process.title: Get the code, the tier and the calculator rules
process.description: Ask the examinations officer which specification your child is entered for, at which tier, and what the calculator permissions are on each paper. Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1 are different examinations, and Core and Extended are different papers. Practice aimed at the wrong one is polite, expensive and useless.

process.title: Sit one full paper under timing
process.description: Not a worksheet and not a topic test. A complete past paper from the official board site, under examination conditions, marked against the real mark scheme. One hour of this produces more usable information than a term of lessons, and it costs nothing but the hour.

process.title: Count the lost marks by error type
process.description: Sort every lost mark into content, method, arithmetic, precision or timing. The pattern is usually clear within twenty minutes. A script dominated by method and arithmetic losses means a grade is genuinely available in weeks; a script dominated by content losses across the syllabus means a different conversation.

process.title: Buy the narrowest fix the script justifies
process.description: Aim the work at the largest column rather than at the subject in general. Four or five sessions on written method, or six to eight on non-calculator fluency, with a stated target and an end point. An arrangement with no end point has stopped being a repair and become a standing order.

process.title: Set fluency homework and keep the slot
process.description: Mathematics rewards frequency over duration, so short daily arithmetic between sessions does more than a longer lesson. Fix a weekly time fifteen minutes after your child is actually home - later for Mudon and Arabian Ranches than for JVT - and hold it through mock season rather than renegotiating it each week.

whyPoints.title: Diagnosis before teaching
whyPoints.description: The first thing produced is a count of lost marks by error type, taken from your child's own timed script. That count decides what is bought and for how long. A page that only talks about mathematics being difficult cannot tell you whether you need four sessions or a term.

whyPoints.title: The non-calculator paper taken seriously
whyPoints.description: Almost every pupil revises with a calculator to hand and then sits a paper without one. Fractions, surds, standard form and multi-step arithmetic are the predictable casualties, and because the content is already known this is the fastest-moving work available at Extended tier.

whyPoints.title: Codes and tiers, not subject names
whyPoints.description: Work starts from the specification code and tier on the exam entry: 0580 or 4MA1, Core or Extended, Foundation or Higher. These are different examinations with different calculator rules, and a prospectus that says only 'IGCSE Mathematics' has not told you which one your child is sitting.

whyPoints.title: An end point, stated in advance
whyPoints.description: Every recommendation carries a number of sessions and a target drawn from the script. Where the honest recommendation is to stop, or to talk to the school about tier first, that is said. An open-ended weekly arrangement with no stated finish is a subscription rather than a repair.

whyPoints.title: Delivery and coverage stated plainly
whyPoints.description: Lessons are one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai; home visits are an India-only service. Where a brief such as Additional Mathematics 0606 has no specialist free, that is disclosed rather than filled with a generalist.

whyPoints.title: No claim that cannot be evidenced
whyPoints.description: No grade promises, no satisfaction percentages, no self-asserted ratings, and no suggestion that KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, MoE, Cambridge, Pearson or the IB has approved or partnered with IB Gram. Board documents are linked at source rather than copied and handed over.

faqs.question: What do the Cambridge 0580 papers ask a Jebel Ali School pupil to do?
faqs.answer: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 is examined by two written papers at each tier, with no coursework, and the syllabus is examined across both. A Core candidate sits the Core pair and cannot reach the top grades; an Extended candidate sits the Extended pair and has the full scale available. Calculator permissions differ between the papers, so confirm the current arrangement on the live Cambridge syllabus for your child's series. The practical consequence is that there is no weak topic a pupil can decide to skip and no component that can be banked before the series.

faqs.question: Is Extended-tier Maths 0580 worth attempting for a pupil currently at grade 5?
faqs.answer: It depends on what the lost marks are made of, not on the grade itself. A pupil at grade 5 whose script shows marks going to unshown method, non-calculator arithmetic and rounding has considerable headroom, because none of that requires new content. A pupil at grade 5 who cannot start the extended-content questions at all is in a different position, and Core entry may well produce a better certificate than a weak Extended attempt. The decision needs a timed Extended paper marked properly, and it needs to happen before the centre's entry deadline.

faqs.question: Which is harder for most pupils, the non-calculator paper or the calculator one?
faqs.answer: The non-calculator paper, almost invariably, and not because the mathematics is harder. Pupils revise with a calculator within reach because that is how homework is done, so arithmetic they genuinely could do has not been done for a year or more. Fractions with unlike denominators, surds, standard form and reverse percentages are the usual casualties, plus long arithmetic buried inside a method question. The marks lost are real and the repair is fast, because nothing needs teaching - only re-fluency, which is six to eight sessions of deliberate practice.

faqs.question: How do we find out whether marks are being lost to method or to arithmetic?
faqs.answer: Read the script rather than the report. Go through the last marked paper question by question and put each lost mark into one of five columns: content, method, arithmetic, precision or timing. A right answer with no working and unawarded working marks is a method loss. Method marks earned with the accuracy mark gone is an arithmetic loss. A correct value with the wrong rounding or units is precision. Blank final questions where similar earlier ones were answered is timing. The pattern is usually obvious within twenty minutes and it costs nothing.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Cambridge 0580 and Pearson Edexcel 4MA1?
faqs.answer: They are different examinations with different tier names, structures and calculator rules. Cambridge 0580 runs Core and Extended; Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics A 4MA1 runs Foundation and Higher, and the two sets of names are not synonyms. For a pupil transferring between Dubai schools mid-course, the sensible response is a short reconciliation of three or four sessions: confirm the code on the entry, obtain the right past papers from the official board site, and work through what is additional, absent or examined differently. Both boards offer a November series for a single-subject retake.

faqs.question: How many sessions does it take to stop losing method marks?
faqs.answer: Usually four or five, because it is a habit rather than a knowledge problem. A pupil who gets the right answer without writing the working is not confused; they are rushing, and the mark scheme cannot reward reasoning it cannot see. The fix is mechanical insistence: every question written out in full, every session, with the unshown steps pointed at until writing them becomes automatic. It is unglamorous work and it is some of the cheapest grade movement available, because nothing new has to be taught at any point.

faqs.question: Does my child need to memorise formulae for IGCSE mathematics?
faqs.answer: Some are provided and some are not, and the split differs between boards and can be revised, so check the live syllabus or specification for your child's series rather than relying on what an older sibling remembers. What matters more than the list is fluency: a pupil who has to stop and recall a formula has lost the thread of a multi-step question, and a pupil who can rearrange it confidently once recalled loses nothing. The practical test is whether the formula can be used under timing, not whether it can be recited.

faqs.question: Which Extended-tier topics carry the most marks worth chasing?
faqs.answer: Algebra, by a wide margin, because it is embedded inside geometry, trigonometry, probability and function questions rather than confined to its own section. A pupil who cannot rearrange confidently loses marks in places the paper does not label as algebra. Trigonometry and Pythagoras come next, largely through lost exact-form answers. Functions, sequences and vectors sit at the top end and decide the difference between a good grade and a top one, which is why a pupil moving a 4 to a 6 should generally leave them until algebra and arithmetic are secure.

faqs.question: How does an IGCSE maths grade feed into IB Maths AA and AI?
faqs.answer: The IB Diploma splits mathematics into two genuinely different courses, each at Higher and Standard Level. Analysis and Approaches is algebraic and proof-oriented, and competitive engineering, physics, mathematics and economics courses generally expect it. Applications and Interpretation is modelling and data-oriented, and suits business, social sciences and design routes where statistics matter more than proof. Both assume Extended-tier fluency, and Higher Level Analysis and Approaches assumes a good deal of it. Cambridge Additional Mathematics 0606, where a school offers it, is the best available bridge.

faqs.question: My child's maths set changed in Year 10. Does that affect the tier entry?
faqs.answer: Often, yes, because set placement is the main evidence a department uses when proposing a tier. A set change made on one term's assessments can quietly become a grade ceiling eighteen months later, and the change itself may reflect a short-term dip rather than a settled level. The response is to produce a second instrument: a timed Extended-tier paper marked against the real mark scheme, which is a different measurement from classroom assessment. Ask the department what evidence it wants and when its internal entry deadline falls, then meet it.

faqs.question: Can mathematics practice continue through Ramadan?
faqs.answer: Yes, and for a June-series candidate it should. The heaviest useful revision window sits eight to twelve weeks before the paper, which lands in the spring term and in some years overlaps Ramadan. School days shorten and evenings restructure around Iftar, so sessions move to a post-Iftar slot rather than disappearing. A family that reschedules keeps the most valuable quarter of the two-year course intact; a family that pauses loses six weeks at the point when timed practice and marked rewriting are the only interventions still capable of moving a grade.

faqs.question: Is a maths tutor still useful in the last three weeks before the June paper?
faqs.answer: For some things, yes, and for others no. Timed paper practice with marking and immediate re-working remains productive right up to study leave, and so does a precision checklist applied to every final answer. What does not work in three weeks is teaching a topic the pupil has never understood, and a provider willing to take the money for that is selling comfort. The honest version is narrow: pick the two highest-yield error types from the script, work only on those, and leave the rest alone.

faqs.question: Do you send maths tutors to Damac Hills or Arabian Ranches addresses?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; sending a tutor to a family's address is a service offered only in India. Tutoring for Dubai families is one-to-one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time. For mathematics that works particularly well, because the session is spent annotating the pupil's own marked script on a shared screen and re-working the questions they lost marks on. It also means the tutor is chosen for the specification and tier rather than for living within a drivable radius of your community.

faqs.question: How do we check that a maths tutor actually knows the 0580 specification?
faqs.answer: Ask three questions and listen for specifics. Which code and tier is my child entered for, and what are the calculator permissions on each paper? Having read this marked script, how many marks went to method as against arithmetic? And what is the end point of the work you propose, as a number of sessions and a target? A tutor who answers all three concretely has read the specification and the script. A tutor who answers in general terms about building confidence has read neither, and will charge the same rate.

dubai/ib-igcse-tutor-for-jebel-ali-schoo.closingHeading: Bring one marked paper, not a list of worries
dubai/ib-igcse-tutor-for-jebel-ali-schoo.closingBody: The most useful thing you can do this week costs nothing. Ask the school for your child's last marked mathematics paper, then sort every lost mark into content, method, arithmetic, precision or timing. The pattern usually appears within twenty minutes, and it tells you whether you are looking at four sessions or a term. A free trial lesson is one session, with no card details required, and the right thing to bring to it is that script. Lessons are one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time, and where a brief such as Additional Mathematics 0606 has no specialist free, that will be said rather than filled.

Each teaches one subject at one level and works from the criteria or the mark scheme that will actually be applied, not from a general sense of the subject.

intro.heading: Two edges, and the one that catches good students
paragraphs: The Middle Years Programme does something unusual: it reports in a language most parents have never been taught to read. A report arrives with criterion scores out of eight under letters rather than percentages, and a summary grade from 1 to 7 that averages them. A student can score 7 on criterion A and 3 on criterion D and land on a 5 overall, which looks unremarkable and conceals a specific, nameable weakness. Nobody is hiding anything. The information is there and the vocabulary for using it is not widely shared.

The second edge is the step into the Diploma, and it catches students who have never had academic trouble. A Year 11 student holding criterion scores of six and seven moves into Mathematics Analysis and Approaches or Chemistry Higher Level and finds the first term difficult in a way nothing warned them about. This is predictable and it is not a collapse. The Middle Years Programme assesses inquiry, communication and application against descriptors; the Diploma assesses those plus an accumulated technical fluency that the descriptors never explicitly demanded.

At a continuum school like Jumeirah Baccalaureate School both edges arrive in the same building, which means a family can be reading unfamiliar criterion reports for four years and then meet an external examination for the first time in Year 12. There is no mock IGCSE to serve as a reality check along the way. The first hard external mark is the one that counts, and by then the habits are five years old.

This page is built around that pair of problems. It explains what each Middle Years Programme criterion actually rewards and how to act on a low one. It maps the Diploma gap subject by subject rather than in the abstract, so a family can see what a student moving into Biology Higher Level needs that Middle Years Programme science did not require. It covers the Personal Project, which is many students' first long independent piece of work and often their first encounter with a word limit that bites.

It also covers the British-route comparison honestly, because plenty of Dubai families hold one child in an IB continuum and another in an IGCSE school, and the two are not variations on a theme. IGCSE grades come from terminal papers marked against a published scheme question by question. Middle Years Programme and Diploma grades come from criterion-referenced judgements plus, in the Diploma, external papers. What counts as good work differs, and so does what a tutor should be doing.

Delivery, stated once. Tutoring for Dubai families is one-to-one, live, over video, in Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service offered only in India. An Al Safa family therefore chooses a specialist in the criterion or the paper that is causing trouble rather than whoever can reach Jumeirah by five o'clock.

dubai/ib-igcse-tutor-for-jumeirah-baccal.programmesIntro: Jumeirah Baccalaureate School runs the IB continuum. The three stages that generate tutoring requests are the upper Middle Years Programme, the transition year, and the Diploma itself, and each needs something different.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Four criteria per subject, each marked out of eight against published descriptors. In mathematics they are knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. In the sciences the second and fourth shift to inquiring and designing, and reflecting on the impacts of science. The letters matter more than the summary grade because they are actionable.
programmes.countryNote: At a Dubai continuum school this is where the cheap fixes live. A student weak on the communication criterion is losing marks for presentation of reasoning rather than for mathematics, and that is weeks of work rather than months. Left alone it compounds into the Diploma, where written justification carries real weight in every subject.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects with three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Subject grades total 42 points and the core adds up to three more. Internal Assessments are marked against lettered criteria; final papers are externally marked. Both reward a visible chain of reasoning rather than a correct endpoint.
programmes.countryNote: UAE schools sit the May session. No IB examination or results date appears on this page, because ibo.org blocks automated verification and an unverified date on a page a family plans around is worse than none. Work from the school's own internal deadlines, which sit ahead of the IB's and are what actually governs a student's term.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE
programmes.description: Included here because many Dubai families hold children in both systems or transfer between them. Two years ending in terminal papers graded 9-1 or A*-G, with tiering in several subjects that caps the available grade before the paper is written. Assessment is point-based against a published mark scheme rather than criterion-referenced.
programmes.countryNote: A student moving from Middle Years Programme Year 9 into Year 10 IGCSE at another Dubai school usually finds the content manageable and the assessment style unfamiliar: nothing in criterion-referenced work requires method to be written out so that method marks can be awarded. That habit is the first four to six sessions of any transfer plan.

dubai/ib-igcse-tutor-for-jumeirah-baccal.subjectsIntro: What the Diploma asks for that the Middle Years Programme did not, subject by subject. These are the courses Al Safa and Jumeirah families most often bring, and the gap is specific in each.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The gap is algebraic automaticity. Middle Years Programme work rewards the method and the reasoning; the Diploma assumes the manipulation inside a question is effortless so that calculus and proof have room. Students who understand the ideas still lose marks mid-question. Paper 3 at Higher Level is an extended investigation marked on written reasoning.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Lighter on proof, heavier on statistics and modelling than most students expect, with technology use assumed throughout. Calculator technique is an assessed skill rather than a convenience, and students arriving from criterion-based work often under-practise it because nothing previously marked it.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: The gap is quantitative. Middle Years Programme science rewards inquiry design and reflection; Diploma Chemistry requires moles, energetics and mechanisms handled with units and significant figures treated as marked content. Organic mechanism arrows are a notation that has to be taught explicitly.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Content volume rises sharply and command words tighten. Distinguish, outline, evaluate and suggest demand different answer shapes, and accurate biology in the wrong shape scores nothing. This is the fastest available fix for a student whose knowledge is sound and whose marks are not.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: The gap is deriving a relationship from data rather than knowing the relationship. Graph-based and extended-response questions cluster the losses, and the skill of reading a gradient as physics is distinct from recall. Four or five focused sessions usually shift it.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The Individual Oral requires sustained analysis of a global issue through two texts, which is a longer piece of structured talking than anything in the Middle Years Programme. Written work must analyse rather than describe, and the difference is visible in whether quotations are interrogated or merely placed.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Mostly new content at Diploma, so the gap is pace rather than prior knowledge. Diagram accuracy carries marks prose cannot recover, and Higher Level evaluation is a separate taught skill with its own allocation rather than a flourish at the end of an essay.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Case-study papers reward application to the stimulus, which suits students trained on Middle Years Programme application criteria. The common failure is reciting theory without touching the company. Higher Level quantitative tools are marked on method shown, not on the final figure.

subjects.name: Visual Arts
subjects.description: Assessment includes a comparative study and a process portfolio, both of which reward sustained documented thinking rather than finished pieces. Students who produce strong work and document it thinly lose marks that are straightforwardly recoverable with a different working habit.

subjects.name: Arabic as an Additional Language
subjects.description: Required in all Dubai private schools whatever the licensed curriculum. KHDA requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs because curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ, so the stream must be confirmed before a plan is written.

sections.heading: What each Middle Years Programme criterion actually rewards
paragraphs: The four criteria are not four aspects of the same thing. Criterion A, knowing and understanding, is closest to a conventional test: can the student recall and use the subject's content and procedures. Most students who are considered good at a subject score well here, which is why a strong A can mask everything else. Criterion B differs by subject group. In mathematics it is investigating patterns, which rewards finding and justifying a general rule. In the sciences it is inquiring and designing, which rewards a well-constructed investigation with controlled variables and a testable hypothesis.

Criterion C is communicating, and it is the one most often dismissed as presentation. It is not. It rewards the use of appropriate notation, terminology and logical structure, which means a student who reaches a correct answer by an unreadable route scores badly on C regardless of the mathematics. This is also the criterion with the most direct Diploma consequence, because every Diploma subject rewards a visible chain of reasoning and penalises an unjustified assertion.

Criterion D is applying the subject in real-life or unfamiliar contexts, and in practice it is the hardest and most predictive. It asks the student to take a procedure learned in one setting and deploy it somewhere it was not taught. A student can hold every technique in the course and score three on D because they have only ever met those techniques in the question types that announce them. That is the profile that struggles most in the Diploma, and it is also the one least likely to be flagged, because the summary grade looks fine.

The practical move for a parent is simple and free: ask the subject teacher for the criterion breakdown rather than accepting the summary grade, then target the lowest letter. If the breakdown is not on the report, it exists in the school's assessment records and teachers will generally share it on request.

sections.heading: The Year 11 to Diploma gap, mapped per subject
paragraphs: The step into the Diploma is routinely described as a jump in workload, which is true and not very useful, because workload is not what students actually hit. What they hit is a specific technical expectation in each subject that the Middle Years Programme did not require them to make automatic. Naming it per subject turns a vague anxiety into a six-session piece of work.

In mathematics it is manipulation speed and accuracy inside longer questions. A student who can explain differentiation will still lose the marks if the algebra in the middle of the question breaks down, and the Middle Years Programme never demanded that the algebra be effortless. In chemistry it is quantitative handling: moles, energetics and significant figures treated as marked content rather than as arithmetic to be tidied later. In physics it is extracting a relationship from plotted data, which is a different skill from knowing the relationship.

In biology the gap is command-word discipline against a much larger body of content. In the languages it is sustained analysis: the Individual Oral asks for ten minutes of structured argument about a global issue through two texts, which is longer and more independent than anything in Year 11. In the arts it is documentation, because process portfolios reward recorded thinking and students who make strong work and document it thinly lose recoverable marks.

The sensible place to do this work is the summer before Year 12 or the first few weeks of it, when the gap is small and nothing else is urgent. Done then, it is a short block. Done in the second term of Year 12, it competes with the Internal Assessment and the actual course, which is why the same gap costs several times as much to close later.

sections.heading: The Personal Project, and the word limit that bites
paragraphs: The Middle Years Personal Project is the first genuinely independent long piece of work most students produce, and for many it is also their first encounter with a limit that cannot be negotiated. It is assessed against published criteria covering planning, applying skills and reflecting, and the marks go to the process rather than to the object produced. Students who build something impressive and document it thinly score lower than students whose outcome is modest and whose process is clearly evidenced.

The most common failure is scope. A project question broad enough to be interesting is usually too broad to be completed and evidenced within the limit, and the student discovers this late, when the work is done and the report will not fit. Narrowing the question at the start costs one conversation. Narrowing it at the end costs discarded work. This is the same failure that appears two years later in Diploma Internal Assessments and Extended Essays, which is why the Personal Project is worth taking seriously as practice.

Legitimate help is clear here and worth stating because the Personal Project is a student's own work in exactly the way an Internal Assessment is. A tutor may help narrow the question, check the plan is achievable, explain what each criterion rewards, read what the student has written and ask the questions an assessor would ask, and teach how to evidence a process as it happens rather than reconstructing it afterwards. A tutor may not design the project, write the report, or produce the outcome.

The habit worth installing is documentation in real time. A student who keeps a short dated log of decisions and setbacks as they occur has the evidence the reflecting criterion asks for. A student reconstructing it in the final week is writing fiction and it reads as such. That habit, once established, carries directly into the Diploma, where every Internal Assessment rewards the same discipline.

sections.heading: Higher Level or Standard Level: a decision with a two-year tail
paragraphs: Diploma subject choices are made in Year 11 and they constrain university options two years later, which makes them one of the most consequential academic decisions a Dubai family takes. The Higher Level and Standard Level distinction is not simply a matter of difficulty or hours. The courses differ in content, in the weighting of components and in what they prepare a student to do next, and the right choice depends on the student's profile rather than on ambition.

The useful evidence is the criterion breakdown rather than the summary grade. A student with a strong criterion A and a weak criterion D in mathematics is being carried by recall, and Higher Level will expose that in the first term. A student with a moderate A and a strong D has the transfer ability the Higher Level course rewards and may do better than their grade suggests. These two profiles can hold the same summary 5 and should be advised differently.

University requirements are the other half of the decision and they are specific rather than general. Medicine, engineering and economics courses commonly specify Higher Level subjects and sometimes which mathematics route, and a Standard Level choice made in Year 11 can quietly close a course two years later. The place to check is each university's own published entry requirements rather than general advice, and the time to check is before the choice is locked.

What tutoring contributes here is evidence rather than persuasion. A short block of Diploma-style questions in the candidate subject, marked honestly, tells a family far more than a prediction does. If the student is collecting marks on Higher Level material, the choice is straightforward. If they are not, the family is making an informed decision instead of a hopeful one.

sections.heading: What a Dubai IB family should know about the examination calendar
paragraphs: UAE schools sit the Diploma in the May session. This page publishes no IB examination or results date, and that is deliberate: ibo.org returns an error to automated checking, so no IB date in this project has been confirmed from the IB itself, and an unverified date on a page a family plans around is worse than silence. Confirm every Diploma deadline with the Jumeirah Baccalaureate School coordinator, who holds the internal calendar that actually governs the year.

For the British-route sibling, the dates are published and checkable. Cambridge International runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level examinations in a June series and a November series, with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests in March, May and October. The February and March series is offered to India only, so a UAE candidate sits June or November. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May and June and again in November.

Verifiable past dates are worth citing precisely because they can be checked. The Pearson November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. For a future series, read the live official timetable on the board's site; provisional timetables are revised and a restated date goes stale on its own.

One administrative point applies to Cambridge candidates. Every centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones, and Cambridge states it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone and that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after using the wrong one. Get the zone from the exams officer rather than from a search result.

sections.heading: KHDA, the mandatory subjects, and what a regulator does not do
paragraphs: Dubai private schools are overseen by the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, which the UAE government describes as responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate, inspecting annually across six bands from Outstanding to Very Weak. Abu Dhabi and Al Ain sit under ADEK, Sharjah under the Sharjah Private Education Authority, Ras Al Khaimah under its Department of Knowledge, and Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah under the federal Ministry of Education.

Alongside any licensed international curriculum, KHDA requires Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies in all Dubai private schools. Schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, because curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ, and combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited. Teachers of Arabic and Islamic Education must hold appropriate KHDA approval for those subjects, and the use of different or additional content without prior Ministry permission is prohibited.

That last point has a direct consequence for tutoring in these subjects. The content is set and a tutor cannot substitute their own material, so support has to work within the prescribed curriculum rather than around it. A parent should also know which stream their child sits in, because the Arabic first-language and additional-language routes are different courses with different expectations.

What a regulator does not do is endorse a tutoring company. A tutoring operation with premises and staff in Dubai requires a KHDA Educational Services Permit issued to training institutes, with initial approval first and annual renewal requested at least thirty days before expiry. IB Gram holds no such permit, operates no UAE office or centre, and no tutor here is described as KHDA-approved or IB-approved. Any provider using those phrases should be asked to produce the permit.
