sections.heading: Why a primary search lands on an IGCSE page
paragraphs: It lands here because the two are connected by a chain nobody draws. A primary pupil's arithmetic fluency determines how much of their attention a Year 9 algebra lesson consumes. That determines the set they are placed in at the end of Year 9. That set, in most Dubai schools, informs the tier they are entered for at IGCSE. And a Core-tier entry caps the grade scale, whatever the pupil does on the day of the paper.

Each link in that chain is reasonable on its own and the cumulative effect surprises people. Nobody decides in Year 5 that a child will be entered at Core tier in Year 11. The decision emerges from a sequence of defensible judgements made on the evidence available at each point, and the evidence at each point was shaped by the fluency the pupil brought into the room. That is why the earliest work is the cheapest, and the latest work is the most expensive and least effective.

The second reason is subject-level. Four of the things primary schools work on are the direct ancestors of specific IGCSE assessment objectives, not vague prerequisites. Science enquiry at ten becomes the alternative-to-practical paper at sixteen, which carries around a fifth of each Cambridge science grade. Inferential reading at nine becomes the reading analysis question. Planning before writing becomes the structure marks in every essay subject. The lineage is traceable.

None of this is an argument for tutoring a nine-year-old as a matter of course. Most primary pupils in Dubai need no paid help at all, and a child who is fluent, reads beyond the literal and plans their writing should be left alone to enjoy being nine. The argument is narrower: if one of those four things is genuinely insecure, dealing with it now is a fraction of the cost of dealing with it later. The table draws the chain explicitly.

sections.heading: Cambridge Checkpoint: what it is, when it runs, what it means
paragraphs: Cambridge Primary Checkpoint and Lower Secondary Checkpoint are diagnostic tests marked by Cambridge, taken at the end of the primary and lower secondary stages. They are offered in March, May and October. They report scaled scores with strand-level feedback rather than grades, and that structure is the point: the useful output is which parts of mathematics, English and science are weak, not a single number.

Not every Dubai school enters pupils, and those that do use the results differently. Some use them to inform setting for the next stage, some purely for internal tracking and reporting to parents, and some as evidence in a secondary transfer. Those three uses have very different consequences, and the only way to know which applies is to ask. A result used for setting carries forward; a result used for tracking does not.

What Checkpoint feedback is good for is targeting. A report showing weakness in a specific mathematics strand tells a parent and a tutor exactly where to work, which is far better information than a school report comment. What it is not good for is prediction. It is one performance on one test at one point, and a child who was unwell, or who had not met a topic, will read lower than they are without that meaning anything about Year 11.

The practical move for a primary family is therefore modest. Read the strand feedback rather than the overall score. Compare it against your child's own written work from the same term, which the school will share. If both point the same way on one of the four gaps, that is worth a short block of work. If they disagree, the test is the less reliable instrument and the written work is the better one.

sections.heading: The four primary gaps that become IGCSE grades
paragraphs: Number fluency is the first and most expensive. It means arithmetic performed without conscious effort: times tables, fractions, decimals, percentages, negatives. A pupil who can do these correctly but slowly has a working memory problem later rather than an arithmetic problem now, because every Year 9 algebra step will be competing for attention with a calculation that should have been free. At IGCSE it shows up as the non-calculator paper and as timing failures that look like laziness.

Inferential reading is the second. Literal retrieval - finding the answer that is stated in the text - is the skill primary assessment measures most and secondary assessment rewards least. The step to saying what a text implies, and what effect a word has on a reader, is a different skill, and a pupil who never makes it will earn comprehension marks at IGCSE and leave the analysis marks unclaimed in every reading component for five years.

Written structure is the third. A primary pupil who begins writing immediately and finds their shape as they go produces strong first paragraphs and loses coherence, which is charming at nine and costs structure marks at sixteen in every essay subject. The habit worth installing is unglamorous: agree the shape before writing anything. It takes a term of insistence at primary age and considerably longer later.

Precision is the fourth and the most teachable. Units written, answers labelled, rounding considered, the question actually answered rather than a nearby question answered well. Primary marking is often generous about this because the mathematics was right. IGCSE marking is not: a correct value with the wrong unit or the wrong rounding scores nothing. Building the habit of checking the final answer is five minutes per session for a year, and it pays in every subject.

sections.heading: Reading comprehension at ten and analysis at sixteen
paragraphs: The gap between these two is the one families notice least and pay for most. A Year 5 pupil who reads fluently, enjoys books and answers comprehension questions correctly looks entirely secure, and in the terms primary assessment uses, they are. The questions being asked are overwhelmingly retrieval questions: what happened, who said it, where was it. A confident reader answers them without effort.

Secondary assessment asks something else. It asks what a word does, what a writer's choice achieves, and what a reader is made to feel. That requires selecting a precise word rather than a whole sentence, naming what is being done with it, and stating an effect. None of those three steps is practised by retrieval questions, and a pupil can spend six years reading widely without ever being asked to perform them.

The transition is teachable at primary age in a form children find enjoyable rather than onerous. Choose one word from a sentence and ask why that word and not a plainer one. Ask what picture it puts in the reader's head. Ask what would change if it were swapped. That is the whole technique, and a child who does it regularly at ten arrives at IGCSE with the habit already formed while their classmates are being taught it under time pressure in Year 10.

This is also the single clearest example of why primary work transfers. The same skill earns marks in IGCSE English reading components, in History source questions, and in the interpretation parts of Geography. One habit built at primary age pays in three subjects six years later, which is a better return than any single-subject intervention available at fifteen.

sections.heading: Number fluency: the most expensive thing to leave
paragraphs: Fluency and accuracy are not the same thing, and primary assessment frequently cannot distinguish them. A child who computes seven eighths minus two thirds correctly in ninety seconds has demonstrated accuracy. A child who does it correctly in fifteen seconds has demonstrated fluency. Both score the mark. Only the second one will be able to do it as an incidental step inside a Year 10 algebra question without losing the thread of the question.

That is the mechanism by which a primary gap becomes a secondary grade. Working memory is finite. A pupil spending it on arithmetic has less available for the method, and the method is where the marks are. This is why apparently careless errors cluster in long questions: the pupil was not careless, they were out of capacity. It also explains why these pupils look fine on short questions and fall away on multi-step ones.

The remedy at primary age is frequency rather than explanation, which is why primary tutoring should look different from secondary tutoring. Twenty-five minutes twice a week beats an hour once a week for fluency work, because fluency is built by repetition under mild time pressure. The content does not need teaching; it needs practising until it is free. A good primary session is mostly the child working, not the tutor talking.

There is a stopping rule, and it matters. Fluency work should end when the skill is automatic, not when the term does. A pupil who can do their fraction arithmetic quickly and reliably does not need more sessions on it, and continuing is how a short intervention becomes a standing arrangement. The test is simple and should be applied monthly: can the child do it fast, under mild pressure, without being reminded how?

sections.heading: Choosing a secondary school from a primary standpoint
paragraphs: Families leaving a primary school in Dubai face a decision that is usually made on reputation and inspection band, and those are the two least useful inputs for an individual child. A KHDA inspection band describes a school's overall provision; it does not say whether that school's mathematics department will place your child in the set their fluency justifies, or whether it enters pupils at Core or Extended tier by default.

The questions that do predict something are narrower and schools will generally answer them. When does setting happen, and on what evidence? How often do pupils move between sets, and what triggers a review? Which boards does the school use for IGCSE, and in which subjects? Does the school enter pupils at Core tier, and in what circumstances? Does it offer Additional Mathematics 0606 or separate sciences? What are its own sixth-form entry grades?

The last two matter disproportionately. A school that does not offer separate sciences has constrained A Level science options for its own pupils, and a school with no Additional Mathematics provision leaves a pupil heading for Higher Level Analysis and Approaches without the designed bridge. Neither is a flaw in a school; both are facts a family should know while choosing rather than discovering in Year 10.

Dubai gives families unusual choice here. KHDA counted 387,441 pupils across 227 private schools offering seventeen different curricula in 2024-25, and the 2026-27 intake adds seven more schools, four UK curriculum and three International Baccalaureate, creating 16,846 places. With that much supply, asking specific questions and declining to be reassured in general terms is a realistic strategy rather than a presumptuous one.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies in the primary years
paragraphs: Dubai primary families meet a requirement that families elsewhere do not, and it is worth understanding properly rather than treating as an administrative detail. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, and KHDA's requirements were to be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, with April 2026 for schools whose academic year begins in April.

The rules are specific. For Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, schools must organise separate classes for Arab and non-Arab pupils, and combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because the curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language, with Arabic as the primary language for Social Studies for Arab pupils and the school's licensed-curriculum language for non-Arabs in Islamic Education and Moral, Social and Cultural studies.

Two further requirements affect what tutoring in these subjects can legitimately look like. Schools must ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold appropriate KHDA approval to teach those subjects, which is a concrete and checkable credential point. And for the mandatory subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited, so no provider may substitute its own syllabus or materials.

On time allocation, KHDA calculates mandatory-subject instructional time on a 40-minute lesson unit, permits schools to vary lesson length provided the total weekly time is met, and advises that any mandatory-subject lesson should be at least 25 minutes. For a parent, the practical use of all this is to know what the school is required to deliver, to ask how it is delivering it, and to treat any tutoring in these subjects as support for the prescribed content rather than an alternative to it.

sections.heading: What primary tutoring should and should not look like
paragraphs: Primary tutoring goes wrong in predictable ways and most of them come from importing a secondary model. An hour is too long. A weekly rhythm is too infrequent for fluency. A curriculum-order syllabus march ignores the fact that one specific thing is weak. And a session where the tutor explains for forty minutes and the child works for ten has reversed the only ratio that matters at this age.

What works is short, frequent and productive. Twenty-five to thirty minutes, twice a week, with the child working for most of it under mild time pressure and the tutor marking, prompting and raising the difficulty. One target per block, stated in words a nine-year-old can repeat. A monthly test of whether the skill has become automatic, and a stop when it has. That shape is unfashionable because it sells fewer hours, and it is what the evidence of the child's own work supports.

There are things nobody should be paying for at primary age. Homework completion is not tutoring; it is outsourcing, and it teaches a child that difficulty is someone else's problem. Preparation for a school entrance assessment by drilling that assessment's format teaches format rather than mathematics. And a general weekly arrangement with no named target, continuing indefinitely, is a subscription that will quietly run for four years.

The honest recommendation for most Dubai primary families is no paid tutoring at all. A child who is fluent, reads beyond the literal, plans their writing and checks their answers needs time, books and a reasonable bedtime rather than a tutor. Where one of the four gaps is genuinely insecure, a short targeted block is excellent value. Those are different situations and a provider who cannot tell you which one you are in should not be given the hour.
bullets: Twenty-five to thirty minutes twice a week beats an hour once a week for fluency

sections.heading: Coverage, permits and the first session
paragraphs: Primary and lower secondary mathematics and English are well covered in this set, and a match is usually quick. Thinner briefs exist: Arabic as a first language at primary level, Islamic Education within the prescribed MoE content, and specific Cambridge Primary strand work for a school following that curriculum closely. In a given week the honest answer may be that nobody suitable is free, and that is better said than filled with a generalist.

Three outcomes are possible. The brief is covered and a trial lesson is scheduled within days. The brief is covered by a specialist working into Gulf Standard Time from outside the UAE, which is disclosed rather than hidden behind a local-looking telephone number. Or the brief is not currently covered, in which case it is named. Rates do not change because a tutor is based outside the UAE, and for the mandatory UAE subjects any support must follow the prescribed content rather than substitute for it.

One credential is checkable, and at primary level it is the only one on offer. The private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and issued through MoHRE free of charge for two years, is what makes paid private tuition lawful in the UAE. Its eligibility list reaches further than most parents of a nine-year-old assume: teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school pupils aged fifteen to eighteen. So a permitted sixteen-year-old may lawfully hear a Year 5 pupil read, which is useful work and tends to be priced as such. It is not the same purchase as a trained primary teacher diagnosing a number-fluency gap, and the permit draws no distinction between the two. Tutoring without any permit attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no schedule of amounts has been published, so no figure should be quoted at you as fact.

Starting is small by design. A free trial lesson is one session, with no card details required, and the useful thing to bring is a sample of your child's own written work from this term plus any Checkpoint or assessment report. Within that session it should be possible to say which of the four gaps, if any, is genuinely insecure, and what a short block aimed at it would consist of. A recommendation of no paid work is a legitimate and common outcome at this age.

process.title: Collect two pieces of evidence, not one
process.description: Ask the school for a sample of your child's own written work from this term, and read any Checkpoint or internal assessment report for its strand feedback rather than its overall score. Where both point the same way on one of the four gaps, that is strong evidence. Where they disagree, trust the written work.

process.title: Test fluency, not accuracy
process.description: Give your child a handful of fraction or times-table questions and watch the clock rather than the answers. Correct but slow is a fluency gap, and fluency is what secondary content assumes. This distinction is invisible to most primary marking and it is the single most predictive thing you can check at home.

process.title: Name one target, in words the child can repeat
process.description: Not 'improve at maths' but 'know every times table without counting' or 'say what a word does to a reader'. A target a nine-year-old can state is a target they can notice themselves meeting, and it gives the arrangement a visible end rather than an indefinite middle.

process.title: Buy short and frequent, then stop
process.description: Twenty-five to thirty minutes twice a week for a defined block, with the child working for most of it. Test monthly whether the skill has become automatic under mild time pressure. When it has, stop. Continuing past that point is how a six-week intervention becomes a four-year standing arrangement.

process.title: Ask the secondary school the narrow questions
process.description: When setting happens and on what evidence, how pupils move sets, which boards and codes are used, whether Core-tier entry is used, whether separate sciences and Additional Mathematics 0606 are offered, and what the sixth-form entry grades are. Those answers predict more than any inspection band does.

whyPoints.title: The chain drawn explicitly
whyPoints.description: Primary fluency, Key Stage 3 setting, IGCSE tier and the grade ceiling are connected by a sequence of defensible decisions. Naming that chain is what justifies early work, and it is more useful than a general claim that foundations matter.

whyPoints.title: Short and frequent, as the age requires
whyPoints.description: Twenty-five to thirty minutes twice a week, with the child working for most of it. Fluency is built by repetition under mild time pressure, not by explanation, and a primary child's attention does not survive an hour of anything demanding.

whyPoints.title: A stopping rule, applied monthly
whyPoints.description: Fluency work ends when the skill is automatic, not when the term does. The monthly test is whether the child can do it fast, under mild pressure, unprompted. A block that passes that test is finished, and continuing anyway is a subscription rather than a repair.

whyPoints.title: Checkpoint feedback used properly
whyPoints.description: Strand-level feedback targets work; the overall score predicts little. Checkpoint tests are offered in March, May and October, and whether a result informs setting or only tracking is a question for the school, with very different consequences either way.

whyPoints.title: The UAE mandatory subjects respected
whyPoints.description: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies are required in Dubai private schools whatever the licensed curriculum, with separate classes by group, KHDA-approved teachers, and no substitution of content without MoE permission. Support follows the prescribed content rather than replacing it.

whyPoints.title: Delivery and the honest answer
whyPoints.description: Lessons are one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time; IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai, since home visits are an India-only service. For most primary pupils the honest recommendation is no paid tutoring at all, and that answer is given when it is the right one.

faqs.question: Why would a Victory Heights Primary School family be thinking about IGCSE at all?
faqs.answer: Because the chain between them is shorter than it looks. Primary fluency decides how much attention a Year 9 algebra lesson consumes. That shapes the set a pupil is placed in at the end of Year 9. In most Dubai schools that set informs the IGCSE tier a department proposes, and a Core-tier entry caps the grade scale whatever the pupil does on the day. Nobody decides in Year 5 that a child will be capped; it emerges from a sequence of reasonable judgements made on the evidence available at each step.

faqs.question: What are the four primary gaps that actually matter later?
faqs.answer: Number fluency, meaning arithmetic performed without conscious effort rather than merely correctly. Inferential reading, meaning saying what a text implies rather than what it states. Written structure, meaning planning a piece before writing it. And precision, meaning units written, answers labelled and the question actually answered. Each of these is the direct ancestor of a specific IGCSE assessment demand, and each is cheap to build at nine and expensive to retrofit at fifteen, because by then other subjects have inherited the weakness too.

faqs.question: My child gets the right answers but takes a long time. Is that a problem?
faqs.answer: It is the most predictive thing you can notice, and primary marking usually cannot see it. Accuracy and fluency are different: both score the mark, and only fluency survives being an incidental step inside a Year 10 algebra question. Working memory is finite, so a pupil spending it on arithmetic has less available for the method, which is where the marks are. This is why apparently careless errors cluster in long questions - the pupil was not careless, they were out of capacity.

faqs.question: When are Cambridge Checkpoint tests taken and what do they tell us?
faqs.answer: They are offered in March, May and October, and they report scaled scores with strand-level feedback rather than grades. The useful output is which parts of mathematics, English and science are weak, in a form a school and a parent can both read. They are a good targeting instrument and a poor predictive one, because they measure one performance at one point. Read the strand feedback against your child's own written work from the same term; where both agree, that is worth acting on.

faqs.question: Does a Checkpoint result affect which set my child goes into?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on the school, which is why it is worth asking directly. Some Dubai schools use Checkpoint results to inform setting for the next stage, some use them purely for internal tracking and parent reporting, and some treat them as evidence in a transfer application. A result used for setting carries forward and has consequences; a result used for tracking does not. Ask the head of year what else informs the setting decision, because the answer is usually a combination rather than one test.

faqs.question: How is tutoring a nine-year-old different from tutoring a teenager?
faqs.answer: Shorter, more frequent and far more productive. Twenty-five to thirty minutes twice a week beats an hour once a week, because fluency is built by repetition under mild time pressure rather than by explanation. The child should be working for most of the session while the tutor marks, prompts and raises the difficulty. A session where an adult explains for forty minutes and the child writes for ten has reversed the only ratio that matters at this age, and it will sell more hours while achieving less.

faqs.question: Should a tutor help with primary homework?
faqs.answer: No, and this is worth being firm about. Homework completion is outsourcing rather than tutoring, and it teaches a child that difficulty is somebody else's problem to solve. It also removes the main signal a teacher uses to see what a class has and has not understood. Paid time at primary age should go on one named skill being drilled to automatic, with the child producing the work. If a homework task reveals a gap, the gap is the thing to work on later, not the task.

faqs.question: What should we ask a secondary school before choosing one?
faqs.answer: Six narrow questions that predict more than any inspection band. When does setting happen and on what evidence. How do pupils move between sets and what triggers a review. Which boards and specification codes are used, subject by subject. Whether the school enters pupils at Core tier and in what circumstances. Whether separate sciences and Additional Mathematics 0606 are offered. And what its own sixth-form entry grades are. Schools will generally answer all six, and the answers shape the next six years.

faqs.question: Does taking Combined Science later matter when choosing a primary leaver's school?
faqs.answer: It can, because a school that does not offer separate sciences has already constrained A Level science options for its own pupils. Combined Science covers reduced content from all three sciences for one grade, which several Dubai sixth forms treat as below the entry requirement for A Level Chemistry or Physics. That is not a flaw in a school, and it is a fact worth knowing while choosing rather than discovering in Year 10. The same applies to Additional Mathematics 0606, which is the designed bridge to Higher Level mathematics.

faqs.question: What does KHDA require Dubai schools to teach in Arabic and Islamic Education?
faqs.answer: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, with the requirements to be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year and April 2026 for April-start schools. Schools must organise separate classes for Arab and non-Arab pupils in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ between them.

faqs.question: Can a tutor use their own materials for Islamic Education or Arabic?
faqs.answer: No. For the mandatory UAE subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited, so support must follow the prescribed content rather than substitute an alternative syllabus. KHDA also requires schools to ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold appropriate approval to teach those subjects, which is a concrete credential point. Any tutoring in these areas should therefore be reinforcement of what the school is required to deliver, not a parallel course.

faqs.question: Is the summer before Year 7 worth spending on?
faqs.answer: For a pupil with a genuine fluency or structure gap, it is the best-value block in the whole sequence. Six to eight short sessions aimed at times-table automaticity, fraction and decimal fluency, planning a piece of writing, and answering the question asked. It works because the receiving school's Year 7 curriculum assumes those things from the first week and does not revisit them. Availability is also loose over the summer. For a pupil who already has all four, the summer is better spent reading and being eleven.

faqs.question: Do you send tutors to Victory Heights, Motor City or Sports City addresses?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; sending a tutor to a family's address is a service offered only in India. Tutoring for Dubai families is one-to-one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time. At primary age the format has a specific advantage: short sessions twice a week are practical over video and awkward to arrange as visits, because nobody will drive for forty minutes to deliver twenty-five. The published AED 180-500 in-home band exists largely to pay for that drive.

faqs.question: Does our child actually need a tutor at this age?
faqs.answer: Probably not, and that is the honest answer for most Dubai primary families. A child who is fluent with number, reads beyond the literal, plans their writing and checks their answers needs time, books and a reasonable bedtime rather than paid sessions. Where one of those four is genuinely insecure, a short targeted block is excellent value and has a visible end. Those are different situations, and a provider who cannot tell you which one you are in before taking money should not be given the hour.

dubai/ib-igcse-tutor-for-victory-heights.closingHeading: Test fluency at home before buying anything
dubai/ib-igcse-tutor-for-victory-heights.closingBody: Give your child half a dozen fraction or times-table questions and watch the clock rather than the answers. Correct but slow is a fluency gap, and fluency is what every later stage assumes. Then ask the school for a sample of this term's written work and read any Checkpoint report for its strand feedback rather than its headline score. Where two instruments agree on one of the four gaps, a short block is worth buying. Where they do not, the likely answer is no paid work at all. A free trial lesson is one session with no card details required. Lessons are one-to-one over live video in Gulf Standard Time.

intro.heading: Start with the number, then work out what you are buying
paragraphs: A Wellington International School family in Al Sufouh who rings three tutoring providers on the same afternoon will be quoted three very different hourly figures, and usually none of the three will explain the gap. The honest explanation is that there is no single market rate in Dubai. There is a budget tier, a qualified-subject tier, a specialist exam tier and a premium tier, and the distance between the cheapest and the dearest is roughly a factor of ten. Knowing which tier your child's problem actually sits in is the whole of the decision.

Published market figures, read in October 2026, put a budget online tutor or university student at roughly AED 45 to AED 150 an hour, with EdFlik advertising from AED 45 to AED 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to AED 52. A qualified subject tutor working online sits around AED 150 to AED 300, and Unitors publishes IGCSE tuition from AED 150 and IB tuition from AED 200. A dedicated IB, IGCSE or A-Level specialist runs AED 200 to AED 450 and higher, with TutorChase quoting AED 270 and Bestimate's Dubai rate table landing at AED 200 to AED 450 plus. A named or examiner-level tutor at the premium end can reach AED 650, the figure BartyED publishes. Those are market rates from other providers, not an IB Gram price list.

The tier that fits is set by the question you are asking. A Year 9 student who has lost the thread in algebraic fractions does not need an examiner at AED 650; a confident Year 11 chasing the top band in Chemistry 0620 Paper 4 is poorly served by the cheapest hour available. Most Wellington families who contact us are somewhere in the middle: one subject is dragging, the mock result came back lower than the predicted grade, and nobody at home can diagnose whether the problem is content, exam technique or timing.

The second number that matters is the one nobody quotes: travel. An in-home visit in Dubai carries the tutor's drive time inside the fee, which is why published in-home bands run from AED 180 to AED 500 an hour against AED 150 to AED 300 online. On the Al Sufouh and Al Barsha corridor, a tutor crossing from Mirdif or Silicon Oasis at five o'clock loses most of an hour each way, and that hour is priced into the quote whether anyone names it or not. Removing the drive removes the premium and, more usefully, removes the geographic limit on who can teach your child.

So this page is built around cost. It gives the AED bands by format and by level, it converts them into monthly budgets, it shows what the travel premium actually buys, and then it deals with the three things that quietly change the number in Dubai specifically: the exam series your child is entered for, the KHDA-mandated subjects that sit alongside the British curriculum, and the Ministry of Education equivalency rules that decide which IGCSE grades count later. IB Gram delivers tuition to Dubai online, one-to-one, over live video; home visits are a service offered only in India, and no tutor is sent to a UAE address.

dubai/ib-igcse-tutor-for-wellington-inte.programmesIntro: Wellington International School runs a British curriculum, so most families arrive here with an IGCSE question. A smaller group is weighing the IB Diploma for sixth form, or has transferred in from an IB continuum school. The cost of support differs by programme, and so does the work itself.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson International GCSE
programmes.description: Two years of linear courses assessed almost entirely by terminal written papers. Cambridge splits most sciences and maths into Core and Extended tiers, which cap the achievable grade differently; Pearson Edexcel International GCSE is untiered in several subjects and offers a modular route in others. The specification code on the front of the paper, not the subject name, decides what is examinable.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai centres enter candidates for the Cambridge June and November series; the February/March series is offered to India only and is not available here. Pearson International GCSE runs May/June and November. Entry deadlines sit months ahead of the papers, so a Year 11 who wants a November resit is making that decision long before results day.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Criterion-referenced assessment across eight subject groups, marked A to D on 1-8 scales rather than against a percentage. Students coming into a British curriculum school from MYP often have strong inquiry and reflection habits and weak timed-paper stamina, because MYP rarely asks for a closed-book paper under clock pressure.
programmes.countryNote: Several Dubai schools run MYP to Year 11 and then move into the Diploma, so a transfer into Wellington's Year 10 or Year 11 means picking up two years of IGCSE specification content partway through. That transition is the most common reason an Al Sufouh family books a block of sessions rather than a weekly slot.

programmes.name: IB Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects at Higher or Standard Level plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Internal assessment carries real weight in most subjects, and the written papers reward command-term precision far more than IGCSE does. Higher Level courses add both content and a third paper in several sciences.
programmes.countryNote: The IB Diploma accounts for roughly 7 per cent of Dubai's private-school enrolment, and the emirate's 2026-27 intake adds three new IB schools among seven new openings. UAE schools sit the May session. We do not publish IB exam or results dates, because the IB's own site blocks automated checking and an unverified date on a page is worse than no date.

programmes.name: International A Level, sixth form route
programmes.description: The usual continuation for a British curriculum student who does not take the Diploma. Three or four subjects studied in depth, with AS and A2 structures varying by board. The jump from an IGCSE Extended grade 8 to an A Level A is larger than the grade labels suggest, particularly in Maths and Physics.
programmes.countryNote: For Ministry of Education equivalency on the British track, a student must show one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or better, or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade, alongside five accredited IGCSE or GCSE subjects at no less than E or grade 3. That requirement shapes sixth-form subject choice for families who intend to apply to a UAE university.

dubai/ib-igcse-tutor-for-wellington-inte.subjectsIntro: Subject scarcity is one of the clearest drivers of price in Dubai. Maths and the three sciences are widely covered and competitively priced; Business Studies, Computer Science and the second-language subjects have far fewer specialists and quote higher. These are the courses Wellington families ask for most often.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580, Pearson 4MA1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended · Higher and Foundation tier
subjects.description: Extended Paper 2 and Paper 4 carry the algebra, trigonometry and vectors that decide the top grades. Marks go missing in non-calculator fluency, in setting up a problem rather than solving it, and in method marks lost to unshown working. Tier choice is a grade ceiling decision made in Year 10.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics and Maths AA
subjects.levels: IGCSE Additional · IB HL and SL
subjects.description: The bridge subjects between IGCSE and a quantitative sixth form. Calculus notation, proof and the discipline of writing a solution someone else can follow are what separate a pass from a strong grade. Families planning engineering or economics at a UAE university usually need this route rather than Applications.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625, Pearson 4PH1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended · IB HL and SL
subjects.description: Electricity and circuits are where Extended candidates lose most marks, followed by moments and momentum. The practical and data-handling paper rewards graph discipline, unit consistency and significant figures, none of which are taught by solving more problems; they are taught by marking the student's own paper against the scheme.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620, Pearson 4CH1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended · IB HL and SL
subjects.description: Moles and stoichiometry gate everything after them, and organic chemistry is where Year 11 confidence collapses. Extended Paper 4 asks for explanation in chemical language rather than recall, so answers that are factually right and linguistically vague still score zero on the explanation marks.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610, Pearson 4BI1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended · IB HL and SL
subjects.description: A content-heavy course where marks are lost to imprecise terminology more than to misunderstanding. Transport in plants, homeostasis and genetics crosses need exact wording. Extended candidates also need the skill of reading how many marks a question carries and writing exactly that many points.

subjects.name: English Language and Literature
subjects.levels: First Language · Second Language · IB Language A
subjects.description: The directed-writing and composition tasks are scored on audience, register and structure, not vocabulary display. For second-language candidates the summary question is the highest-yield single task on the paper, because its mark scheme is mechanical once a student knows how it is applied.

subjects.name: Business Studies and Economics
subjects.description: Application marks depend on using the case study in front of the student rather than a memorised example, and evaluation marks depend on a judgement with a reason attached. One of the thinner subject pools in Dubai, which is why these sessions sit at the higher end of market bands.

subjects.name: Computer Science and ICT
subjects.description: Pseudocode, trace tables and the theory paper's exact definitions carry the marks. Students who code fluently in Python often underperform because the paper wants the board's notation and the board's definitions, which is a learnable gap and usually a short block of work rather than a year of lessons.

subjects.name: Arabic as a second language
subjects.description: Required in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed curriculum, and organised in separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students under KHDA's rules. Non-Arab students are taught in the school's licensed-curriculum language of instruction, and schools must ensure their Arabic teachers hold the appropriate approval from KHDA.

subjects.name: Geography and History
subjects.description: Case-study recall plus source handling. The highest-yield work is almost always the extended-response question, where structure and a sustained argument earn the level-descriptor marks that short factual answers cannot reach however accurate they are.

sections.heading: What IGCSE and IB tuition actually costs in Dubai, in AED
paragraphs: An hour of qualified online subject tuition in Dubai sits in a market band of roughly AED 150 to AED 300, read in October 2026 from providers who publish their rates. Below that band is a budget tier of AED 45 to AED 150, mostly university students and non-specialist generalists. Above it is a specialist tier of AED 200 to AED 450 and a premium named tier that reaches AED 650. Those four bands are the whole market, and every quote a Dubai family receives lands in one of them.

The table below sets out what each tier is and who publishes a figure in it. Every number belongs to the provider named beside it; none of them is an IB Gram price. We publish them because three of the six best-ranking tutoring pages for Dubai searches give no price at all, and two of the three that do quote in US dollars, a currency no family here transacts in. A parent cannot judge value against silence.

What the bands do not show is the unit. Some providers quote per hour, some per 90-minute lesson, and some only per monthly package, so a figure that looks cheap can be dearer once converted. Ask for the price per 60 minutes of teaching, ask whether marking between sessions is inside or outside that figure, and ask whether the rate changes closer to a series. Those three questions make two quotes comparable, and most providers will not volunteer any of the three answers.
bullets: Always convert a quote to a price per 60 minutes of teaching before comparing
Ask whether marking between sessions is included or billed separately

sections.heading: The five things that change the number in this emirate
paragraphs: Subject scarcity moves a Dubai quote more than anything else. Maths and the three separate sciences have the deepest pool of tutors in the emirate, so they price competitively. Business Studies, Computer Science, Economics, Psychology and the second-language subjects have far fewer specialists available on a Tuesday at 4pm, and a thin pool prices at the top of the band regardless of how straightforward the content is.

Level comes second. Cambridge Extended and IB Higher Level work costs more per hour than Core or Standard Level, because fewer tutors can teach the last two grade bands with authority. The third driver is proximity to a series: demand for exam-subject hours climbs steeply through the mock season and the weeks before the papers, and a tutor whose diary is full in that window has no reason to discount it. Booking a term ahead is the only reliable way to hold a rate through that period.

The fourth is session structure, which is where families overpay without noticing. A 45-minute session at a low hourly rate can cost more per unit of teaching than a 90-minute block at a higher one, because the first ten minutes of any session are spent re-establishing where the student got to. The fifth is delivery format, and it is the largest single lever available: a Dubai in-home visit carries travel inside the fee, and the published in-home bands sit AED 30 to AED 200 an hour above the online equivalent for identical teaching.

sections.heading: Monthly budgets rather than hourly rates
paragraphs: Families do not plan in hours, they plan in months, and a quote per hour hides the number that matters. Bestimate's Dubai estimates for a weekly one-hour session land at AED 240 to AED 600 a month at the budget end, AED 600 to AED 1,200 in the middle, and AED 1,000 to AED 2,000 and above for specialist support in an exam year. Monthly packages advertised elsewhere in the market include AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home visits.

The spread between one session a week and two is not double in practice, because the second session usually runs at the same rate but produces more marked work per month, which is where the useful gain sits. A Year 11 Chemistry student doing one hour a week completes roughly three past-paper questions under timed conditions in a month. The same student at two hours a week completes a full paper and a review of it, which is a materially different piece of evidence to take to a parents' evening.

Set the budget against the school year rather than the calendar. A British curriculum year in Dubai has three intense stretches: the autumn assessment window, the mock season in the new year, and the run to the June series. Most families are better served by a modest weekly commitment across the year plus a defined block in one of those stretches, rather than a heavy commitment started in panic eight weeks before a paper.

sections.heading: What the travel premium buys, and what it does not
paragraphs: The case for an in-home tutor is real and worth stating properly. A tutor in the room can see a student's page without being shown it, can intervene on handwriting and working out as it happens, and holds a younger child's attention more easily than a screen does. For a Year 3 reader or a child who genuinely cannot settle to a video call, that is a strong argument and parents should weigh it.

What the premium does not buy is a wider choice of teacher. A Wellington family that insists on a tutor who drives to Al Sufouh is choosing from the people willing to make that drive at 4pm, which is a small subset of the emirate's specialists. The same family online chooses from every tutor available at that hour, which is how a Chemistry 0620 Extended specialist becomes available instead of a general science graduate who lives nearby. On a thin subject the difference is not marginal; it is the difference between a specialist and whoever is left.

IB Gram does not offer in-home visits anywhere in the UAE. Home visits are an India-only service, and no tutor is sent to a Dubai address. Our tuition for Dubai runs online, one-to-one, over live video, with a shared screen, a document camera or tablet for working, and the student's own marked scripts on screen. That position is published on every UAE page on this site, which is why the comparison below sets out the trade honestly rather than pretending the in-home option has no merits.

sections.heading: Where Years 10 and 11 marks actually go at a British curriculum school
paragraphs: Cost is easier to judge once you know what the money has to fix. At IGCSE the losses are predictable and they are rarely about intelligence. In Mathematics 0580 Extended, method marks disappear into unshown working and into problems the student can solve but cannot set up. In Physics 0625, electricity and circuits account for more lost marks than any other topic, and the practical paper punishes graph axes, units and significant figures rather than physics.

Chemistry 0620 has two choke points. Moles and stoichiometry gate everything that follows, so a student who never became fluent there loses marks in topics that look unrelated. Organic chemistry then arrives in Year 11 and asks for mechanism and language precision at the point when revision pressure is highest. Biology 0610 loses marks almost entirely to vocabulary: an answer that describes the right process in everyday words scores nothing against a mark scheme that names the term.

English is the subject where a single task carries the most recoverable marks. For second-language candidates the summary question has a mechanical mark scheme, and a student who learns how it is applied can gain several marks in one session. For first-language candidates the directed-writing task is scored on register and structure, which is coachable in a way that vocabulary is not. Knowing which of these your child's paper actually shows is what a first diagnostic session is for, and it is also what decides whether you need four sessions or forty.

sections.heading: The Cambridge and Pearson calendar, counted backwards
paragraphs: Almost every tutoring page for Dubai ignores the exam calendar entirely, which is strange, because the calendar is what determines when tuition is worth buying. Cambridge International runs IGCSE and O Level exams in a June series and a November series. The February/March series exists but is offered to India only, so no Dubai candidate sits it; a page that tells a UAE parent otherwise is giving them a date they may act on. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs May/June and November.

Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones, and the board states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, adding that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. That is a sentence worth reading twice before trusting a timetable found on a forum. Ask the school's exams officer which zone it sits in, and work from the school's own copy.

Recent dates give a sense of the rhythm without pretending to predict the next ones. The Pearson International GCSE November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results reached centres on 19 August 2026 and students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Final entries close months before the first paper, which is why a resit decision is effectively made before results arrive. Always work from the live official timetable rather than a restated date.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies alongside the British curriculum
paragraphs: Every Dubai private school teaches Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies regardless of which international curriculum it is licensed for. This is a federal requirement, implemented through KHDA in Dubai, and the authority's guidelines required implementation by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, with April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April. For a Wellington family this means the timetable carries subjects that do not appear on any Cambridge specification and still produce a report grade.

KHDA's rules are specific about organisation. For Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, schools must organise separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students, and combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because the curriculum expectations and language of instruction differ. Standard Arabic is the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arab students and for Arabic as a first language, while non-Arab students are taught Islamic Education and Moral, Social and Cultural studies in the school's licensed-curriculum language.

Instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided the weekly total is met, and the guidance advises that any mandatory-subject lesson runs at least 25 minutes. Schools must also ensure that teachers of Arabic and Islamic Education hold the appropriate approval from KHDA. For these subjects the use of different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is strictly prohibited, so tutoring here means working with the school's own material and the Ministry's curriculum, not substituting something else.

sections.heading: What a tutor may and may not touch on coursework
paragraphs: Dubai's tutoring market contains providers who sell completed Internal Assessments. One of them advertises a finished IA at AED 3,750. Buying that is academic malpractice under IB rules, the consequence falls on the student rather than the seller, and the risk is loss of the Diploma. A page about the cost of tutoring has an obligation to say so plainly, because the price difference between real support and a purchased document is the reason some families are tempted.

The honest boundary is simple. A tutor teaches the assessment criteria, explains what the criterion letters reward and what the mark allocations mean, reads a draft the student has written and says where it falls short, and coaches the process of choosing a question, planning data collection and structuring an argument. A tutor never writes a sentence of the submitted work, never edits a draft into its final state, and never supplies a topic, a data set or a conclusion for the student to adopt.

The same line applies to IGCSE coursework components, to the Extended Essay and to Theory of Knowledge. It also applies to past papers and mark schemes: these are the boards' copyright material, so a tutor references them and links the official source rather than distributing copies of the documents. If a provider's offer sounds like it removes the student's work rather than improving it, that is not a cheaper service, it is a different and far more expensive product bought under a misleading label.

For families weighing the cost, the practical consequence is that coursework support is billed as teaching hours like anything else. An IB Internal Assessment block is usually three to five sessions spread across the drafting window rather than a single long sitting, because the student needs time to write between them. Scoping that block in writing before the first session keeps the total predictable and stops an open-ended arrangement running for a term.
bullets: Teaching the criteria and mark allocations: yes
Reading and giving feedback on the student's own draft: yes
Writing, rewriting or completing any submitted text: never
Supplying a topic, data set or finished conclusion: never

sections.heading: Equivalency, permits and the two checks worth making before you pay
paragraphs: Two regulatory facts change decisions and almost no competing page mentions either. The first is Ministry of Education equivalency, which decides whether a school-leaving certificate is accepted in the UAE. On the British track a student must pass five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade no lower than E or grade 3, and Arabic and Islamic education are not included among those five. Alongside that, one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or better, or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade, is required. A ranking competitor states that UAE candidates must take six IGCSE subjects; the sourced figure is five.

On the American track, English proficiency is shown by a score of 5 in the IELTS academic test, 61 in the TOEFL iBT, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT, and mathematics requires at least 450 in the SAT Math test. No IB points threshold is published here, because we have not read one on the Ministry's own site, and an unverified threshold is exactly the kind of number a family would plan around to their cost. Verify your own case with the Ministry, which runs the process; IB Gram neither performs nor guarantees equivalency, and tutoring is not a requirement for it.

The second check is the tutor's permit. Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated: the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation issues a private tuition work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. It is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, government and private-sector employees, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18 and university students. Individuals tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws; no fine schedule is published, so no amount should be quoted to you. Abu Dhabi's professional-ethics rules additionally bar school staff from paid tutoring of students at their own school, and the permit's code of conduct carries a similar restriction, so a request for your child's own class teacher privately is one to decline.

Plus one A Level at E, or two AS Levels at E, on the British track
The MoHRE private tuition permit is free and valid for two years
No official fine schedule is published, so treat any quoted amount with suspicion

faqs.question: How much does an IGCSE tutor cost for a Wellington International School family in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Market rates read in October 2026 put a qualified online subject tutor at roughly AED 150 to AED 300 an hour, with Unitors publishing IGCSE tuition from AED 150. A budget or university-student tutor runs AED 45 to AED 150, and a dedicated IGCSE specialist sits at AED 200 to AED 450 and above, with TutorChase quoting AED 270. Those are other providers' published figures, not an IB Gram price list. Which band fits depends on the subject, the tier and how close the series is. Ask for the price per 60 minutes of teaching so quotes become comparable.

faqs.question: Why do two tutoring quotes for the same Year 11 subject differ by three times?
faqs.answer: Because they are from different tiers of the same market, and almost nobody labels the tier. A budget tutor supervises homework and revises content. A subject specialist knows the paper structure, the mark scheme wording and the two or three places that particular paper loses marks. The hourly rates reflect that, and so does the pool size: Maths has many available tutors in Dubai and prices competitively, while Economics or Computer Science has few and prices at the top. Session length, included marking and proximity to a series account for most of the rest of the gap.

faqs.question: Is it cheaper to book an in-home tutor or online tuition in Al Sufouh?
faqs.answer: Online is cheaper, and the reason is travel rather than quality. Published in-home bands in Dubai run from AED 180 to AED 500 an hour because the tutor's drive time is inside the fee; equivalent online teaching sits at AED 150 to AED 300. A tutor crossing the city at five in the afternoon can lose most of an hour each way, and that cost appears in the quote whether anyone itemises it or not. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE at all. Lessons for Dubai run online, one-to-one, over live video.

faqs.question: What does a month of tuition cost rather than an hour?
faqs.answer: Bestimate's Dubai estimates for a weekly one-hour session land at AED 240 to AED 600 a month at the budget end, AED 600 to AED 1,200 in the middle and AED 1,000 to AED 2,000 or more for specialist support in an exam year. Monthly packages advertised in the market include AED 799 for eight online sessions. Doubling to two sessions a week roughly doubles the figure, but it buys a full timed paper plus a marking review each month rather than a few individual questions, which is the more useful unit to plan against.

faqs.question: Which IGCSE specification codes should I check before booking a tutor?
faqs.answer: Ask the school which board and code each subject sits on, then quote it when you book. Cambridge uses 0580 for Mathematics, 0620 for Chemistry, 0625 for Physics and 0610 for Biology; Pearson Edexcel International GCSE uses 4MA1, 4CH1, 4PH1 and 4BI1. The code decides what is examinable and how the papers are structured, and Core versus Extended also sets a grade ceiling. A tutor who teaches the right subject on the wrong specification will still teach well and still waste some of your money.

faqs.question: Can a Wellington student sit the Cambridge February or March series?
faqs.answer: No. Cambridge offers the February/March series to India only. Candidates in the UAE sit the June series and the November series, and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs May/June and November. This matters because some tutoring pages aimed at Gulf parents restate Indian dates, and a family planning around a February window would miss an entry deadline. Cambridge also allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and states that it cannot accept responsibility for a candidate who misses an exam after using the wrong zone timetable, so always work from the school's own copy.

faqs.question: Will the hourly rate we agree in September still hold in the weeks before the June papers?
faqs.answer: In practice yes, because demand for exam-subject hours climbs through the mock season and the weeks before the papers, and a tutor whose diary fills has no reason to discount. The effect is strongest in the scarcer subjects and at Extended or Higher Level. Two things protect against it: book a term ahead rather than in the panic window, and ask directly whether the quoted rate holds through the series. A provider that will not answer that question in writing is telling you something useful about what happens in March.

faqs.question: What should I send when asking for a tutoring quote?
faqs.answer: Send the subject with its specification code, the year group, the paper numbers your child will sit, the board, and a recent marked script or mock result. The script is the most valuable item, because it turns a vague request into a diagnosable problem and lets a tutor say honestly whether this is a four-session fix or a year of work. Add the days and times that are realistically free after the school run, and say whether another sibling needs a slot on the same evening.

faqs.question: Which permit should I ask a Dubai tutor to confirm before paying for a block of lessons?
faqs.answer: Yes. Private tutoring in the UAE requires a private tuition work permit from the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023. The permit is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, students aged 15 to 18 and university students. Those tutoring without one are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws. No official fine schedule is published, so treat any specific amount you see quoted with care and apply through the MoHRE channel.

faqs.question: Can my child's own Wellington teacher tutor them privately for a fee?
faqs.answer: That is an arrangement to avoid. The MoHRE private tuition permit carries a code of conduct that bars serving students affiliated with the tutor's own school, and Abu Dhabi's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff prohibit paid private tutoring of students enrolled at the teacher's own school. Beyond the rules, it puts a teacher in the position of assessing work they were paid to help produce. An independent specialist who does not grade your child's reports is a cleaner arrangement for everyone, including the teacher.

faqs.question: How many IGCSE grades does the Ministry of Education count for equivalency?
faqs.answer: Five. On the British track a student must pass five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade no lower than E or grade 3, and Arabic and Islamic education are not counted among those five. Alongside that, one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or better, or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade, is required. One ranking competitor publishes six as the subject count. Verify your own case with the Ministry directly, since it runs the process and we neither perform nor guarantee it.

faqs.question: Will a tutor help my child write the Chemistry Internal Assessment?
faqs.answer: No, and any provider offering that is selling something that puts the Diploma at risk. A tutor teaches what each criterion letter rewards and how the marks are allocated, discusses a research question the student has proposed, reads a draft the student has written and says where it falls short against the criteria. The student writes every word that is submitted. One Dubai operator advertises completed Internal Assessments at AED 3,750; that is malpractice under IB rules and the consequence lands on the student rather than the seller.

faqs.question: Does online tuition work for a Year 10 student who says they focus better in person?
faqs.answer: Often yes, once the setup is right, and the honest answer is that it depends on the child rather than the format. What makes it work is a quiet room, headphones, a second surface for working such as a tablet or a document camera, and the student's own marked scripts shared on screen rather than described. What makes it fail is a laptop at the kitchen table with a sibling nearby. The free trial exists to test this cheaply: one real session shows whether the format fits before any money moves.

faqs.question: What happens if there is no specialist free for a scarce subject at our preferred time?
faqs.answer: We say so instead of substituting a generalist. Maths and the sciences are covered widely at most hours. Computer Science, Economics, Psychology and some second-language subjects have thinner coverage, and the 4pm to 6pm window in Dubai is the busiest. Usually the answer is a different slot on the same week, sometimes a weekend morning, and occasionally a wait of a week or two for the right teacher. A subject specialist at an inconvenient hour beats a convenient hour with someone who does not know the paper.

faqs.question: Do Arabic and Islamic Education need separate tutoring alongside the British curriculum?
faqs.answer: They often do, because they sit outside the Cambridge specifications and still carry report grades. Dubai private schools teach Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies whatever international curriculum they are licensed for, and KHDA requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students, with Standard Arabic as the language of instruction for Arabic as a first language and for Islamic Education for Arab students. Instructional time runs in 40-minute lesson units. Support here has to work from the school's own material, since substituting content needs prior Ministry permission.

dubai/ib-igcse-tutor-near-me.tutorsIntro: Judge the tutors below on the same thing a parents' evening should be judged on: what they can show you. Each profile names the specifications taught and the levels marked, and the free first lesson exists so the first evidence you see is your own child's work.

intro.heading: Near me is a logistics question. The grade is an evidence question.
paragraphs: A Dubai parent types tutor near me for sound reasons. The evening is short, the roads are full between five and seven, and a plan that needs somebody to cross the emirate twice a week will fail by the third week whatever anybody promises. Proximity is a real constraint and this page is not going to pretend it is irrational. It will, though, separate it from the thing families usually confuse it with, which is quality.

Here is the separation. Proximity determines whether a session happens at all in the in-home model, and nothing else. It does not determine whether the tutor has taught your child's specification, whether they mark to the board's scheme, whether anything is written down between sessions, or whether the errors identified in September have closed by December. Those four things determine the grade, and none of them has an address. Over video, proximity stops being a constraint at all, which is what makes the other four the only questions left.

So the useful reframe is this: instead of asking who is near me, ask what should exist in my hands after four weeks, and then buy from whoever can produce it. The answer is specific. An annotated script with marks awarded and withheld at named points. A timed attempt with the minutes recorded per question, not just the total. A short written note after each session saying what the hour changed. And by week four, three named causes of mark loss, ranked, each labelled content, method or timing.

That file is also the thing that makes the school take you seriously. A Dubai Year 11 parent who arrives at a consultation evening saying their child is struggling gets sympathy. A parent who arrives saying their daughter is losing method marks on structured algebra questions, here are four scripts showing it, and we are drilling it weekly, gets a different conversation and sometimes a different set. In a class of twenty-five, the specific request is the one that gets acted on. That is not a trick and it is not adversarial. A head of department with a hundred and fifty students is making decisions on the information in front of them, and a dated folder of scripts is simply better information than a worried sentence at the end of a long evening. The file is there to inform the school, never to argue with it.

Everything below is built around that file: what proximity does and does not buy, a twelve-week evidence ledger, how to read a marked script the way an examiner reads it, how to tell real grade movement from noise, how drafts of an internal assessment work as evidence without crossing the academic-honesty line, what a weekly note should contain, and the questions that expose a tutor who has no evidence to show. Lessons here run one to one over live video; IB Gram does not provide home visits in the UAE, where home visiting is a service we offer only in India.

subjects.levels: Core and Extended, Foundation and Higher

subjects.description: Look at the six-mark extended responses specifically. Evidence of progress is a causal chain appearing where three unlinked statements used to be, and it is visible to a parent without any physics knowledge at all.

subjects.name: English Language
subjects.description: Evidence here is annotated text, not a grade. Look for the student naming a method and commenting on its effect, and for shorter embedded quotations replacing long retold extracts across successive pieces.

subjects.name: English Literature
subjects.description: Compare two essays six weeks apart and count the paragraphs that start with a technique rather than with a plot event. That single count tracks the grade more faithfully than any mark out of thirty.

subjects.name: Economics and Business
subjects.levels: IGCSE and DP SL or HL
subjects.description: Diagrams make excellent evidence because they are either correct, labelled and shifted or they are not. Keep the marked diagram sheets; the improvement curve in these subjects is usually steep and visible within a fortnight.

subjects.description: Timed paper data matters more here than anywhere, because Higher Level students frequently know enough for a 6 and produce a 4 on timing alone. Minutes per question is the column to watch.

subjects.name: Internal assessment and coursework
subjects.description: Evidence is the draft history and the feedback trail: criteria referenced, questions asked, changes made by the student. The work stays theirs throughout, and a trail that shows their own decisions is both better evidence and the only legitimate kind.

sections.heading: What proximity actually buys in Dubai
paragraphs: Take the near-me question seriously enough to answer it properly. The table lists what families are really trying to secure when they search that phrase, says whether being close helps with each, and names what actually determines it instead. Three of the seven rows are genuinely improved by proximity. The other four are not, and two of them are made worse by it, because a short list of nearby tutors is a short list.

The rows worth reading twice are the subject-match ones. For mainstream Year 10 mathematics or Year 11 biology, enough people teach those in this emirate that proximity costs you almost nothing. The arithmetic changes at the edges: further pure mathematics, Higher Level chemistry, an unfamiliar Pearson code, Arabic first language for a student who moved streams, or diploma economics with a key-concept evaluation problem. Those are exactly the cases exam-year families need, and they are where a twenty-minute radius leaves you choosing from almost nobody.

There is also a cost to getting this wrong that does not show up until January. A family hires the best nearby option in September, the match holds for a term while the work is general, and then the work gets specific and the tutor cannot follow it. Changing tutor mid-year costs four to six weeks of rebuilding in the most expensive term of the year, which is why the evidence questions in this page's later sections are worth asking in September rather than in February.

None of that argues against convenience. It argues for ordering the questions correctly: specification and level first, evidence second, hour of the evening third, and geography only where it still matters after those three. Over video the fourth question disappears entirely, which is the honest reason this site exists rather than a claim that screens are inherently better than rooms.

sections.heading: The twelve-week evidence ledger
paragraphs: Below is what should exist, and when, if tutoring is working. It is deliberately a ledger rather than a promise: each row names an artefact, how to read it and the red flag that tells you something is wrong. Nothing in it requires you to understand the subject, which is the point. A parent who cannot do quadratics can still see whether the number of marks lost to missing working fell between September and November.

Week four is the decision point and it should be treated as one. By then you either have three named, ranked causes of mark loss from your child's own work, or you have an impression that things are going well. The first is a product. The second is a feeling, and it is the single most common reason Dubai families spend a full term discovering that the tutoring was pleasant and ineffective. If week four produces nothing nameable, change the tutor or the shape rather than adding hours.

Week twelve is where you should see closure rather than activity. The same three errors, tracked across dated scripts, should be measurably less expensive. Not absent, because habits regress under pressure, but cheaper. If the errors are the same size in December as in September while the sessions continued weekly, the diagnosis was wrong or the work between sessions was not happening, and both of those are fixable conversations rather than reasons to abandon the plan.

Keep every artefact in one folder, dated. It takes no effort and it does three jobs: it makes the four-week and twelve-week tests possible, it hands a replacement tutor a diagnosis on day one if the first one becomes unavailable, and it is the document that makes a Dubai school conversation specific rather than general.

sections.heading: Reading a marked script the way an examiner does
paragraphs: Most parents look at the number in the corner. The number is the least informative thing on the page. What matters is the distribution: where in the paper the marks were lost, whether they were lost to not knowing or to not writing, and whether the last two questions are blank because time ran out or because they were skipped on sight.

Four quick checks need no subject knowledge. First, count blank spaces and incomplete final questions: that is a timing problem, not a knowledge problem. Second, look for correct answers with no working in subjects where method is credited: those are given-away marks and the cheapest to recover. Third, read the long-answer questions and see whether sentences connect to each other or merely sit next to each other. Fourth, check whether the same topic appears in the lost column across several papers.

Then look at the annotation itself, because its quality tells you about the tutor rather than the student. Credible marking quotes the scheme's own phrasing, says what would have earned the mark, and distinguishes between a mark not available and a mark available and missed. Weak marking is a tick, a cross and a score out of sixty. If what arrives is the second kind, you are paying for attendance, and that is as true of a visiting tutor in Dubai as of a video session.

One caution about marks and grades. Grade boundaries move between series, so a mark of 62 is not a fixed grade and no honest tutor will convert one for you with confidence. What a mark does tell you reliably is direction: 62 after 48 on comparable papers is real movement. Treat boundary conversions as estimates and insist that progress is reported in marks and errors rather than in predicted letters.
bullets: Blanks and unfinished final questions mean timing, not knowledge

sections.heading: Grade movement: signal against noise
paragraphs: Progress claims in this market are mostly noise, and it is worth knowing how to tell. A higher score on an easier paper is not progress. A better mock after a mock season where the whole cohort improved is partly the cohort. A two-grade jump in three weeks is almost always a difficulty difference between papers, or a topic the student happened to have revised. None of that means tutoring is failing; it means the measurement was weak.

Real signal looks different and it is slower. The cost of a named error falls across dated scripts on comparable papers. Timing data improves: fewer minutes on low-mark questions, fewer blanks at the end. A student starts annotating the question before answering it. In essay subjects, paragraphs begin with a method rather than a plot event. Those are structural changes and they persist, which is exactly why they are worth more than a single flattering score.

The table separates the two. Use it when a provider reports progress, and use it on yourself when a mock result arrives and feels like either a triumph or a disaster. Dubai mock seasons generate a great deal of unnecessary panic in November, most of which is a difficulty effect, and a great deal of unwarranted relief in February for the same reason.

One timescale worth internalising, because it prevents most mid-term crises of faith: technique habits move in two or three sessions, structural writing changes in four to six weeks, and content gaps take a term, sometimes two if a year was genuinely lost. A plan judged on the wrong timescale gets abandoned a fortnight before it would have worked.
