sections.heading: The university question, and how to check it properly
paragraphs: Mathematics-heavy degree routes commonly specify Analysis and Approaches, and some specify it at Higher Level. The pattern across engineering, mathematics, physics, computer science and parts of economics is that Analysis and Approaches is the expected course, with Applications and Interpretation accepted in fewer places and sometimes only at Higher Level. That is a general pattern and not a rule, which is exactly why it must be checked case by case.

No named institution's requirement appears on this page. Requirements differ between institutions, between campuses of the same institution, between intakes, and sometimes between routes within one department. A figure published on a tutoring site goes stale without anyone noticing, and a family that plans two years around it has no recourse. The reliable method is to read the programme's own published entry requirements for the intake in question, and to keep a copy.

The practical discipline is to check the fallbacks as well as the first choice. A course choice that satisfies a student's preferred route and quietly eliminates the insurance route is the expensive version of this decision, and it is common because families research the aspiration rather than the safety net. Check three or four routes, including one in the UAE and one abroad if both are in play.

sections.heading: Switching course, and the clock nobody mentions
paragraphs: Schools set their own deadlines for changing mathematics course or level, generally within the first Diploma year, and those deadlines pass quietly. The student who is struggling in the first term and waits for the end-of-year internal examinations has usually waited past the point where the school can still move them, which converts a solvable placement problem into a two-year one.

A switch between courses is not a small administrative act. The content diverges, so a student moving from Applications and Interpretation to Analysis and Approaches part way through has algebra and calculus to acquire that the class has already covered, and a student moving the other way has statistics to acquire. Either way there is a catch-up block, and it should be priced and planned rather than assumed.

The decision should rest on three things in order. Whether any university route names a course, read from the written requirement. Whether the school's deadline has passed. And what a marked diagnostic task actually shows about the student's engagement with proof against their engagement with data. That third item is the one families skip, and it is the only one that measures fit rather than grade.

Where a switch is not possible, the plan changes rather than ending. A student stuck in Analysis and Approaches with no appetite for proof can still be funded effectively by concentrating on method writing and non-calculator fluency, which are the recoverable marks. A student in Applications and Interpretation who needs Analysis and Approaches for a route should be looking at the route's alternatives, including foundation entry, rather than at more tutoring.

sections.heading: The exploration: five criteria, twenty marks, named
paragraphs: Both courses carry the mathematical exploration, an internally assessed piece of the student's own mathematical writing. It is marked against five criteria lettered A to E, totalling twenty marks, and the allocation is uneven in a way that changes how the work should be done. Nobody in the competitor set for these searches names a single criterion, which is strange, because this is the one part of the grade a student can work on calmly with time to revise.

The practical consequence of the mark distribution is that the mathematics itself carries the largest single allocation, so an exploration built on a topic too simple to allow sophisticated work caps its own mark regardless of how well it is written. Equally, a technically ambitious exploration with no personal engagement and no reflection throws away a meaningful share of the available marks. Both failures are extremely common and both are preventable at the topic-choice stage.

The length guidance, recommended at roughly twelve to twenty pages, is the other thing students get wrong in both directions. A six-page exploration cannot demonstrate the depth criterion E rewards; a thirty-page one buries the argument and loses communication marks. Your school will confirm the current guidance and its own deadlines, and those deadlines are the operative ones.

A tutor's role here is bounded and worth stating. A tutor can discuss whether a topic allows the level of mathematics the criteria expect, explain what a criterion descriptor actually asks for, question whether a piece of reasoning holds, and comment on a draft naming the criterion and the band. A tutor cannot write, rewrite or produce any part of it, and a service offering a finished exploration is selling a malpractice risk that lands on the student.

sections.heading: What the two courses cost to support in Dubai
paragraphs: Published rates in this city do not distinguish between the two mathematics courses, and the market behaves as though they do. The general band for a qualified online subject tutor is AED 150 to 300 an hour, with Unitors publishing IB from AED 200. Specialist IB work sits at AED 200 to 450 and above in Bestimate's 2026 Dubai rate table, TutorChase quotes AED 270, and BartyED's premium named tier reaches AED 650. Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level is quoted towards the upper half of that range, for a simple reason: fewer people can teach it.

Applications and Interpretation at Standard Level sits comfortably in the general band, and that is worth knowing because families frequently pay a specialist rate they do not need. A Standard Level Applications and Interpretation student whose losses are interpretation and statistical writing is well served by a competent subject tutor and gains nothing from a calculus specialist's premium.

The component view changes the arithmetic further. The highest-return purchases in this subject are narrow: four sessions on non-calculator technique for an Analysis and Approaches candidate, four on the Higher Level third paper, or four on the exploration against criteria A to E. At published bands those blocks are roughly AED 800 to 1,800 each, which is a fraction of a term and often produces more measurable movement.

sections.heading: Choosing from evidence rather than from reputation
paragraphs: The reliable way to choose between these courses takes about ninety minutes and costs almost nothing. Put two items in front of the student. The first is an algebraic proof question of modest difficulty: show that an identity holds, or prove a result about consecutive integers. The second is a modelling question with real data: fit something to a small dataset, say what it predicts, and state one reason the prediction might be wrong.

Then watch, rather than mark. The signal is not which one the student gets right; it is which one they stay with when it becomes uncomfortable, and which one they abandon. Students who persist with the proof and find the data commentary tedious belong in Analysis and Approaches. Students who enjoy arguing about what the data means and resent the proof's formality belong in Applications and Interpretation. This is a better predictor than an IGCSE grade, which rewards neither behaviour distinctively.

The secondary signal is the writing. Applications and Interpretation requires a student to write about mathematics continually, in the papers and in the exploration, and a student who writes reluctantly will find that a persistent tax. Analysis and Approaches requires sustained symbolic manipulation without a device, and a student who is careless with algebra will find that a persistent tax. Both taxes are payable; the question is which one the student can pay for two years.

Record the result in writing and take it to the school. A marked script with an observation about engagement is the kind of evidence a coordinator can act on, and it is considerably more useful than a parental impression or a classroom rumour about which course is easier. Where the school's placement differs from what the script suggests, the conversation is at least about the same evidence.

sections.heading: Buying this honestly
paragraphs: Four questions make a mathematics quote comparable. Which of the two courses and which level does the tutor actually teach. Have they marked the Higher Level third paper against the published scheme. Is setting and marking work between sessions included. And how many sessions, ending when. A provider who answers all four in writing is quoting a service; one who answers mathematics, IB, flexible is quoting a subscription.

Two things are worth refusing. A quote that treats both courses as interchangeable, because the specialism is precisely what is being bought at Analysis and Approaches Higher Level and precisely what is not needed at Applications and Interpretation Standard Level. And any offer to write or complete an exploration, which transfers the entire risk to your child while the provider keeps the fee.

One thing is worth insisting on: that the first session produces a marked artefact rather than a conversation. In mathematics the marks are in the method, and a script with the working visible tells a tutor and a parent more in one hour than a term of reassurance. It is also the only evidence that a school will weigh in a placement or level discussion.

Every AED figure on this page belongs to the provider or source that published it, including Unitors, TutorChase, Bestimate and BartyED, and none is an IB Gram price. Our rate is quoted after the free trial lesson, with the course, level, session length and marking inclusion stated. No university requirement is reproduced here, no success rate or average grade appears, and no tutor can promise a grade in either course.

faqs.question: What is the actual difference between IB Maths AA and AI?
faqs.answer: Analysis and Approaches builds from algebraic technique, functions and calculus, with proof as a running theme and proof by induction at Higher Level. Applications and Interpretation builds from modelling, statistics and the interpretation of real data. They share a common core and then diverge in depth, so one goes much further in calculus and the other much further in statistics. Neither is simply the harder version of the other, and a student can be genuinely strong in one and uncomfortable in the other for reasons of temperament rather than ability.

faqs.question: Which course allows a calculator in every paper?
faqs.answer: Applications and Interpretation permits technology across its papers. Analysis and Approaches sits Paper 1 without technology and Paper 2 with it, and that single rule has the biggest practical effect on how a student must revise. An Analysis and Approaches candidate who always works with a calculator to hand will not have built the surd, logarithm, exact trigonometry and algebraic fraction fluency that Paper 1 assumes. The remedy is a weekly sheet of non-calculator work, marked, with the working written out in full.

faqs.question: Everyone at the school gates says one course is softer. Is that true?
faqs.answer: It is a different course with a different failure mode, which is why the question misleads. Applications and Interpretation asks students to write about mathematics continually: what a result means in context, what a model assumes, where it stops being valid. A student who computes fluently and writes reluctantly finds that a persistent tax. Analysis and Approaches asks for sustained symbolic manipulation without a device. Both taxes are real; the question is which one your child can pay across two years without resenting it.

faqs.question: Which maths course do engineering and medicine routes expect?
faqs.answer: The common pattern is that engineering, physics, mathematics and computer science routes expect Analysis and Approaches, often at Higher Level, because calculus and algebraic technique are assumed from the first year of the degree. Medicine routes are usually constrained by chemistry and biology rather than by mathematics. Those are patterns, not rules. Requirements differ by institution, campus, intake and route, so read the programme's own published requirement for the intake in question and keep a copy, including for the fallback choices.

faqs.question: What is the mathematical exploration and how is it marked?
faqs.answer: It is the internally assessed component in both courses: an independent piece of the student's own mathematical writing. It is marked against five criteria lettered A to E for twenty marks in total, covering presentation, mathematical communication, personal engagement, reflection, and use of mathematics. The allocation is uneven, with the mathematics itself carrying the largest single share, which is why a topic too simple to allow sophisticated work caps its own mark however well written it is. Read the criteria before choosing a topic rather than afterwards.

faqs.question: How long should the exploration be, and does length matter?
faqs.answer: The recommended range is roughly twelve to twenty pages, and students get it wrong in both directions. A very short exploration cannot demonstrate the depth that the use-of-mathematics criterion rewards. A very long one buries its own argument and loses communication marks for structure and focus. Your school confirms the current guidance and sets the internal deadline, which is the date that actually binds. Allocate the length across the criteria before writing, because the commonest structural fault is extensive working with almost no reflection.

faqs.question: Can my child switch from one maths course to the other?
faqs.answer: Schools set their own deadlines for course and level changes, usually within the first Diploma year, so the first thing to establish is whether the window is still open. If it is, the decision rests on whether a university route names a specific course, what a diagnostic task shows about engagement with proof against engagement with data, and whether the catch-up block is affordable. A switch is not administrative: the content diverges, so there is genuine material to acquire in whichever direction the student moves.

faqs.question: Does Applications and Interpretation at Higher Level satisfy a maths prerequisite?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it must be checked rather than assumed. Some programmes accept Applications and Interpretation at Higher Level where they would not accept it at Standard Level, and others specify Analysis and Approaches explicitly. Because this varies between institutions and between intakes, no requirement is reproduced on this page. Read the published requirement for every route the student is considering, including the insurance choices, and keep copies. Eliminating the fallback route is the expensive and common version of getting this wrong.

faqs.question: Why does Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level cost more to tutor here?
faqs.answer: Supply. Fewer tutors in this market can teach Higher Level calculus and proof to a candidate chasing a 7, and fewer still have marked the Higher Level third paper against the published scheme. Published Dubai bands put a qualified subject tutor at AED 150 to 300 an hour and a specialist at AED 200 to 450 and above, with a premium named tier reaching AED 650, and this specialism sits in the upper half. A Standard Level Applications and Interpretation student does not need that premium and should not pay it.

faqs.question: My child computes well but dislikes proof. Which course suits them?
faqs.answer: On that description, Applications and Interpretation, provided no university route names Analysis and Approaches. The useful test is not the preference stated at the kitchen table but behaviour under mild difficulty: give the student one modest algebraic proof question and one modelling question with real data, and watch which they persist with when it becomes uncomfortable. That signal predicts two years of experience far better than an IGCSE grade, which rewards neither behaviour distinctively.

faqs.question: Do tutors come to our home in Dubai for maths sessions?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not run home visits anywhere in the UAE, since that is an India-only service, and all sessions are delivered online over live video. Mathematics is the subject where this matters least as a compromise and most as an advantage: the student's own working is shared on screen and annotated live, and the annotations stay in the file, which is exactly what a subject whose marks sit in the method needs. It also widens the pool for the scarcest specialisms well beyond driving distance.

faqs.question: How many hours does the exploration need?
faqs.answer: Fewer than families expect if the topic is chosen against the criteria, and many more if it is not. Four sessions is a realistic plan: one on topic selection tested against the use-of-mathematics criterion, one on structuring the work so presentation and communication marks are available, one on a draft with comments naming criterion letters and bands, and one on the reflection section, which is the most commonly thin part. The student writes everything between sessions; a tutor comments and never produces any of it.

faqs.question: Is the Higher Level third paper the same in both courses?
faqs.answer: No. In Analysis and Approaches it is short and investigative, with extended questions that award marks for setting out and justifying an approach. In Applications and Interpretation it is a long data-led investigation requiring structured commentary alongside calculation. What the two share is that fewer past versions exist than for the other papers, so both are routinely under-practised. Two properly marked attempts is one of the highest-return purchases available in either course, and it takes four sessions at most.

faqs.question: What if we discover in the final year that the course choice was wrong?
faqs.answer: Then the plan changes rather than the course, because the switching window has almost certainly closed. For a student in Analysis and Approaches without an appetite for proof, concentrate the funded hours on method writing and non-calculator fluency, which are the recoverable marks regardless of temperament. For a student who needs Analysis and Approaches for a route they cannot access, the conversation should be about the route's alternatives, including foundation entry and related degree pathways, rather than about buying more mathematics hours.

faqs.question: What should a mathematics quote state in writing?
faqs.answer: Four things. Which of the two courses and which level the tutor teaches. Whether they have marked the Higher Level third paper against the published scheme, if your child sits one. Whether setting and marking work between sessions is included, since in mathematics the marked script with the working visible is the product. And the number of sessions with an end date. A provider who will also state what the block will not cover is giving you a plan rather than a subscription.

dubai/ib-math-aa-vs-ai-guidance.closingHeading: Watch the student, read the requirement, then spend
dubai/ib-math-aa-vs-ai-guidance.closingBody: Two cheap steps settle this better than any amount of discussion. Put one modest algebraic proof question and one modelling question with real data in front of your child and watch which they stay with when it gets uncomfortable; that signal predicts two years better than a grade does. Then read the published entry requirement for three or four degree routes, fallbacks included, and check whether a specific mathematics course and level are named. Ask the school for its change deadline while you do it. Book the free trial lesson, bring the script, and ask for a quote that names the course, the level, the component, the session count and the end date.

dubai/ib-math-ia-help.tutorsIntro: The tutors here supervise mathematical explorations in both Diploma maths courses. Each has read explorations against the five criteria, knows which topics cap criterion E at higher level, and will tell a student in the first session if their chosen topic cannot reach the top band of the course they are sitting.

intro.heading: The exploration is twenty marks, and six of them are decided before writing begins
paragraphs: Every Diploma mathematics student, in Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation, at standard or higher level, submits one mathematical exploration. It runs to roughly twelve to twenty pages, it is marked by the school teacher against five published criteria totalling twenty marks, and the IB moderates a sample of the school's marking. It is worth about a fifth of the final Mathematics grade, and unlike a paper it is worked on over months rather than hours.

The criteria are not evenly weighted and the distribution is the single most useful thing a family can know. Presentation carries four marks. Mathematical communication carries four. Personal engagement carries three. Reflection carries three. Use of mathematics carries six, the largest single block, and it asks whether the mathematics in the exploration is at the level of the course and whether it is correct and thorough. A student whose topic resolves with mathematics below their course level has capped those six marks in week one, and nothing written afterwards lifts them.

That makes the exploration unusual among assessed tasks: the most consequential decision is the earliest one, and it is made when the student knows least. A Maths AA HL candidate who picks a topic about the optimal angle for a basketball shot will produce something readable, will earn presentation and engagement marks, and will be marked against a criterion that asks for higher level mathematics by an examiner looking at projectile motion a standard level student could handle. The work was fine. The topic was not.

The second pattern worth knowing is that six of the twenty marks, personal engagement and reflection, are the ones students leave to the final evening. Those six marks reward ownership and mathematical thinking about the mathematics, and they are the cheapest marks in the exploration to earn properly because they require no new mathematics at all, only a student who wrote down their actual decisions as they made them.

Our work is narrow. We test a topic against criterion E before any writing, teach the notation conventions criterion B rewards, read the student's own draft letter by letter and state the band each criterion sits in, and name the next job. The student does the mathematics and writes the pages. Nothing is supplied and nothing is rewritten, because the exploration carries an academic honesty declaration and the student is the one who signs it.

Sessions run online, one-to-one, over live video with a shared screen. An exploration session is two people looking at the same graph, the same derivation or the same spreadsheet, which works better shared on screen than over a shoulder, and the student keeps the annotated file afterwards. It also means a Dubai family can book a tutor who has supervised explorations in their child's exact course and level, rather than whichever mathematics tutor happens to live within a drivable distance of their community at seven in the evening.

dubai/ib-math-ia-help.programmesIntro: Mathematics is assessed differently at each stage of the IB continuum, and Dubai families moving between schools or arriving from other systems meet the exploration with very different preparation. Here is what mathematics assessment looks like at each level.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Two mathematics courses, Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation, each at standard and higher level. All four combinations submit the same kind of mathematical exploration against the same five criteria, but criterion E is read against the level and content of the specific course, which is why the same topic can be strong in one course and weak in another.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai schools often run all four mathematics combinations with small higher level groups, sometimes taught together with standard level for part of the week. The practical effect is that a higher level student may receive topic guidance calibrated to a standard level audience, which is precisely the situation where criterion E gets capped without anybody noticing.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: MYP mathematics is assessed against four criteria including investigating patterns and applying mathematics in real-life contexts, which is recognisably the exploration in miniature. Students who have written MYP investigations already know what it means to justify a general rule rather than to compute an answer.
programmes.countryNote: The continuum schools in Dubai produce DP students who have written criterion-marked investigations since Year 7. Students who join at Year 12 from an IGCSE mathematics course have usually never written mathematics as prose, and the first two sessions on an exploration with those students are about writing conventions rather than about mathematics.

programmes.name: Career-related Programme
programmes.description: CP students take Diploma courses alongside career-related study, so a CP student taking a Diploma mathematics course submits the same exploration against the same criteria as any Diploma candidate. The core differs, with a reflective project rather than TOK and an Extended Essay.
programmes.countryNote: Where a Dubai school offers the CP, mathematics is often taken at standard level as part of the course package. The exploration requirement is unchanged, which surprises some families who assume the career-related route reduces the internally assessed load.

dubai/ib-math-ia-help.subjectsIntro: An exploration's topic has to fit the course, and the practical question is which areas of each syllabus actually support higher level mathematics. These are the areas Dubai students draw topics from most, with what each one can and cannot reach.

subjects.name: Calculus and optimisation
subjects.description: Reliable ground for higher level explorations if the problem genuinely needs calculus rather than decorating it. Optimisation problems that resolve with a single derivative and a sign check sit at standard level, so the higher level version needs constrained or multivariable structure.

subjects.name: Complex numbers and polar forms
subjects.description: Strong for criterion E because the mathematics is unambiguously higher level. The risk is a student who can manipulate the algebra but cannot explain what the result means, which costs reflection rather than use of mathematics.

subjects.name: Series, sequences and proof
subjects.description: Proof by induction and convergence arguments earn criterion E cleanly. These topics also reward mathematical communication, because the notation conventions are strict and a student who follows them picks up criterion B almost automatically.

subjects.name: Vectors and three-dimensional geometry
subjects.description: Good for explorations with a physical setting, and strong on presentation because the diagrams carry real information. Students lose marks by computing with vectors without ever stating what the result tells them about the situation.

subjects.name: Statistics and regression
subjects.description: The natural home for most Applications and Interpretation explorations. Marks are decided by whether the student interrogates the model: residuals examined, assumptions stated, and the limits of the fit discussed rather than a correlation coefficient quoted and accepted.

subjects.name: Probability and distributions
subjects.description: Flexible across courses. The common failure is treating a distribution as an assumption that needs no justification, when explaining why this distribution fits this situation is exactly where reflection marks live.

subjects.name: Graph theory and networks
subjects.description: Distinctive and under-used, and it maps naturally onto real Dubai settings such as metro connectivity or delivery routing. The mathematics is genuinely higher level, which secures criterion E if the student can handle the algorithms correctly.

subjects.name: Matrices and transformations
subjects.description: Useful for modelling topics and strong on criterion B because matrix notation is unforgiving and rewards precision. Students must be careful that the matrices are doing work rather than restating something simpler.

subjects.name: Financial and exponential modelling
subjects.description: Accessible and often well executed at standard level. At higher level it usually needs more: a comparison of competing models, a sensitivity analysis, or a derivation rather than an application of a standard formula.

subjects.name: Trigonometry and periodic modelling
subjects.description: A frequent choice for topics involving tides, daylight or sound. The mathematics sits at standard level unless the student goes beyond fitting a sinusoid, which is the single most common criterion E cap we see.

The student brings three or four candidate topics and we establish, for each, what mathematics it would actually require and whether that mathematics reaches the level of their course. Roughly half of candidate topics fail this test, and discovering that in week one costs an hour rather than a term.

sections.heading: The five criteria and where the twenty marks sit
paragraphs: No competitor page ranking for this query names a single exploration criterion, which is why so many Dubai students produce a polished document that scores in the middle. The exploration is marked letter by letter and the total is the sum, so the question that matters in any given week is which letter the available hours can move.

Read the allocation as a budget. Four marks for presentation and four for mathematical communication are eight marks that depend on craft rather than on mathematical ability, and both are reliably winnable by any student willing to follow conventions. Three marks for personal engagement and three for reflection are six more that require no new mathematics at all. Six marks for use of mathematics are the ones constrained by the topic. A student who understands that distribution spends their last week very differently from one who does not.

The implication for a struggling student is encouraging. Fourteen of the twenty marks are not about mathematical difficulty. A student in the middle of a standard level set who writes carefully, defines their variables, labels their graphs, reflects on the mathematics and documents their own decisions can score well above where their examination performance would predict.

Treat the allocations below as the structure to plan against, and confirm the current figures in the mathematics subject guide your child's teacher is working from. The IB publishes the authoritative version and revises it on a cycle; where this page and the guide differ, the guide is right.

sections.heading: Criterion E: why the topic sets the ceiling
paragraphs: Criterion E asks whether the mathematics used is commensurate with the level of the course and whether it is correct and thorough. Those two requirements behave differently. Correctness can be fixed by checking the work. Level cannot be fixed at all once the topic is chosen, because the level is a property of the problem rather than of the write-up.

This produces the most common and most avoidable disappointment in Diploma mathematics. A higher level student picks a topic they find interesting, executes it carefully, and receives four of six on criterion E because the mathematics never left the standard level syllabus. The exploration reads well. The teacher's comments are positive. The mark is capped, and it was capped in the first fortnight.

The test that catches it is concrete. Write down the specific pieces of mathematics the topic will require: not the subject area, the actual techniques. Then check each one against the syllabus for the student's own course and level. If every technique appears in the standard level syllabus and the student is sitting higher level, the topic needs extending or replacing before any writing begins.

The table below shows the pattern with topics Dubai students choose often. In every row the fix is the same shape: keep the context, deepen the mathematics. A tide-modelling exploration that fits a sinusoid is standard level; the same tide data analysed with a Fourier-style decomposition, or with a model comparison and a residual analysis, is a different exploration about the same subject.

sections.heading: Analysis and Approaches versus Applications and Interpretation
paragraphs: The two Diploma mathematics courses submit the same exploration against the same criteria, but what counts as a good exploration differs, and students who copy a model exploration from the other course go wrong in predictable ways. Analysis and Approaches rewards structure, derivation and proof. Applications and Interpretation rewards modelling, data and interpretation of results in context.

The practical difference shows up in criterion E and criterion D. An Analysis exploration demonstrates level through the sophistication of its mathematical argument, so an unproven assertion is expensive. An Applications exploration demonstrates level through the sophistication of its modelling and the honesty of its interpretation, so an unexamined model is expensive. A student in Applications who writes a proof-heavy exploration is working hard in the wrong direction, and vice versa.

There is also a data question. Applications explorations usually need real data, and where that data comes from matters for reflection marks: a student who collected their own measurements, or who can state the provenance and limitations of a public dataset, has something honest to reflect on. A dataset pulled from an unattributed source leaves reflection with nothing to say except that the data might be imperfect.

For Dubai students specifically, the data advantage is real and underused. Public transport timetables, municipal weather records, utility pricing structures and the published statistics of a rapidly growing city all provide datasets with genuine local specificity. An exploration using Dubai data a student collected or sourced themselves earns personal engagement marks that a generic international dataset does not.

sections.heading: The four marks almost nobody collects: mathematical communication
paragraphs: Criterion B is worth four of twenty and it is almost pure craft. It asks for correct mathematical notation, variables that are defined before use, consistent symbols throughout, and graphs and tables that carry information. None of that requires mathematical ability beyond the student's course, and yet it is routinely the second weakest criterion on a Dubai exploration after criterion E.

The faults are consistent. Calculator and software syntax appears in the body text, so a student writes an expression the way they typed it into a graphing tool rather than the way it is written in mathematics. Variables appear without definition, so a reader meets a symbol and has to guess what it stands for. Symbols drift, with the same quantity acquiring two names across twenty pages. Graphs arrive without axis labels, units or captions, which means they decorate rather than inform.

Each of those takes an evening to fix and the fix is mechanical. Read the exploration once looking only at notation. Define every symbol at first use and keep a short notation list. Replace every piece of software syntax with proper notation. Caption every figure and label every axis with a quantity and a unit. Students who do this pass from the lower bands of criterion B to the upper ones without touching the mathematics.

This is also the criterion where an external reader helps most cheaply, because the author of a document cannot see its notation problems. A student has been staring at their own symbols for weeks and has stopped noticing that two of them mean the same thing. One hour of someone else's eyes, with no mathematical discussion at all, routinely recovers two marks out of twenty.
bullets: Define every variable at first use and keep a notation list
No calculator or software syntax anywhere in the body text
Every axis labelled with a quantity and a unit; every figure captioned
One symbol per quantity, consistently, across the whole document
Read the document once for notation alone, ignoring the mathematics

sections.heading: Personal engagement and reflection: six marks written in the wrong register
paragraphs: Together these two criteria are worth six of twenty, nearly a third of the exploration, and they are the ones most often written in the last hour. They also require no new mathematics, which makes them the best value marks in the task for a student who is short of time or of mathematical confidence.

Personal engagement is evidenced by choices, not by enthusiasm. A sentence explaining that the student has always loved mathematics earns nothing. A paragraph explaining that they first tried a linear model, found the residuals patterned, and switched approach for a stated reason is engagement, because it shows the student's own thinking at work. The evidence has to be in the mathematics the student actually did.

Reflection must be about the mathematics. The commonest version in Dubai drafts is a closing paragraph on how much the student learnt and how they would manage their time better next time, which is reflection about the project rather than about the subject. What earns marks is thinking about the mathematics itself: why this method rather than another, what the result implies, what assumption the conclusion depends on, what would change if that assumption were relaxed, where the model breaks down.

The practical method is to keep a short log while working. Three lines a week recording what was tried, what failed and what was decided produces, by the end, exactly the material both criteria ask for. Students who do not keep a log have to reconstruct their decisions afterwards, and reconstructed decisions read as generic because they are.
bullets: Engagement is shown by decisions, never by stated enthusiasm
Reflection must be about the mathematics, not about the experience
Abandoned approaches are evidence; include them rather than hiding them

sections.heading: Where Dubai exploration drafts lose marks
paragraphs: The pattern across drafts from Dubai schools is stable. Criterion E caps from topics chosen below course level come first, and they are the single largest loss. They are also the most frustrating, because the student usually worked hard and the cap was set before the work started. Testing the topic against the syllabus in week one is the entire defence.

Second is criterion B, where notation and labelling carelessness costs marks that have nothing to do with mathematical ability. Third is the engagement and reflection pair written as an afterthought in the wrong register. Those three account for most of the gap between a mid-band exploration and a strong one, and none of them is about being better at mathematics.

Fourth is a specifically Dubai issue: topic imitation. Small higher level cohorts and young Diploma departments mean fewer internal exemplars, so students go looking online and arrive with topics that are both widely used and, because they were written for a general audience, usually pitched at standard level. Teachers in these departments see the same four topics every year. Originality is not a criterion, but a topic nobody else chose tends to produce genuine engagement evidence, and a topic everybody chose tends not to.

Fifth, and smallest, is structural: an exploration with no stated aim at the start, no conclusion that answers it, and pages that arrive in the order the work happened rather than in the order a reader needs. Criterion A is four marks and this is what it measures. It takes a single reorganisation session to fix and almost nobody does it.

sections.heading: What exploration support costs in Dubai, and why it runs online
paragraphs: Published Dubai market rates, read in October 2026, start at AED 33-52 at Tutopiya and AED 45-65 at EdFlik for budget online tutoring, rise through Unitors at AED 150 for IGCSE and AED 200 for IB, TutorChase at AED 270, and Bestimate's AED 200-450 and above for specialist IB and IGCSE work, reaching AED 650 at BartyED for premium examiner-branded provision. Bestimate quotes in-home visits at AED 180-350, with independent home tutors up to AED 500 once travel is priced in. These are market figures, not an IB Gram price list.

A mathematical exploration is a project cost rather than a monthly one. Four to six sessions covers it for most students: one or two on topic viability, one on notation and communication, one or two criterion reviews of the student's own draft, and a short engagement and reflection session. Compare that with the AED 1,000-2,000 a month Bestimate attributes to specialist exam-year weekly tutoring and the exploration looks like what it is, a short targeted piece of work rather than a subscription.

The question worth asking a prospective tutor is whether they can say, in the first session, where a proposed topic sits relative to the student's course level. That is the service. A tutor who is strong at mathematics but has never read an exploration against the criteria will help with the mathematics and leave criterion E exactly where it was, which is where most of the available marks are.

IB Gram does not sell home visits anywhere in the UAE; sending a tutor to a family's address is a service we run only in India. For exploration work that costs nothing. The session is a derivation, a graph or a spreadsheet on a shared screen, annotated live, with the file staying in the student's hands. What the online format buys is a tutor who has supervised explorations in the student's own course rather than whoever can reach Mirdif or Dubai Hills by seven in the evening, which for a small higher level cohort is frequently nobody at all.

The service in the first session is a judgement about whether a topic reaches the level of the student's own course, which requires someone who has read explorations against criterion E. Where nobody suitable is free at your preferred hour we say so rather than substituting.

It ends with a clear statement of what mathematics each would require and where that mathematics sits relative to their course. Half the time a topic survives and the student starts writing; half the time it needs extending, and knowing that in week one is worth the hour on its own.

whyPoints.title: We test the topic first
whyPoints.description: Six of twenty marks depend on whether the mathematics reaches the level of the course, and that is decided before any writing. The first session exists to catch a capped topic in week one rather than in the teacher's comments three months later.

whyPoints.title: Criterion B is treated as free marks
whyPoints.description: Notation, definitions, labelled graphs and consistent symbols are four marks of pure craft, winnable by any student. Most drafts arrive leaking two of them, and an hour of someone else's eyes on notation alone is the cheapest mark gain in the task.

whyPoints.description: An Analysis exploration and an Applications exploration fail criterion E differently, one through unproven assertion and one through untested models. Advice calibrated to the wrong course is worse than no advice, so the tutor is matched to the course.

faqs.question: How long does the IB mathematical exploration have to be?
faqs.answer: The expected length is roughly twelve to twenty pages, which is a page count rather than a word count and therefore includes graphs, tables and worked mathematics. A shorter exploration is not automatically weaker, but an exploration of six pages rarely contains enough mathematics to show thoroughness on criterion E, and one of thirty pages usually contains repetition that costs presentation marks. Aim for the mathematics to determine the length and then check it falls in the expected range, rather than writing to fill pages.

faqs.question: What is the maths IA actually worth towards the final grade?
faqs.answer: Roughly a fifth of the Mathematics grade, at both standard and higher level and in both Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation. The exploration is marked out of twenty by the school teacher against five criteria and a sample of the school's marking is externally moderated by the IB, which means the mark has to be defensible against the band descriptors rather than simply generous. Confirm the exact weighting in the current subject guide your child's teacher is working from.

faqs.question: Why does my child's topic choice matter so much?
faqs.answer: Because criterion E, worth six of the twenty marks, asks whether the mathematics used is at the level of the course. Level is a property of the problem, not of the write-up, so a topic that resolves with standard level techniques caps that criterion for a higher level student no matter how well the exploration is written. The defence is a half-hour exercise in week one: list the specific techniques the topic requires and check each against the student's own syllabus and level.

faqs.question: What is the difference between an AA and an AI exploration?
faqs.answer: The criteria are identical and the expectations differ. Analysis and Approaches demonstrates level through derivation, proof and structural argument, so an unproven assertion is costly. Applications and Interpretation demonstrates level through modelling, data handling and interpretation in context, so a model applied without being tested is costly. Students who copy a strong exploration from the other course go wrong predictably, working hard in the wrong direction. Check which course a model exploration came from before learning anything from it.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with the mathematics in my child's exploration?
faqs.answer: Yes, within the rule that the work must be the student's own. A tutor may teach a technique the exploration needs, explain what a criterion rewards, ask whether a topic reaches the course level, flag that a derivation has an error for the student to find, and report where each criterion currently sits. A tutor may not perform the mathematics, write any passage, build the spreadsheet or supply the graphs. The student signs an academic honesty declaration, and it has to be true.

faqs.question: What does criterion B, mathematical communication, actually want?
faqs.answer: Correct notation, variables defined before use, consistent symbols throughout, and graphs and tables that carry information rather than decorate. In practice it means no calculator or software syntax in the body text, every symbol defined at first use, one symbol per quantity across all twenty pages, and every axis labelled with a quantity and a unit. It is four of twenty marks and it requires no mathematical ability beyond the student's course, which makes it the most reliable mark gain available.

faqs.question: How do personal engagement and reflection earn marks?
faqs.answer: Engagement is evidenced by choices the student made, not by stated enthusiasm, so a paragraph explaining that a first model was abandoned for a specific reason earns where a sentence about loving mathematics does not. Reflection must be about the mathematics: why one method rather than another, what the result implies, what assumption the conclusion rests on, where the model breaks down. Together they are six of twenty marks and they need no new mathematics, which makes them the best value in the task.

faqs.question: When should my child start their exploration?
faqs.answer: Topic work should begin nine to twelve months before the school's internal submission deadline, which for most Dubai schools means during the first Diploma year. The topic conversation is the part that cannot be compressed, because testing a topic against the course level and finding it short means starting again. Writing can be done in a few concentrated weeks; choosing well cannot. Ask the mathematics teacher for the internal deadline early and count backwards from it rather than forwards from today.

faqs.question: My child is struggling with Maths HL. Is a difficult topic a mistake?
faqs.answer: A topic should be demanding enough to reach the higher level syllabus and no more demanding than that. Choosing something exotic to look impressive usually damages criterion E through errors rather than helping it, because the criterion asks for mathematics that is correct and thorough as well as at level. The better strategy for a struggling higher level student is a topic at the lower end of the higher level syllabus, executed meticulously, with the fourteen marks outside criterion E collected in full.

faqs.question: Can my child use a dataset they found online?
faqs.answer: Yes, provided it is cited properly and its provenance can be stated. The reflection criterion rewards honest discussion of the data's limitations, which requires knowing where it came from, how it was collected and what it excludes. A dataset from an unattributed source leaves reflection with nothing to say. For Dubai students, locally available data on transport, weather, utilities or the city's published statistics often works better, because it is specific and the student can describe its origin accurately.

faqs.question: How should the hours be split between topic work and draft review?
faqs.answer: Roughly half and half for most students, with the topic half coming first. One or two sessions establish whether the proposed mathematics reaches the course level, then one covers notation and communication, one or two review the student's own draft criterion by criterion, and a short final session handles engagement and reflection. Spreading the same hours as a standing weekly arrangement across a year works less well, because criterion feedback only means something when there is something written to apply it to.

faqs.question: What do Dubai families pay for maths exploration support?
faqs.answer: Published market rates read in October 2026 run from about AED 33-65 an hour at the budget online platforms up to AED 650 for premium examiner-branded providers, with Unitors listing IB from AED 200, TutorChase at AED 270, and Bestimate putting specialist IB and IGCSE support at AED 200-450 and above. In-home visits are quoted at AED 180-350 with independent tutors up to AED 500 once travel is included. Those are the market's figures. An exploration block of four to six sessions is a project cost rather than a monthly commitment.

faqs.question: Does the teacher's exploration mark always stand?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. The exploration is marked by the school teacher and the IB moderates a sample of each school's marking. If the sample suggests a school has marked generously or harshly against the band descriptors, marks for that component can be adjusted across the cohort. This is why a mark needs to be defensible criterion by criterion rather than reflecting how hard a student evidently worked, and why criterion language matters more than general quality impressions.

faqs.question: Is it too late to start if the deadline is a month away?
faqs.answer: Not too late to improve the mark, but be clear about what a month can reach. Criterion E is fixed by then, since the topic cannot change, which leaves fourteen marks genuinely in play across presentation, mathematical communication, engagement and reflection. A month is comfortable for all four. What a month cannot do is lift a topic that sits below the student's course level, and any tutor suggesting otherwise is selling hope rather than help.

dubai/ib-math-ia-help.closingHeading: Test the topic before writing a page
dubai/ib-math-ia-help.closingBody: If your child has a topic in mind and nothing written, the single most valuable hour available is the one that establishes what mathematics the topic requires and whether it reaches the level of their course. If a draft already exists, a criterion review will report the band each of the five letters sits in and name the one job that moves the mark. Sessions run over live video on Gulf Standard Time, the student keeps the annotated file, and every page submitted is theirs. If the answer is that the exploration is already strong and needs a notation pass, that is what we will say.

intro.heading: Four courses, one subject name
paragraphs: The phrase 'IB maths' covers four distinct courses, and the most common waste of money in Dubai maths tutoring is a tutor who has taught one of them being booked for another. Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches and Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation each run at Standard and Higher Level. They share five syllabus topics by name — number and algebra, functions, geometry and trigonometry, statistics and probability, calculus — and they treat them so differently that a strong Analysis teacher can be poorly placed to teach Applications, and the reverse.

The sharpest practical difference is the calculator. In Analysis and Approaches, Paper 1 is sat without a graphic display calculator. In Applications and Interpretation, a calculator is permitted in every paper. That single rule reshapes revision entirely: an Analysis student needs algebraic fluency, exact-value work and by-hand differentiation to be automatic, while an Applications student needs calculator command sequences to be automatic and a different kind of discipline about interpreting what the machine returns.

The second difference is what the papers reward. Analysis and Approaches leans toward proof, algebraic structure and abstraction. Applications and Interpretation leans toward modelling, statistical inference and reading a real context correctly. A student who enjoys mathematics but cannot sustain abstraction frequently does better in Applications at a higher level than in Analysis at a lower one, and in Dubai that student has often been placed in Analysis by default because it carries more prestige in staffroom conversation.

At Higher Level both courses add a third paper. Paper 3 is an hour long, carries 20 per cent of the grade, and consists of extended problem-solving questions that build across many parts from a single scenario. It is the component Dubai students most often arrive unprepared for, because it rewards something the other two papers do not: holding a long chain of reasoning together while the question keeps changing what it asks. Dubai students typically meet it properly for the first time in a Year 13 mock, long after the habit of abandoning a question at its first unresolved part has set. Practised deliberately from the start of Higher Level, it is among the more coachable twenty per cent of any Diploma subject, because the behaviour it rewards can be taught directly rather than accumulated.

Lessons are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service offered only in India. For mathematics this is a practical advantage rather than a compromise. Working through a Paper 3 on a shared screen keeps a long solution visible in full, annotations are saved, and a Dubai family in Mirdif or Dubai Hills gets a tutor matched to Analysis Higher Level specifically rather than whichever maths tutor is within driving distance.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor.programmesIntro: Mathematics appears in every stage of the IB continuum a Dubai family passes through, and each stage hands the next one a different set of strengths. These are the stages that matter when planning maths support.

programmes.name: MYP Mathematics, Years 4 and 5
programmes.description: Standard and extended mathematics assessed against four criteria: knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. Students arrive at the Diploma comfortable with investigation and communication, often light on algebraic fluency and almost always light on timed-paper speed.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai IB World Schools running the full continuum feed MYP students straight into Diploma maths, and the common shock is Paper 1 in Analysis and Approaches. A student used to a calculator in every assessment meets a paper where it is prohibited, and the first mock reflects that rather than their mathematical understanding.

programmes.name: IGCSE Mathematics into Diploma maths
programmes.description: Cambridge 0580 Extended or Edexcel 4MA1 Higher leaves a student fluent at timed non-calculator work and short structured questions, which transfers well into Analysis and Approaches. What it does not build is the extended modelling and the statistical reasoning that Applications and Interpretation and Paper 3 both require.
programmes.countryNote: Most British-curriculum schools in Dubai run IGCSE at 16, and a meaningful share of their leavers join Diploma programmes elsewhere in the emirate. Additional Mathematics 0606, where a school offers it, is the single best preparation for Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level available before the Diploma.

programmes.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
programmes.description: Algebraic and proof-oriented. Paper 1 is sat without a calculator at both levels. Higher Level adds Paper 3 and substantially more content, particularly in calculus, complex numbers, proof and vectors. The route specified by some engineering, physics, mathematics and economics degrees, which is why the choice is a university decision as well as an academic one.
programmes.countryNote: The most over-chosen course at Higher Level in Dubai. A student scoring in the low teens on a Paper 1 in the first term of Diploma Year 1 has a decision available for a limited period, and the school's change window is usually earlier than families expect. Ask the IB coordinator for the actual date in September.

programmes.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
programmes.description: Modelling and statistics-oriented, with a calculator permitted throughout. Higher Level is demanding in its own right, adding substantial statistical inference, graph theory and matrices. The right course for a large share of students placed in Analysis by default, provided the universities on their list accept it for the intended course.
programmes.countryNote: Check the stated requirements of the universities actually on the student's list before switching. Some courses specify the Analysis route explicitly, others accept either, and a few state a Higher Level requirement without naming a route. The requirement is published by the university, not by the school or by a tutoring page.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor.subjectsIntro: Maths support in Dubai is booked by course, by level and increasingly by component. These are the units a session plan is built from, with the thing each one actually assesses.

subjects.name: Number and algebra
subjects.levels: All four courses; substantially extended at AA HL
subjects.description: Sequences, series, exponents, logarithms, binomial expansion, and at Analysis Higher Level complex numbers, proof by induction and systems of equations. The topic where a weak Key Stage 3 or IGCSE foundation does the most damage, because every later topic assumes the manipulation is automatic.

subjects.name: Functions
subjects.description: Domain and range, composite and inverse functions, transformations, and the graph behaviour that Paper 1 tests without a calculator in Analysis. Sketching from an equation rather than reading from a screen is the specific skill, and it is the one calculator-dependent students have never built.

subjects.name: Geometry and trigonometry
subjects.levels: All four courses; vectors at Higher Level
subjects.description: Triangle rules, radian measure, trigonometric identities and equations, and at Higher Level vectors in three dimensions. Marks go on exact values, on solving in the correct interval, and on knowing which identity shortens the work before starting it.

subjects.name: Statistics and probability
subjects.levels: All four courses; heavily extended at AI HL
subjects.description: Data presentation, correlation and regression, probability distributions and hypothesis testing. The dominant topic in Applications and Interpretation and the one Analysis students treat as an afterthought until Paper 2. Interpreting a result in context, not just producing it, is where the marks sit.

subjects.name: Calculus
subjects.levels: All four courses; extensive at AA HL
subjects.description: Differentiation, integration and their applications, with Analysis Higher Level adding implicit differentiation, differential equations and Maclaurin series. By-hand technique matters disproportionately because Paper 1 in Analysis forbids the calculator that would otherwise do the work.

subjects.name: Paper 1
subjects.levels: AA: no calculator · AI: calculator permitted
subjects.description: Short and extended response questions across the whole syllabus. 40 per cent at Standard Level, 30 per cent at Higher. In Analysis this is the paper that exposes algebraic fluency, and it is the paper most Dubai students practise least because practising it properly means putting the calculator away.

subjects.name: Paper 2
subjects.levels: Calculator permitted in all four courses
subjects.description: Same structure as Paper 1 with technology allowed. 40 per cent at Standard Level, 30 per cent at Higher. Marks are lost here to calculator command sequences the student half-remembers and to answers reported without the degree of accuracy the question specified.

subjects.name: Paper 3, Higher Level only
subjects.levels: AA HL and AI HL · 20 per cent · one hour
subjects.description: Two extended problem-solving questions, each building through many parts from a single scenario. It rewards sustained reasoning and the confidence to continue after a part that did not resolve. The component Dubai students most often meet for the first time in a Year 13 mock.

subjects.name: The Exploration
subjects.levels: All four courses · 20 per cent · 20 marks
subjects.description: An individual written mathematical investigation of a student-chosen topic, usually around twelve pages, assessed against five criteria. It is a fifth of the grade awarded for work done without time pressure, which makes it the most recoverable marks in the course.

subjects.name: Technology and the calculator
subjects.levels: Course-dependent, and the difference is decisive
subjects.description: Graphic display calculator command fluency is a taught skill, not an intuition. Applications and Interpretation students need it in every paper; Analysis students need it in Papers 2 and 3 and must be able to work without it in Paper 1. Mixing the two habits is a reliable source of lost marks.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor.regionsIntro: Delivery is online, so geography does not limit which maths specialist a Dubai student works with. What geography changes is when a session can realistically start and how long a student has been awake by then.

regions.name: Dubai Marina and JLT
regions.note: Short commutes and apartment study space. Paper 1 practice needs a quiet hour and a desk, so afternoon slots work better here than evening ones in a shared living room with a calculator within reach.

regions.name: Al Barsha and Dubai Hills Estate
regions.note: Several IB World Schools within a short radius, which means large Diploma cohorts and maths sets that move. A student moved from Analysis Higher to Standard mid-year has a decision pending, and marked Paper 1 evidence is what makes it a decision rather than an acceptance.

regions.name: Arabian Ranches, Mudon and Damac Hills
regions.note: Long bus routes and heavy after-school sport. Maths sessions here are usually 6.30pm or later, which suits worked-example teaching better than a timed Paper 1; the timed paper gets set for a weekend morning instead.

regions.name: Jumeirah, Umm Suqeim and Al Safa
regions.note: Established Diploma programmes with both maths routes offered at both levels, so a course change is usually administratively possible. Families here benefit most from an early audit, because they actually have options to act on.

regions.name: Mirdif, Al Warqa and Al Qusais
regions.note: A high share of students arriving from IGCSE rather than MYP, which generally means solid non-calculator algebra and little exposure to statistical modelling. That combination points toward Analysis, and the diagnostic should test it rather than assume it.

regions.name: Dubai Silicon Oasis and Academic City
regions.note: Short commutes make a 4.30pm maths slot realistic, which is the best time of day for Paper 1 work. Families here often book a Diploma student and an IGCSE sibling back to back on the same evening.

regions.name: Al Furjan, Discovery Gardens and Dubai South
regions.note: Newer Diploma provision where one teacher sometimes covers both maths routes. With no parallel set to benchmark against, an independently marked Paper 1 is often the only external data a family has about where their child actually sits.

schoolClusters.city: Dubai schools offering both maths routes at both levels
schoolClusters.note: Mature Diploma programmes where Analysis and Applications both run at Standard and Higher Level. A course change is a timetable question rather than an impossibility, which makes an early marked diagnosis genuinely actionable.

schoolClusters.city: Newer Diploma provision with narrower maths offerings
schoolClusters.note: Schools whose Diploma cohorts are smaller, where one route may run at only one level or where both routes share a teacher. Here the audit often concludes that the right course is not available on the timetable, which is a different conversation and worth having early.

schoolClusters.city: IGCSE feeder schools with strong non-calculator foundations
schoolClusters.note: British-curriculum schools whose Year 11 leavers join Diploma programmes elsewhere. Students from this group typically arrive with secure algebraic manipulation and no modelling experience, which shapes which route suits them.

modes.description: Sixty minutes a week aimed at a single component. For an Analysis student that usually means Paper 1 without a calculator; for an Applications student it is more often Paper 2 technique and interpretation. The student writes every word and performs every calculation; the tutor questions and marks.

sections.heading: Which IB maths course is the student actually sitting?
paragraphs: An IB maths tutor in Dubai should not teach a lesson before this is settled in writing. There are four courses: Analysis and Approaches at Standard and Higher Level, and Applications and Interpretation at Standard and Higher Level. They share five topic headings and differ in content depth, in calculator rules, in what the papers reward and in which university courses accept them. Booking a tutor without naming the course is like booking a physics tutor without naming the level.

The calculator rule is the fastest way to tell the difference in practice. Analysis and Approaches sits Paper 1 without a graphic display calculator at both Standard and Higher Level. Applications and Interpretation permits the calculator in every paper. That one rule changes what a revision hour should contain, and it changes it completely: exact-value trigonometry and by-hand integration for one student, calculator command fluency and interpretation discipline for the other.

Content depth is the second axis. Analysis Higher Level carries substantially more material than its Standard Level version, particularly in calculus, proof, complex numbers and vectors. Applications Higher Level carries a large additional load in statistical inference, matrices and graph theory. Neither Higher Level course is the easy option, and a student who finds one overwhelming may be well suited to the other.

The third axis is the university requirement, which is the only one a family cannot adjust after the fact. Some engineering, physics, mathematics and economics courses specify Analysis and Approaches by name; others accept either route; a few state a Higher Level requirement without specifying which course. Those requirements are published by the universities themselves and should be read from their own pages rather than inferred from a school's reputation or a tutoring site's summary.

sections.heading: The assessment structure, paper by paper
paragraphs: The weightings are the first thing that should go on a Dubai student's wall, because most maths revision is organised by topic while the grade is decided by paper. At Standard Level the two papers carry 40 per cent each and the Exploration carries 20. At Higher Level the papers carry 30, 30 and 20, with the Exploration again at 20. That last figure is the one families underestimate: a fifth of the maths grade is awarded for a written investigation produced without time pressure.

Paper 1 and Paper 2 cover the same syllabus and differ in technology. In Analysis and Approaches the absence of a calculator in Paper 1 is not a minor inconvenience; it is the design of the paper. Questions are written so that exact values, algebraic simplification and recognised identities do the work a calculator would otherwise do. A student who has revised the content but always with technology available will score below their understanding, consistently, and the first mock will look like a knowledge problem.

Paper 3 at Higher Level is an hour for two extended problem-solving questions. Each builds from a single scenario through many parts, often introducing an unfamiliar definition in the stem and asking the student to work with it. It rewards persistence and the ability to continue to part (d) after part (c) did not resolve, which is a specific examination behaviour rather than a mathematical skill, and it can be taught directly.

The Exploration is assessed against five criteria carrying twenty marks in total. Almost no competing tutoring page in this market names a single one, which is difficult to explain given that they are the entire basis on which the mark is awarded. Naming them changes how a student works: knowing that personal engagement and reflection together carry six of the twenty marks stops a student treating both as padding around the mathematics.

sections.heading: Where IB maths marks are actually lost in Dubai scripts
paragraphs: The first category is algebraic fluency, and it is the largest. A Diploma maths question is rarely one step; it is a chain, and a sign error or a mishandled fraction in step one takes the remaining marks with it even where the method was entirely correct. The diagnosis is straightforward and uncomfortable: set twenty short manipulation items with no context, time them, and count. A student who is slow and inaccurate on those is not losing marks on Diploma content.

The second is calculator dependence in Analysis and Approaches. Students who have met every topic with technology available cannot sketch a function from its equation, cannot produce an exact value for a trigonometric ratio, and reach for decimals where the mark scheme wants a surd. This shows up as a gap between Paper 2 and Paper 1 performance, and that gap is the single most diagnostic number in a maths file. Where it is wide, the fix is weeks of practice with the calculator physically out of reach.

The third is accuracy and reporting. Diploma mark schemes specify how answers should be given, frequently to three significant figures, and marks are lost for rounding early in a multi-step calculation or for reporting an answer in a form the question did not ask for. It is a mechanical habit, worth two or three marks per paper, and across four papers over two years it is a grade boundary's worth of marks for no mathematics at all.

The fourth is Paper 3 behaviour at Higher Level. The paper introduces unfamiliar definitions deliberately and then asks the student to work with them. Students who treat an unfamiliar stem as evidence that they have not been taught something stop, and the remaining parts of a long question go unattempted. Students who have practised the component know that the stem contains everything required. That is the whole difference, and it is a taught behaviour.

sections.heading: The Exploration: twenty marks, five criteria, named
paragraphs: The Exploration is an individual written mathematical investigation on a topic the student chooses, typically around twelve pages, carrying 20 per cent of the maths grade in all four courses. It is marked against five criteria totalling twenty marks. Criterion A covers presentation, B mathematical communication, C personal engagement, D reflection, and E use of mathematics, which carries the largest single allocation. Those letters and their weights should be in front of a student from the first session, because they describe the task more accurately than any amount of advice about choosing something interesting.

The dominant failure in Dubai Explorations is a topic that does not permit mathematics at the course level. A student picks something they genuinely care about, writes well about it, and ends up producing arithmetic and a graph. Criterion E rewards mathematics commensurate with the course, which means a Higher Level Exploration needs Higher Level mathematics in it. Testing a topic for that before any writing begins is the single highest-value session in the whole process.

The second failure is treating reflection as a conclusion. Criterion D is not a summary of what was done; it is evidence of the student considering the significance and the limitations of their own results, ideally throughout rather than in a final paragraph. Criterion C, personal engagement, is similarly misunderstood as a statement of interest in the introduction, when it is assessed through the choices visible across the whole piece.

The boundary matters here more than anywhere else in the course. A tutor may teach the mathematics a topic requires, question whether the topic can carry it, name the criteria and their allocations, and give written feedback on a draft the student produced. A tutor may not choose the topic, perform the mathematics, or rewrite a draft into its final form. Work that is not the student's own carries a malpractice finding against the student. One UAE-facing site advertises completed Internal Assessments at AED 3,750, and what is being sold there is a risk to the Diploma rather than a shortcut to a mark.

sections.heading: Choosing between Analysis and Applications in a Dubai school
paragraphs: The route decision gets made in the spring before Diploma Year 1, usually from IGCSE or MYP performance plus a provisional university idea, and in many Dubai schools it can still be changed for a limited period in the first term. The window is the thing to know about in September rather than in February, because afterwards the set, the timetable and the completed work have all settled around the original placement.

The right order of operations is university requirements first, then marked evidence, then preference. Reading the stated maths requirement of each course on the student's actual list takes an afternoon and removes most of the uncertainty: if a target engineering course names Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, the decision is made and the question becomes how to support it. If every course on the list accepts either route, the decision belongs entirely to the evidence and the student.

The evidence that matters is a Paper 1 sat under the correct calculator rule. For Analysis that means without a calculator, which is the part students resist and the part that produces the honest number. Where the losses are concentrated in two or three named topics, the issue is content and content responds to teaching. Where they are spread evenly across every question type and every topic, the course is the wrong fit and no realistic quantity of tutoring changes that over eighteen months.

One thing worth saying plainly, because the market does not: Applications and Interpretation is not the remedial option. At Higher Level it carries substantial statistical inference and modelling, and students who are fluent algebraically sometimes find it harder than Analysis because it asks them to sustain a context rather than manipulate a symbol. Choosing it should be a positive match to how a student thinks, not a retreat.

sections.heading: What IB maths tutoring costs in Dubai
paragraphs: Maths is the most requested Diploma subject in this emirate and Higher Level Analysis and Approaches is among the scarcest, which places it at the top of the qualified band and often into the specialist band. Read from providers' own published pages in October 2026: Unitors lists IB tuition from AED 200 an hour and IGCSE from AED 150, TutorChase quotes AED 270 for specialist work, and the Bestimate rate survey puts IB and IGCSE specialists at AED 200-450 and above. Budget online provision starts at AED 45-65 at EdFlik and AED 33-52 at Tutopiya, and premium named listings reach AED 650 at BartyED.

Those bands reward precision in what is bought. A student whose Paper 1 and Paper 2 marks differ widely needs calculator-free practice and marking, which is perhaps eight to ten focused hours rather than a year of weekly content review. A student whose Exploration topic cannot carry Higher Level mathematics needs three or four sessions before writing starts, placed early. Both of those are small, specific purchases that move a fifth or a third of the grade.

The in-home comparison is worth making once and then setting aside. Bestimate puts qualified in-home one-to-one in Dubai at AED 180-350 an hour and independent home tutors at AED 200-500, against AED 150-300 for comparable work online. The premium pays for a commute. For mathematics specifically there is a second argument: a long Paper 3 solution stays visible in full on a shared screen and the annotated version is saved, where a worked solution on paper at a kitchen table is gone by the following week.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; home visits are a service offered only in India. No IB Gram rate card is published here, because a maths plan is priced by course, level, component and hour count. The free 30-minute trial lesson, one per family with no card details taken, is where a plan and a figure are discussed together, and every AED figure above belongs to the provider or survey that published it.
