sections.heading: The Dubai market in dirhams, read from the providers' own pages
paragraphs: Here is the uncomfortable fact about tutoring prices in this city: three of the six best-ranking pages on these queries publish no price at all, and the two that do quote in US dollars, which is not a currency a Dubai family transacts in. The table below is the AED version, and each row names the provider who published the figure so you can verify it rather than take it on faith.

Read it from the bottom of the market upwards, because that is where most decisions actually sit. A university-student tutor working online is advertised from AED 45 to 65 an hour by EdFlik, with Tutopiya's published panel starting lower again. A qualified subject tutor online is a different band: Unitors publishes IGCSE tuition from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. A named IB or IGCSE specialist runs from roughly AED 200 to 450 and above, with TutorChase at AED 270. At the top, BartyED publishes AED 650 for its premium tier. For a Higher Level Analysis and Approaches student in DP2, the realistic band is the specialist one, and pretending otherwise is how a family ends up paying twice.

None of these is an IB Gram price. We do not publish a rate card on these pages, partly because the right figure depends on the course, the level and how many sessions a week, and partly because a number on a page at this scale goes stale and then misleads. The free trial lesson and the conversation after it is where you find out what your child's arrangement would cost. sections.heading: AA or AI: the choice that moves the bill most
paragraphs: The commonest expensive mistake in IB maths tutoring is buying help for the wrong course. Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation share five topic areas and almost nothing else about how they feel to study. A tutor fluent in AA Higher Level calculus can be genuinely weak on AI Higher Level statistics, and the reverse holds too. If a parent books on the subject name alone, there is a real chance of paying specialist rates for a mismatch.

The second expensive mistake is choosing the course on difficulty rather than on destination. Applications and Interpretation is not the easy option; its Higher Level course is demanding and its statistics load is heavier than most students expect. But course choice closes doors: engineering, physics and mathematics degrees commonly expect Analysis and Approaches, often at Higher Level. A student who picks AI for comfort in DP1 and discovers in DP2 that their target degree wants AA has a problem that no amount of tutoring fixes cheaply.

The route out of both mistakes is the same and costs nothing. Find out which course and which level your child is actually registered for, write it down, and check the published entry requirements for two or three specific university courses they might apply to. Requirements differ by institution and change between years, so read the university's own page rather than any summary, including this one. Then buy tutoring against that, not against a general sense that maths needs help.

sections.heading: Three papers, and where the hours have to go to earn marks
paragraphs: Standard Level students sit two written papers and Higher Level students sit three, with the exploration carrying twenty per cent of the final grade in every course. The split matters for budgeting because the papers are not equally coachable. Paper 1, sat without a calculator, rewards drilled fluency and is the fastest place to find marks. Paper 3, which only Higher Level students sit, rewards familiarity with an extended scaffolded format that a student may never have met.

The distribution of effort families choose is usually upside down. A student who feels weak will ask for more content teaching, and content teaching is the most expensive way to buy marks late in the course. The cheaper route is technique: exact values and surds for Paper 1, reading the question and stating the context for the interpretation marks, and sitting two or three Paper 3 investigations before the real one so the format holds no surprises. None of that is glamorous and all of it is recoverable in weeks.

Confirm the current weightings and durations with your school's IB coordinator before planning around them, because subject guides are revised and a tutoring page is not a syllabus. The point of the table is the pattern rather than the precise percentage: three components, three different skills, and an exploration that sits outside all of them and is handled on its own timeline.

One habit is worth building from the first lesson regardless of paper. IB mathematics awards method marks, and a student who writes down a substitution or a rearrangement before reaching for the calculator keeps marks that a student working in their head loses whenever the arithmetic slips. That is a behaviour rather than knowledge, which means it is trained by being corrected every week for a term, not explained once. Ask any tutor how they handle it; the answer tells you whether they have taught this course under examination conditions.

sections.heading: Where Al Rashidiya families waste money on maths tutoring
paragraphs: Every item below has been paid for by somebody, repeatedly. None of them is a scam; they are all reasonable-looking decisions that produce no grade movement, which makes them worse than an obvious waste because nobody notices for a term.

The pattern underneath most of them is buying reassurance rather than diagnosis. A parent who is worried books an hour a week and feels better, and nobody establishes which paper the marks are leaving from or why. Six weeks later the arrangement is still running and the mark is unchanged, and the tutor is blamed when nobody ever asked them to fix anything specific. A diagnosis costs one lesson and saves a term of that.

The corrective is unglamorous: get a marked past paper, identify the two or three repeating errors, state what the tutoring is for, and review against marks after six lessons rather than against how the sessions felt. If the pattern has not shifted, change the tutor or the approach instead of extending the arrangement. We would rather lose a booking at week six than hold one that is not working.

There is a seventh waste that deserves naming separately, because it looks like prudence. A family worried about cost buys the cheapest available hour for a Higher Level student, on the reasonable theory that some help beats none. A university-student tutor advertised from AED 45 an hour is a genuine service for MYP consolidation and the wrong purchase for Higher Level Analysis and Approaches, where the content runs past what most undergraduates have revised recently. The hour is cheap and the term is not, and the family usually ends up buying the specialist anyway, two months later and closer to the papers.

sections.heading: The exploration: twenty per cent that is cheap to protect and expensive to rescue
paragraphs: The mathematical exploration carries twenty per cent of the final maths grade in all four courses. It is assessed on criteria that include presentation, mathematical communication, personal engagement, reflection and the use of mathematics, and those criteria are published and specific. A student who has read them properly in DP1 is in a completely different position from one who meets them in DP2 with a deadline three weeks away.

The economics are stark. Protecting the exploration costs perhaps four sessions early: one on what the criteria actually reward, one on choosing a topic that has enough mathematics in it to reach the higher bands, one on structure, and one reviewing the student's own draft with questions rather than corrections. Rescuing it costs far more, arrives at exam-year rates, and still cannot recover a topic choice that was too thin for the mathematics required.

The boundary here is not negotiable and it is worth stating plainly, because this is where the UAE tutoring market is at its worst. A tutor may explain the criteria, model the method on a different example, ask questions about the student's draft and point out where the mathematics is unsupported. A tutor may not write, draft, rewrite or edit to completion any part of the exploration. One page in the researched competitor set sells completed Internal Assessments outright. That is a malpractice route and the student carries the finding, not the seller.

Topic choice is where a parent can usefully intervene without knowing any mathematics. Ask your child what the mathematics in their chosen topic actually is, and listen for whether the answer names techniques or only names a subject they find interesting. An exploration about a sport with one average calculated in it has nowhere to go; the same interest routed through a model, a derivation and a reflection on the model's limits has room to reach the higher bands. That conversation costs nothing and happens best in DP1.

sections.heading: One session a week against two: the two-year arithmetic
paragraphs: Families ask whether to start with one session a week or two, and the honest answer depends on how long they intend to keep going. Two sessions a week sustained through the whole Diploma is a serious financial commitment, and most households that start there reduce it by the second term, usually at the worst possible moment.

The pattern that works better is one weekly session held for the full two years, with a second session added for a defined block when there is something specific to do: the exploration in DP1, Paper 3 format work before the final series, or a recovery block after a predicted grade that blocks an offer. That shape costs less in total than two sessions a week for one year and produces more, because continuity is what lets a tutor see a pattern rather than react to a test.

Whatever shape you choose, cancel the thing that is not working rather than adding to it. A family paying for two weekly sessions in a subject where the diagnosis was never made is spending twice as much on the same absence of a plan. Run the review at six lessons, against marks on questions of the type that were going wrong, and be willing to stop.

Siblings change the arithmetic, and in the eastern suburbs they often do. Two children on different programmes in the same household are two separate arrangements, and the household budget tends to be set by whichever one is closer to final papers. The usual sensible answer is a weekly slot for the exam-year student and short defined blocks for the younger one, rather than halving both into something too thin to be useful. Book the two slots back to back if you can; one quiet hour in the house is easier to produce than two on different evenings.

sections.heading: Fitting a maths lesson into an Al Rashidiya weekday
paragraphs: A session that does not happen costs the same as one that does, so scheduling is a money question as much as a logistics one. Al Rashidiya sits against the airport's southern edge, and its Diploma students travel north to Al Garhoud or east to Mirdif, which are two very different afternoons. A family running towards Garhoud can plausibly hold a 4.30pm slot. A family on a Mirdif bus route is realistically looking at 5.30pm or later.

Pick the slot that survives a bad traffic day rather than a good one. The arrangement that quietly dies is the one booked for the earliest time that ever worked, which then fails every third week and is rescheduled until it stops existing. Online delivery removes the tutor's journey from the equation entirely, which means the only variable left is your child's arrival home, and that is a variable you can actually measure.

Hold the slot like a school commitment. Across two years, a weekly session that is missed once a month has lost roughly twenty sessions, which at mid-tier market rates is a sum worth protecting. Ramadan and school holiday periods are worth planning rather than improvising: sessions can shift later in the evening during Ramadan, and holiday weeks are usually better used for a short block on one topic than for keeping a weekly slot limping along.

The room matters as much as the hour. A Diploma maths lesson needs a desk, a closed door, paper and a pen, and a laptop on a stable surface rather than a phone on a sofa. Households in this corridor are often busy at 6pm with younger siblings and visiting family, and a lesson held in the middle of that produces half of what the same hour produces at a bedroom desk. Families who settle that in the first week get noticeably more from the same spend than families who never quite do.

sections.heading: What the money cannot buy, and what we will tell you instead
paragraphs: No tutor can promise a grade, a band of improvement or a specific mark, and anybody who does is telling you something about themselves rather than about your child. What tutoring can reliably do is find the repeating error, drill the technique that recovers method marks, and get the exploration started on time. Those are real and they are worth paying for; a number is not on offer.

Nor can money buy a specialist who does not exist for a given slot. Higher Level Analysis and Approaches Paper 3 work at a fortnight's notice, or a particular combination of course and schedule, sometimes has no good match available. When that is the case we say so and give a realistic match time rather than putting a general maths tutor in a specialist slot. A mismatch costs a family the fee and the weeks, and in DP2 the weeks are the expensive part.

The first step is cheap and specific. Send the course and level, a photograph of a marked paper or the most recent report, and the weekday that works on a bad afternoon. The trial lesson is free, takes about forty minutes, runs on a past question from the right course, and ends with the tutor's written read on what the loss pattern is and how many weeks it implies. Then you decide, with a number in front of you and a plan attached to it.

Two last things we will not do, both of which are on offer elsewhere in this market. We will not describe a tutor as an IB examiner unless that status can actually be evidenced, because examiner claims are made loosely here and are used to imply access to marking and boundaries that nobody has. And we will not claim approval, accreditation or a licence from KHDA, the Ministry of Education, the MoHRE or the IB, because IB Gram holds none and the phrase is the single most dangerous thing a tutoring page in Dubai can say. What we will do is explain what each body actually governs and link you to its own pages.

faqs.question: What does an IB maths tutor in Al Rashidiya actually cost per month?
faqs.answer: Think in monthly terms, because a Diploma arrangement runs for two years. Bestimate's Dubai rate table puts weekly one-hour tutoring at AED 240 to 600 a month at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 in the middle, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or above for exam-year specialist support. Packages advertised locally sit around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions against AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four in-home sessions of two hours. None of those is an IB Gram price; they are the market, published by others, and each is checkable on the source's own page.

faqs.question: Is Higher Level Analysis and Approaches more expensive to tutor than Standard Level?
faqs.answer: In practice yes, because the pool of people who teach it well is smaller. Higher Level AA adds proof by induction, complex numbers, vectors and a considerably harder calculus load, plus Paper 3, and that specialism sits in the market's AED 200 to 450 and above band rather than the AED 150 to 300 qualified-tutor band. The honest framing is that you are paying for scarcity rather than for effort. For Standard Level work and for most of DP1, a qualified subject tutor at the lower band is usually the right purchase.

faqs.question: My child is on Applications and Interpretation. Can any maths tutor teach it?
faqs.answer: No, and assuming otherwise is the commonest waste in this market. Applications and Interpretation carries a much heavier statistics and modelling load than Analysis and Approaches, including hypothesis testing and regression, and assumes technology throughout. A tutor whose strength is AA calculus can be genuinely weak here. Ask a prospective tutor which of the two courses they teach and how many cohorts of it they have taken through, then ask them to describe the statistics content. A specialist answers immediately; a generalist asks which course you mean, which is a fair answer honestly given.

faqs.question: Where do families here most often waste money on maths tutoring?
faqs.answer: Six places, in rough order of frequency: paying specialist rates without confirming the course and level; spending the weekly hour on the student's stronger topic while the failing paper goes untouched; buying exploration help in the final fortnight; paying the in-home travel premium of AED 180 to 500 an hour for teaching available online at AED 150 to 300; group classes for a problem nobody else in the group has; and extending an arrangement that has produced no mark movement because stopping feels like quitting. All six are prevented by a diagnosis and a six-lesson review.

faqs.question: How many sessions a week should we start with?
faqs.answer: One, almost always, held for the full two years, with a second session added for a defined block when there is something specific to do. That shape costs less in total than two weekly sessions for a single year and tends to produce more, because continuity lets a tutor see a pattern rather than react to whichever test came back badly. Two sessions a week sustained across the whole Diploma is a large commitment, and households that start there usually cut back by the second term, often at the worst possible moment.

faqs.question: Why is in-home maths tutoring quoted so much higher in the eastern suburbs?
faqs.answer: Because the rate includes a car journey and in this corridor it is a slow one. A tutor driving into Al Rashidiya from Al Garhoud or Mirdif between 3pm and 6pm loses a real part of the chargeable hour on Algeria Street or at the Garhoud interchange, and recovers it in the price. The published gap tells the story: AED 180 to 500 an hour in-home against AED 150 to 300 for a qualified tutor working online. The premium buys travel, not teaching. IB Gram does not sell home visits anywhere in the UAE.

faqs.question: Does the exploration really justify spending tutoring money on it?
faqs.answer: It carries twenty per cent of the final maths grade, which makes it the single largest component outside the written papers. Four early sessions, one on what the published criteria reward, one on choosing a topic with enough mathematics in it, one on structure and one reviewing the student's own draft through questions, is a small spend that protects a large share of the grade. Leaving it until the term it is due costs considerably more, arrives at exam-year rates, and cannot undo a topic choice that was too thin to reach the higher bands.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help write my child's mathematical exploration?
faqs.answer: No, and you should decline the offer wherever you hear it. A tutor may explain the assessment criteria, model the method on a different example, ask questions about your child's draft and point out where the mathematics is unsupported. A tutor may not write, draft, rewrite or edit to completion any part of it. The practical test is simple: if the feedback arrives as sentences your child could paste in, the line has been crossed. One page in this search result sells finished Internal Assessments outright, and it is the student who faces the malpractice finding.

faqs.question: Is Paper 1 or Paper 3 the better place to spend limited hours?
faqs.answer: Paper 1 first, for most students. It is sat without a calculator, so it exposes fluency directly, and exact values, surds and clean algebraic manipulation under time pressure respond quickly to drilling. It is the highest return per hour available in the subject. Paper 3, sat only by Higher Level students, is worth a short dedicated block rather than ongoing work: sitting two or three past investigations removes the format shock, which is where those marks are usually lost rather than in the mathematics itself.

faqs.question: My child's predicted maths grade is below a university offer. What now?
faqs.answer: Act on the papers, not on the content. A predicted grade that sits a band low usually reflects two or three repeating errors across past papers rather than a general gap, and finding them takes one diagnostic lesson with a marked paper in front of the tutor. From there a defined block of two sessions a week to the final series, spent almost entirely on timed past-paper work marked against published criteria, is the shape that moves marks. Tell the school too, since predicted grades are theirs to revise on evidence.

faqs.question: What time can a maths lesson realistically start for an Al Rashidiya student?
faqs.answer: It depends on which direction the school run goes. Families whose child attends a school in Al Garhoud can usually hold a 4.30pm slot, because the run north is short outside peak. Families on a Mirdif, Al Mizhar or Al Warqa bus route are realistically looking at 5.30pm or later, since those routes can take the better part of forty minutes once school finishes. Choose the time that works on a bad traffic day rather than the earliest that has ever worked, because that is the slot still running in month four.

faqs.question: Do you teach the exact course my child's school follows?
faqs.answer: We teach the IB course your child is registered for, at the level they are registered at, and we follow the school's own sequence rather than running a parallel syllabus. Tell us the school and the tutor will work against its scheme of work and internal deadlines where you want that. What we do not do is reproduce or supply IB subject guides, past papers or mark schemes as downloads; those belong to the IB, and the right place to get them is through the school or the official site. Confirm current structure with your IB coordinator.

faqs.question: Is a group maths class cheaper and good enough?
faqs.answer: Cheaper per hour, and the right answer only when the whole group shares the same gap. A group class works for revising a topic the class is collectively weak on. It works badly for the situation most families are actually in, where one student is losing marks on a specific thing that the others handle fine, because the hour then runs at the group's pace. Judge it on the question: can you name the single topic the class will cover, and is that the topic your child's marks are leaving from?

faqs.question: What happens if no Higher Level maths specialist is available for our slot?
faqs.answer: We tell you, with a realistic match time, rather than filling the slot with a general maths tutor. The combinations that run short are predictable: Higher Level Analysis and Approaches at short notice, Paper 3 work a fortnight before the series, and narrow scheduling windows in the late evening. If the wait does not fit your timeline we will say that too. A tutor who does not know the course costs a family the fee and, in DP2, the weeks, and the weeks are the part that cannot be bought back.

faqs.question: What do I need to send before the free trial lesson?
faqs.answer: Three things, and none of them takes long. The course and level, confirmed from the registration rather than remembered. A photograph of a marked mock or school test, which tells a specialist more in two minutes than a paragraph of description. And the weekday slot that works on a bad traffic afternoon. We do not need a photograph of your child, a full academic history or grades across every subject; UAE Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 governs personal data here and the privacy link on this page explains what is held.

intro.heading: Where the content actually lives, and where it gets hard
paragraphs: Both Diploma maths courses are built from five content areas: number and algebra, functions, geometry and trigonometry, statistics and probability, and calculus. That structure is not decoration. It tells a student where a question comes from, which matters under time pressure, and it tells a tutor where to look when a grade is stuck. A student who is losing marks across every paper usually has a problem in number and algebra, because that area underpins the other four. A student losing marks in one paper only usually has a technique problem rather than a content one.

The two courses distribute weight across those five areas differently, and this is the practical difference between them that matters more than reputation. Analysis and Approaches leans heavily into algebra, functions and calculus, with proof running through it as a skill. Applications and Interpretation shifts weight towards statistics and probability and towards modelling with technology. A student placed in the wrong course does not merely find it harder; they find the wrong things hard, which is a worse position because their strengths go unused for two years.

Al Safa is a useful place to write this from, because the community contains an unusual concentration of secondary provision. Jumeirah College, Horizon English School, Safa British School, Latifa School for Girls and Jumeirah Baccalaureate School all sit in or next to it, which means children living in Al Safa, Al Wasl, Jumeirah 3 and Al Manara frequently study maths within a few minutes of home. It also means Higher Level cohorts are spread thin across several institutions rather than concentrated in one, and a small cohort is why a local specialist in Higher Level Analysis and Approaches is hard to find however short the drive would be.

What this page does is work through the subject. The five content areas and where the Higher Level extension sits. Proof, which is a Higher Level skill students rarely practise deliberately. Calculus, which is where Higher Level grades separate. The formula booklet, audited so that nothing gets memorised unnecessarily. Maths teaching for Al Safa families happens one-to-one over live video in a shared workspace where both people write, which suits the subject: a multi-step solution stays on screen, is saved, and can be revisited a week later when the same error reappears.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-al-safa.subjectsIntro: The content a Diploma maths tutor in this cluster spends most time on, organised by the area of the syllabus it sits in, with the error each one tends to produce.

subjects.name: Indices, logarithms and surds
subjects.description: Part of number and algebra, and the foundation most often found missing. Log rules applied in the wrong direction and negative fractional indices mishandled account for marks lost in topics that look unrelated.

subjects.name: Sequences, series and the binomial theorem
subjects.description: Arithmetic and geometric series plus binomial expansion. Losses come from off-by-one errors in the term index and from expansions where the general term is set up correctly and evaluated carelessly.

subjects.name: Proof by induction, contradiction and counterexample
subjects.description: Marks are awarded for structure as much as for the result. An induction proof missing an explicit statement of the inductive step loses marks even when the algebra is correct throughout.

subjects.name: Functions, transformations and inverses
subjects.description: Domain and range restrictions are the recurring loss. Students find an inverse correctly and omit the domain the inverse requires, which the scheme treats as an incomplete answer.

subjects.name: Differentiation techniques
subjects.description: Chain, product and quotient rules used in combination. Optimisation questions lose marks for an unjustified maximum rather than for the calculus, since the scheme wants the nature of the point established.

subjects.name: Integration techniques
subjects.description: Substitution, integration by parts and volumes of revolution. This is the clearest dividing line between a 5 and a 7 in Higher Level Analysis and Approaches, and it rewards volume of practice more than insight.

subjects.name: Trigonometric identities and equations
subjects.description: A non-calculator skill, which is why it punishes AA candidates on the paper where no calculator is allowed. Recognising which identity applies is the taught part; the algebra afterwards is practice.

subjects.name: Vectors, lines and planes
subjects.description: Scalar and vector products and intersections. Notation costs more marks than concepts here: a vector written ambiguously is read by the scheme as a different object and the method mark goes with it.

subjects.name: Complex numbers
subjects.description: Cartesian, polar and exponential forms with De Moivre's theorem. A steep entry and a formulaic payoff: once the representations are secure, questions on it are among the more predictable at Higher Level.

subjects.name: Statistics, distributions and hypothesis testing
subjects.levels: AI most heavily; AA at both levels
subjects.description: In AI this is the centre of the course. Marks sit in stating the hypotheses properly, choosing the right test and interpreting the outcome in context rather than announcing a number.

subjects.name: Regression and modelling
subjects.description: Choosing a model, justifying the choice and naming its limitations. Students operate the technology correctly and omit the justification the criteria explicitly reward.

subjects.name: The mathematical exploration
subjects.description: Around a fifth of the grade, assessed on criteria that do not include topic difficulty. Topic choice is a decision problem, and most of the eventual marks are determined by how narrow the question is.

sections.heading: The five content areas, and where the Higher Level extension sits
paragraphs: Mapping a stuck grade onto the five content areas is the fastest diagnostic available in Diploma maths. Losses spread evenly across all five point at number and algebra, because that area sits underneath the others and a weakness there shows up everywhere. Losses concentrated in one area point at a content gap that can be closed directly. Losses concentrated in one paper rather than one area point at technique, which is a different job again.

The Higher Level extension is not spread evenly either. In Analysis and Approaches it is weighted heavily towards calculus, with substantial additional integration technique, plus proof and complex numbers. In Applications and Interpretation it goes into deeper statistical inference and more demanding modelling. Knowing which area the extension loads changes the order of work: a Higher Level AA student who is weak in integration has a bigger problem than one who is weak in sequences, because the first will recur in every paper and the second will not.

This also answers a question parents ask reasonably often, which is whether a tutor should go through the syllabus from the start. Almost never. Going through five content areas systematically consumes two terms and spends most of them on material the student already knows. Diagnosing which area is leaking and working there is faster, cheaper and more motivating, and it takes one marked paper to establish.

The table maps the areas against where each course puts its weight and where the extension lands. It is the document to look at alongside a marked script, and together they usually settle the question of what the first month should do.

sections.heading: Proof: the Higher Level skill students never practise deliberately
paragraphs: Proof appears in Analysis and Approaches as a genuine assessed skill, and it is the part of the course most students treat as something to read rather than something to rehearse. The result is predictable: a student who can follow a proof in a textbook cannot construct one under time pressure, and the marks for structure go unclaimed even where the algebra is sound.

Proof by induction is the clearest case. The scheme awards marks for the base case, for an explicit statement of the inductive assumption, for the algebraic step, and for a concluding statement that the result holds for all relevant integers. A student who does the algebra beautifully and omits the explicit assumption loses marks that had nothing to do with their mathematics. These are among the most mechanically recoverable marks anywhere in the Diploma, because the structure is fixed and can be learned as a template.

Proof by contradiction and disproof by counterexample behave similarly. Both have a required shape, both reward stating what is being assumed, and both are routinely answered in a conversational style that loses structural marks. A student taught the shape writes shorter answers and scores higher, which is a satisfying combination and an unusual one.

The practical teaching point is rehearsal rather than explanation. Reading three induction proofs teaches less than writing one badly and having it marked properly. An online session suits this well: the student writes in the shared workspace, the tutor marks it against the scheme line by line, and the omission becomes visible immediately rather than two weeks later when a mock comes back.

sections.heading: Calculus, and why Higher Level grades separate here
paragraphs: In Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, calculus carries the largest share of the extension and the largest share of the variance between a 5 and a 7. Differentiation is usually secure by the middle of Diploma 1; integration is where students stall, because the techniques are numerous, the choice between them is not obvious from the integrand, and recognising which to apply comes from volume of practice rather than from understanding a principle.

That has a specific teaching consequence. Integration is not improved much by explanation, and it is improved considerably by doing twenty integrals a week for a month with the choice of technique made explicit each time. A session that explains integration by parts carefully and then sets two examples is less useful than one that works through fifteen varied integrands and names the signal that selects the method in each. Students often prefer the first and need the second.

The errors are predictable enough to list. Substitution attempted without changing the limits in a definite integral. Integration by parts with the parts assigned the wrong way round, producing something harder than the original. Volumes of revolution set up around the wrong axis. Each of those is a habit rather than a gap, and habits respond to repetition with immediate correction, which is exactly what a weekly session with marking can provide.

Differentiation has its own smaller set: chain rule nested inside a product rule and applied once instead of twice, and optimisation questions where the maximum is found and its nature never established. The second of those is scheme behaviour rather than calculus, and it is worth a mark or two per paper to anybody who learns to write one extra line.

sections.heading: The formula booklet: what is given and what must be learned
paragraphs: A formula booklet is provided in every Diploma maths examination, and students waste real hours memorising things it contains while failing to learn things it does not. Auditing the booklet once, early, is one of the highest-return hours available in the course, and almost nobody does it because it feels like administration rather than mathematics.

The audit is simple. Go through the booklet page by page with the syllabus beside it and mark every formula as given or not given. What is given does not need memorising; it needs practice at being located quickly, because finding a formula under time pressure is a skill of its own and a slow search costs a minute a question. What is not given needs learning properly, and that list is shorter than students fear, which is itself reassuring.

There is a second-order benefit. Knowing what the booklet provides changes how a student reads a question. A question that supplies an unfamiliar expression is often signalling that the expression is in the booklet and should be looked up rather than derived. Students who have never opened the booklet outside an examination do not read that signal and try to derive from first principles, which costs time they do not have.

In an online session this is straightforward to practise, since both people can look at the same page and the same question at once. A tutor can watch a student search, time the search, and correct the habit. That is one of several places where a shared screen is at least as good as sitting side by side, because the search becomes an observable activity rather than something happening in somebody's head.

sections.heading: Reading a mark scheme: method marks, accuracy marks and follow-through
paragraphs: Maths mark schemes award marks of different kinds, and a student who does not know this loses marks for reasons they cannot see. Method marks are awarded for a correct approach even where the arithmetic goes wrong. Accuracy marks are awarded for the correct value. The two are tallied separately, which is why a student with the wrong final answer can still score most of a question and why a student with the right answer and no working can score very little.

Follow-through is the mechanism that most changes behaviour once a student understands it. Where an early slip propagates through later parts, the scheme often credits subsequent work that is correct given the earlier wrong value. The practical consequence is that abandoning a question after noticing an early error is almost always the wrong decision: continuing correctly from the wrong number can recover several marks. Students abandon constantly because nobody has told them this.

Two more scheme behaviours are worth teaching directly. Working must be visible for method marks to be awarded, which means a calculator-derived answer with nothing written down forfeits credit that was available. And accuracy expectations are specified, so a correctly computed value quoted to the wrong precision can lose the accuracy mark while keeping the method marks.

The way to teach all of this is to have the student mark their own script against a real scheme, once, under supervision. It is an uncomfortable hour and it changes behaviour permanently, because the student sees for themselves where the marks were and were not. After that, the error log carries the pattern forward, and the table below is the reference to keep beside it.

sections.heading: Past papers in maths, done the way that works
paragraphs: Past-paper practice in maths fails in a characteristic way. A student works through questions by topic, checks answers at the back, feels broadly competent, and arrives at a full paper unable to manage the time. Topic practice builds technique and tests nothing about pace, question order or the decision of what to leave, and all three of those are examined.

The method that works is less comfortable. Sit a full paper to time, in one sitting, with the equipment that paper allows and nothing else. Mark it against the real scheme, separating method losses from accuracy losses. Record every lost mark against one of five causes: content not known, technique not chosen, working not shown, accuracy or rounding, ran out of time. Then read the distribution rather than the total.

That distribution is the whole point. A student losing mostly accuracy marks needs a rounding discipline, not more integration. A student losing mostly to time needs question triage and a decision rule about what to abandon, not more content. A student losing method marks across unrelated topics usually has a foundation gap in number and algebra. Three different students with the same overall score need three different months of work, and only the breakdown tells you which is which.

One source note. Past papers, mark schemes and the formula booklet belong to the IB, and IB Gram does not reproduce or supply them. Your child's school has legitimate access and can provide what is needed. Sessions work from material the student already holds, and any site offering a downloadable bundle of IB assessment material is distributing something it has no right to.

sections.heading: The exploration, treated as a decision problem
paragraphs: Most advice about the mathematical exploration concentrates on writing it. The marks are mostly decided earlier, in the choice of topic and the narrowing of the question, and treating it as a decision problem produces better results than treating it as a writing problem.

Three tests settle a topic. Is the mathematics in it genuinely at the level of the course, neither trivial nor beyond what the student can handle correctly? Is the question narrow enough to be developed properly in the space available rather than surveyed? And is there something real for the student to engage with personally, since personal engagement is an assessed criterion rather than a stylistic preference? A topic that fails any of the three will cap the eventual marks regardless of how carefully it is written up.

The most common failure is ambition. Students choose something impressive, handle the mathematics approximately, and score below a classmate who explored something modest with precision and genuine reflection. Topic difficulty is not among the criteria, and reading the criteria once before choosing is free. The second most common failure is treating reflection as a conclusion: the descriptor wants consideration of the limitations of the student's own approach and what they would do differently, which is a specific kind of writing most students have never been asked for.

On the boundary, stated plainly because it matters. A tutor may explain the criteria, model an exploration on an unrelated topic, test a proposed question against the three tests above, and read a draft and respond with questions. A tutor may not write, rewrite or edit any part of it. Some operators in this market sell finished internal assessments outright, and a student who buys one risks a malpractice finding and the Diploma itself.

sections.heading: What maths support costs around Al Safa, and what a drive adds
paragraphs: Al Safa is one of the few communities in Dubai where a parent could plausibly argue that proximity is easy, since several of the relevant schools are minutes away. So it is worth putting the numbers next to each other properly. In-home one-to-one visits in Dubai are quoted at AED 180-350 by Bestimate and AED 200-500 by independent home tutors, with travel inside the figure. An online qualified subject tutor is published at AED 150-300, with Unitors listing IB from AED 200 and IGCSE from AED 150.

At the specialist end, TutorChase quotes AED 270 for IB, IGCSE and A Level work and Bestimate's specialist band runs AED 200-450 and above, with BartyED publishing AED 650 at the premium end. At the budget end, EdFlik advertises from AED 45-65 an hour and Tutopiya from AED 33-52, which generally means a university student. Monthly, published packages include around AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599-1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions, and Bestimate's monthly estimates for a weekly hour run AED 240-600, AED 600-1,200 and AED 1,000-2,000 or more across the three tiers. These are other providers' own figures with their own dates.

What the travel premium buys in a community like Al Safa is small, because the journeys are short. What it still costs is the match. Higher Level Analysis and Approaches cohorts are spread thinly across the several schools in this area rather than pooled, so the number of people locally who teach that course to examiner depth is very small. Requiring a tutor to be both qualified in it and willing to come to an Al Safa address on a Tuesday evening is a filter that removes nearly everybody.

IB Gram's position: no in-home visits anywhere in the UAE, a free trial lesson first, and a fee discussed once the course, level and problem are known rather than published blind. Where the honest answer after a trial is that a term of focused content work will do and a two-year commitment will not be needed, that is what you will be told.

faqs.question: My child's maths grade is stuck. How do you work out what is actually wrong?
faqs.answer: By mapping the losses onto the five content areas and the five causes. Losses spread evenly across number and algebra, functions, geometry and trigonometry, statistics and calculus point at a foundation gap in number and algebra, because that area sits underneath the rest. Losses concentrated in one area point at a closable content gap. Losses concentrated in one paper rather than one area point at technique. That takes one full marked paper to establish, and the diagnosis determines a completely different month of work in each case.

faqs.question: Should a tutor work through the whole maths syllabus from the beginning?
faqs.answer: Almost never. Working systematically through five content areas consumes two terms and spends most of them on material the student already handles, which is expensive and demoralising. Diagnosing which area is leaking and working there is faster and more motivating, and it takes one marked paper to establish. The exception is a student who has genuinely missed a long stretch of teaching, where a structured rebuild is the right answer and should be planned as one rather than drifted into.

faqs.question: What are method marks and accuracy marks, and why does it matter?
faqs.answer: Maths schemes award them separately. Method marks go to a correct approach shown in writing, even where the arithmetic fails. Accuracy marks go to the correct value at the required precision. This is why a student with a wrong final answer can score most of a question, and why a student with the right answer and no working can score almost nothing. Teaching this changes behaviour fast: once a student knows method marks exist, they write the method down, and that alone recovers marks in every paper.

faqs.question: My child gives up on a question after making a mistake early on. Is that costing marks?
faqs.answer: Yes, often several. Mark schemes operate follow-through: where an early slip propagates into later parts, subsequent work that is correct given the wrong earlier value is frequently still credited. So abandoning a question after noticing an error is almost always the wrong decision, and continuing correctly from the wrong number recovers marks that would otherwise be lost. Students abandon constantly because nobody has explained this to them, and explaining it takes about five minutes.

faqs.question: Why does proof cost my child marks when the algebra is right?
faqs.answer: Because the scheme awards marks for structure as well as for the mathematics. In proof by induction, marks go to the base case, to an explicit statement of the inductive assumption, to the algebraic step, and to a concluding statement that the result holds generally. A student who does the algebra beautifully and never states the assumption loses marks that have nothing to do with their mathematics. Proof by contradiction and disproof by counterexample behave the same way, and both can be learned as templates.

faqs.question: Which part of Higher Level maths separates a 5 from a 7?
faqs.answer: In Analysis and Approaches it is overwhelmingly integration. Differentiation is usually secure by the middle of Diploma 1; integration stalls students because the techniques are numerous and the choice between them is not visible in the integrand. In Applications and Interpretation the equivalent is the deeper statistical inference and modelling content. In both cases the Higher Level extension loads unevenly, which is why the order of work matters more than the quantity of it.

faqs.question: Does the formula booklet really need auditing?
faqs.answer: It is one of the best hours a Diploma maths student can spend. A formula booklet is provided in every paper, and students routinely memorise things it contains while failing to learn things it does not. Going through it page by page against the syllabus, marking every formula as given or not given, shortens the list of what must genuinely be learned and teaches the separate skill of locating a formula in seconds. A slow search costs around a minute a question, which adds up to a grade.

faqs.question: Will a maths tutor come to our villa in Al Safa?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we run in India only. Lessons here are one-to-one over live video in a shared workspace where both people write. For maths that format is genuinely well suited: the whole of a multi-step solution stays on screen, it is saved, and the student can revisit the exact working a week later when the same error reappears, which a sheet of paper cannot do.

faqs.question: Al Safa has several schools within minutes. Does that not make a local tutor easy?
faqs.answer: It makes a local general tutor easy and a local specialist hard, which is the opposite of what you would expect. Several schools sitting close together means Higher Level maths cohorts are spread across them rather than pooled in one, so the number of people in this area who teach Higher Level Analysis and Approaches to examiner depth is very small. Requiring a tutor to be both qualified in that course and willing to come to an Al Safa address on a weekday evening removes almost everybody from the list.

faqs.question: How should my child use past papers to prepare for maths?
faqs.answer: In full, to time, with only the equipment that paper allows, and then marked against the real scheme with method losses separated from accuracy losses. Topic practice builds technique and tests nothing about pace, question order or the decision of what to abandon, and all three are examined. Record every lost mark against one of five causes: content, technique choice, working, accuracy and rounding, or time. Then read the distribution rather than the total, because the distribution is what tells you what to do next.

faqs.question: How do we choose a good exploration topic?
faqs.answer: Apply three tests before writing anything. Is the mathematics genuinely at the level of the course, neither trivial nor beyond what your child can handle correctly? Is the question narrow enough to be developed properly rather than surveyed? And is there something real to engage with personally, since personal engagement is an assessed criterion? A topic failing any of the three caps the eventual marks however carefully it is written. Ambition is the commonest failure: modest and precise outscores impressive and approximate.

faqs.question: Can a tutor mark my child's exploration draft for them?
faqs.answer: A tutor may read it and respond with questions, explain the criteria line by line, and say where the mathematics is not yet at course level. A tutor may not write, rewrite or edit any part of it, or supply sentences that are missing. Marginal questions rather than corrections keep the work the student's own and produce a better exploration anyway, because the student has to resolve the problem and therefore learns what the criterion is measuring. Buying a completed internal assessment risks the Diploma itself.

faqs.question: What time of day works best for a maths session in this area?
faqs.answer: Earlier than families expect, because calculation work degrades with tiredness faster than discussion does. Schools in and around Al Safa finish between roughly 2.30pm and 3.15pm, and many students here are home very quickly given the short distances, so a 4.30pm start is often workable where it would not be further out. For anything heavily quantitative a weekend morning beats a 7pm weekday slot, and online delivery means no tutor journey needs accommodating either way.

faqs.question: Is Standard Level maths a problem for university applications?
faqs.answer: For most courses, no. Standard Level in either maths course is a serious qualification accepted across a wide range of degrees, and a student who takes Standard Level and performs strongly is generally better placed than one who takes Higher Level and cannot cope with the extension. The exceptions are maths-heavy degrees, where Higher Level Analysis and Approaches is frequently specified. Read each shortlisted course's own stated requirement, including at UAE universities, rather than relying on a general pattern.

faqs.question: Can you provide IB maths past papers and the formula booklet?
faqs.answer: No. Past papers, mark schemes and the formula booklet belong to the IB, and reproducing or distributing them is a copyright problem rather than a grey area. Your child's school has legitimate access and can supply what is needed, and sessions work from material the student already holds. Treat any site offering a downloadable bundle of IB assessment material with caution, since distributing it is something they have no right to do, which says something about the rest of the operation.

faqs.question: What if no tutor is free in my child's exact course and level?
faqs.answer: We say so rather than offering an approximate match. Higher Level Analysis and Approaches is the thinnest category and it tightens further in exam terms, when specialists are fully committed. In that situation you get a plain statement that we do not currently have the right person, a realistic estimate of how long a match would take, and a suggestion for the interim, which is sometimes the school's own department. A mismatched maths tutor costs a term and is worse than a short wait.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-al-safa.closingHeading: One marked paper tells us most of it
dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-al-safa.closingBody: Name the course and the level, send one full marked paper, and the diagnosis mostly writes itself: which of the five content areas is leaking, and whether the losses are method, accuracy, technique choice, working or time. A free trial lesson costs nothing and usually settles both questions within the hour, with your child writing and the tutor marking against a real scheme. Lessons run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time in a shared workspace, scheduled around the short Al Safa school run and the mandatory-subject homework rather than around anybody's drive. If a term of focused work would do and two years would not be needed, we will say that.

intro.heading: The maths problem in Satwa starts as a timetable problem
paragraphs: Al Satwa is a small, dense, old part of Dubai sitting between Jumeirah to the west and Bur Dubai to the east, with Satwa Road running through the middle of it and Sheikh Zayed Road along one edge. Almost no family here walks their child to an IB school, because the schools that run the Diploma Programme are in Umm Suqeim, Al Sufouh, Jumeirah and Al Barsha. That single geographic fact shapes everything about maths support in this neighbourhood: the child is in a bus or a car for a meaningful part of the afternoon, and the hour they are freshest is not the hour a tutor is usually free.

Mathematics is the subject least forgiving of that. An essay subject tolerates a long gap and a late start; a student can read a chapter at ten at night and still gain from it. Algebraic fluency does not work that way. It is built by short, frequent, deliberate practice on paper, and it decays when a week is skipped. So the question a Satwa parent is really asking when they search for an IB maths tutor is not only who is good, but when, exactly, in a week that already has a bus, homework, Arabic, Islamic Education and often a sport, can forty-five focused minutes of mathematics actually happen.

Online delivery answers the timetable question before it answers the teaching question. A lesson that needs no travel can start at 4.45pm on a Tuesday and 7.30pm on a Thursday in the same week, and it can move by twenty minutes on the morning of the lesson without anybody losing a commute. It also widens the pool from whoever is within a short drive of Satwa to whoever actually teaches the route your child is on. For a pupil sitting Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, that difference is the entire value of the arrangement, because Paper 3 is a distinct skill that a generalist maths tutor has often never taught.

This page is written for that decision rather than as a brochure. It sets out the AA and AI route choice with the consequences of each, the paper-by-paper weightings at both levels, the five exploration criteria with their mark allocations and the way students lose them, what the Dubai market charges for maths support and who publishes those figures, and a realistic view of when a session can start given where the schools near Satwa actually are. Where a date or a rule matters, the authority that sets it is named so you can check it rather than take our word for it.

One thing is stated plainly before anything else. IB Gram delivers tutoring to UAE families as one-to-one online lessons over live video. We do not send a tutor to an address in Dubai; visits in the home are something we run only in India. The phrase parents type includes the word tutor near the word Satwa, and that is a fair search, but the honest answer to it is an online specialist on your child's exact syllabus route, not a nearby generalist with a car.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-al-satwa.programmesIntro: Maths support in Satwa splits by programme, and the split matters more than it looks. A Year 9 pupil on MYP mathematics, a Year 11 pupil finishing IGCSE and a DP2 pupil writing an exploration need three different tutors, three different session lengths and three different kinds of homework.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme Mathematics
programmes.description: Two courses, each at two levels: Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation, Standard or Higher. Every Diploma candidate takes one of the four. Assessment is Paper 1 and Paper 2 at both levels, Paper 3 at Higher Level only, plus the mathematical exploration, which is internally marked against five criteria and externally moderated. The route is chosen in DP1 and is difficult to change after the first reporting cycle.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai DP cohorts sit the May session, and schools near Satwa set internal exploration deadlines well inside DP2 so that moderation samples can be assembled. Pupils travelling from Satwa to Umm Suqeim or Al Barsha lose part of their afternoon to the commute, so DP maths tutoring here is usually two shorter sessions a week rather than one long one.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme Mathematics
programmes.description: Criterion-referenced rather than paper-based, assessed against four criteria covering knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-world contexts. MYP 4 and 5 split into standard and extended mathematics, and that split is the first real fork in a child's route towards AA or AI. Marks are reported on a 1-8 scale per criterion, converted to a grade boundary set by the school.
programmes.countryNote: Satwa families whose children attend an IB continuum school in Umm Suqeim or Jumeirah often meet the standard-versus-extended decision in Year 9, two years before anybody mentions the Diploma. Getting that call right removes most of the pain of the later AA decision, and it is the cheapest intervention available in the whole five-year sequence.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme Mathematics
programmes.description: Inquiry-led, organised around number, pattern and function, data handling, measurement, and shape and space. There is no external examination. Support at this stage is about number sense, fluency with written methods, and the habit of explaining a result, because the MYP criteria later reward exactly that explanation. Short sessions work better than long ones at this age.
programmes.countryNote: Several primary schools serving Satwa families sit in Jumeirah and Al Wasl, which keeps the primary commute short compared with the secondary one. That makes a late-afternoon PYP maths session genuinely easy to place in this neighbourhood, which is rarely true by DP2.

programmes.name: IGCSE Mathematics into the Diploma
programmes.description: Most British-curriculum pupils near Satwa take Cambridge 0580 Extended or Pearson 4MA1 Higher, then move either to A Level or into the Diploma. The algebra, trigonometry and function work in those syllabuses is the direct foundation of AA SL, and the statistics and modelling strands feed AI. A pupil who scraped a grade 6 on Extended will find AA HL punishing in a way nobody warned them about.
programmes.countryNote: Cambridge candidates in the UAE sit the June and November series; the February and March series is offered to India only, so a Dubai pupil planning a resit is planning for November. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs May/June and November, with the November 2026 timetable finishing on 19 November 2026.

dubai/ib-maths-tutor-in-al-satwa.subjectsIntro: The grid below is weighted to mathematics and the subjects that fail because of it. A pupil losing marks in Physics Paper 2 or Economics HL quantitative questions is frequently losing them to algebra rather than to the subject itself, and treating that as a maths problem is usually faster.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Algebra, functions, trigonometry, calculus, and proof at HL. Paper 1 is sat without a calculator at both levels, which punishes anyone who has outsourced arithmetic to a screen. HL adds Paper 3, two extended problem-solving questions worth a fifth of the grade.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling, statistics, regression and interpretation, with a calculator permitted in every paper. The marks here are lost less to manipulation than to reading: a context described in four lines, and a student who models the wrong quantity. HL Paper 3 is two extended modelling investigations.

subjects.name: Mathematical exploration (IA)
subjects.description: A 12 to 20 page individual piece worth a fifth of the final grade, marked on presentation, mathematical communication, personal engagement, reflection and use of mathematics. Most of the damage is done at topic choice, weeks before a single line is written.

subjects.name: MYP Mathematics
subjects.description: Four criteria, each on a 1-8 scale, with investigating patterns the one that catches strong arithmetic students out. Extended mathematics in MYP 4 and 5 is the honest preparation for AA; standard mathematics points towards AI unless something changes.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Mechanics, waves, electricity and fields, plus the internal assessment. Satwa pupils taking AA HL alongside Physics HL tend to carry the maths across well; those on AI SL often meet an algebra wall in the fields and circuits topics rather than a physics wall.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Stoichiometry, energetics, equilibrium and organic chemistry. The quantitative sections reward exactly the unit-tracking and rearranging that Paper 1 maths demands, which is why a chemistry grade sometimes rises after a term of maths work and nothing else.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Microeconomics, macroeconomics, the global economy and development. HL adds quantitative questions and a policy paper. Diagram accuracy and calculation discipline decide more marks here than essay style does, and both are trainable in a handful of sessions.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Systems fundamentals, computational thinking, algorithms and the solution development internal assessment. Pupils who can trace an algorithm on paper score consistently better than pupils who can only run one, and that tracing is a mathematics habit.

subjects.name: IGCSE Mathematics (0580 / 4MA1)
subjects.description: Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1. Extended and Higher tiers carry the grade ceiling that matters for DP entry. The commonest reason a Year 11 pupil near Satwa is entered for the lower tier is lost algebra from Year 9, which is recoverable with time.

subjects.name: IGCSE Additional Mathematics (0606)
subjects.description: Taken alongside 0580 in a few Dubai schools as a bridge towards A Level or AA HL. It introduces calculus and more demanding trigonometry a year early, and a pupil who copes with it is the pupil for whom AA HL is a sensible choice.

sections.heading: What a Satwa parent is actually searching for
paragraphs: Someone typing for an IB maths tutor in Al Satwa wants three things answered in order: can my child be taught the exact course they are enrolled on, can the lesson happen at a time that exists in our week, and what will it cost. The literal answer is that IB Gram matches an online one-to-one tutor by route and level, that lessons are scheduled on Gulf Standard Time and can start as early as 4.30pm or as late as 8.00pm, and that market rates for IB maths support in Dubai run roughly AED 150 to AED 450 an hour depending on what tier of tutor you buy.

The reason the order matters is that most tutoring in this part of Dubai is sold the other way round. A parent asks a neighbour, gets a name, and the name teaches maths. Whether that person has taught Analysis and Approaches Paper 3, or has ever marked a mathematical exploration against criterion E, is discovered in week four. By then the family has paid for three sessions and lost a month of DP1, which is the one resource in the Diploma that cannot be bought back.

Satwa makes this worse than average because it is a small neighbourhood with no IB school inside it. The local pool is small, and the schools the children attend are elsewhere, so proximity delivers almost nothing. A tutor who lives two streets away and has never seen an AA HL paper is nearer and less useful than a specialist on a video call. Online delivery is not a compromise on this page; on this specific search, in this specific neighbourhood, it is the better answer and the comparison table further down sets out why in cost and in travel terms.

What follows is organised as a decision rather than a pitch. Route first, because it governs everything after it. Then the papers and their weightings, then where marks go missing, then the exploration criteria by letter, then the money, then the timetable. Read the route section even if your child has already chosen, because a quarter of the difficulty families report in DP1 maths is a route problem wearing a teaching problem's clothes.

sections.heading: AA or AI: the route choice that governs the next two years
paragraphs: Every Diploma candidate takes one mathematics course, and there are four of them: Analysis and Approaches at Standard or Higher Level, and Applications and Interpretation at Standard or Higher Level. They are not a ladder from easy to hard. They are two different subjects that happen to share a name, and choosing between them on the basis of which sounds more impressive is the single most expensive mistake available in DP1.

Analysis and Approaches is about method. Algebra, functions, trigonometry, calculus, and at Higher Level proof. Paper 1 is sat without a calculator at both levels, which means a student who has spent five years typing every calculation into a screen will meet a genuine problem in the first term. Applications and Interpretation is about modelling and interpretation, with statistics, regression and real data, and a calculator permitted in every paper. The marks there are lost to reading a context wrongly far more often than to manipulating an expression wrongly.

The decision should be made against two things: what the child can actually do on paper today, and what the universities they might apply to expect. A strong IGCSE grade is weak evidence for AA HL on its own, because Extended tier algebra and AA HL algebra are a long way apart. A diagnostic hour in the first term of DP1, working through a past Paper 1 under timed conditions, produces better evidence than any report card, and it costs a fraction of what a route switch in DP2 costs in lost teaching.

The table sets the two routes side by side on the dimensions that change what a tutor does. Note the last row in particular: the regret runs in both directions, and the AI SL pupil who meets a maths prerequisite at application stage is as badly served as the AA HL pupil who took the course on pride.

sections.heading: The papers, the weightings and what each one is testing
paragraphs: Grades in IB mathematics are built from three or four components depending on level, and families consistently underweight the exploration and overweight the final paper. At Standard Level the two written papers carry four fifths of the grade between them and the exploration carries the remaining fifth. At Higher Level the exploration still carries a fifth, Paper 3 carries a fifth, and the two main papers carry the rest. A pupil can therefore lose two fifths of the available grade in work that is finished before the examination hall is ever entered.

Paper 1 and Paper 2 both mix short response with extended response. The difference is technology: in Analysis and Approaches, Paper 1 is calculator-free and Paper 2 is not. That single rule reshapes revision, because the two papers reward different habits. Paper 1 rewards clean by-hand work, exact values, and the discipline of not reaching for a decimal. Paper 2 rewards knowing which function on the calculator answers the question and still writing down enough method to earn the method marks.

Paper 3 exists only at Higher Level and is the component most often met for the first time in a mock. It presents two extended questions, each building through several parts towards something a student has not been shown how to do. The skill it tests is persistence under structure: reading part (a) as a hint about part (d), and continuing when a middle part has not resolved. It is trainable, and it is almost never trained in a normal school week, which makes it the highest-yield thing an HL tutor can work on.

The weightings in the table are the published shape of the assessment. Use them to decide where the next ten hours of effort go. A pupil three marks off a boundary with an unfinished exploration and no Paper 3 practice should not be spending those hours on more Paper 2 drill.

sections.heading: Where IB maths marks actually go missing
paragraphs: Marked scripts fail in patterns, and the patterns repeat across schools. The first is accuracy early in a long question. A student who mis-signs a term in line two of a six-mark question can do the remaining four steps perfectly and still take two marks. Examiners award follow-through where the scheme allows it, but not everywhere, and a pupil losing two marks to this in each of eight questions has lost a grade boundary to arithmetic rather than to mathematics.

The second is method invisibility. Both papers award method marks, and a correct final answer with no visible reasoning collects fewer of them than a wrong answer with sound working. In Paper 2 this is acute, because the calculator will produce the number and the student assumes the number is the point. Training a pupil to write one line of justification before the answer is a small change with a large return, and it is usually fixed inside three sessions.

The third is command-term misreading. 'Show that' requires a derivation ending at the given result and nothing else. 'Hence' means use the previous part, and a solution that ignores the previous part can score zero even when correct. 'Comment on' wants a sentence. 'Verify' wants a substitution. These are not style preferences; they are instructions that determine what the mark scheme accepts, and most students have never been shown them as a list.

The fourth is topic avoidance. Every pupil has two or three topics they quietly skip, and in Analysis and Approaches those are usually proof, sequences, or the integration techniques introduced late. Avoidance is invisible in classwork, because classwork follows the teaching order, and it surfaces in a mock when the paper does not. The diagnostic value of the first session is largely in finding these, and the honest first lesson is a lot of short questions rather than a lot of talking.

sections.heading: The mathematical exploration, criterion by letter
paragraphs: The exploration is worth a fifth of the grade at both levels and both routes, and it is marked out of twenty against five criteria lettered A to E. Almost no competitor page in this market names a single one of them, which is strange, because the letters are the whole of the task. A student who has read the criteria and written to them is doing a different piece of work from a student who has written something interesting about mathematics and hoped.

Criterion E, use of mathematics, carries six marks, more than any other, and it asks for mathematics commensurate with the course, correct, and relevant to the aim. Two failures recur. The first is mathematics below the level of the course, which caps the criterion regardless of how neatly it is done. The second is mathematics that is correct and sophisticated but serves no stated purpose, inserted because it looked impressive. Both are decided at topic choice, which is why topic choice is where a tutor's time is best spent.

Criteria A and B carry four marks each and are the easiest to secure. Presentation wants a coherent, organised, concise piece with the aim stated early and followed through. Mathematical communication wants defined variables, consistent notation, and symbols that belong to mathematics rather than to a calculator screen. Criteria C and D carry three marks each: personal engagement wants evidence of independent thinking, which means an original data set or an unusual angle rather than a sentence claiming interest, and reflection wants critical discussion of limitations and next steps throughout, not a closing summary.

What a tutor may do here is bounded, and the boundary is worth stating to a parent before the first session. A tutor reads the student's own draft, points at a criterion, and explains what the descriptor asks for that the draft does not yet show. A tutor does not supply the topic, supply the mathematics, or edit prose into a finished state. IB academic honesty rules make the work the student's own, and a breach is an expulsion risk for the child, not a service feature.

sections.heading: Fitting maths into the Satwa week
paragraphs: This is the part of the decision that gets the least attention and causes the most dropout. A tutoring arrangement fails far more often because the slot was wrong than because the tutor was wrong. In Satwa the slot is determined by where the school is, not where the family lives, and the schools are spread from Jumeirah to Al Barsha. A child at a coastal IB school and a sibling at a Bur Dubai school are home at different times, by different routes, in different moods.

The planning numbers below are indicative rather than published timetables, and they are set out that way deliberately. School dismissal times change by year group and by term, activity programmes add an hour to some days, and the bus route from the coast back into Satwa behaves differently at 3pm and at 4pm. What the table is for is the earliest hour a focused maths session can realistically begin, which is almost always later than a parent's first guess and earlier than a tutor's first offer.

Two practical rules come out of it. First, do not place a weekday maths session before the bus has been home for twenty minutes; a lesson that starts in the doorway is a lesson spent settling. Second, do not put both weekly sessions on consecutive days, because the whole benefit of twice-weekly maths is the gap in which the set work is attempted and the error pattern reveals itself. Tuesday and Thursday works for most Satwa families; Monday and Tuesday does not.

Online delivery is what makes either rule affordable. Moving a lesson by twenty minutes on the day costs nobody a journey, and a specialist on the other side of the city or outside the UAE entirely is as reachable at 7.30pm as at 4.30pm. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a Satwa address and does not run home visits anywhere in the UAE; that service exists only in our India operation, and the comparison in the next section prices out what the difference is actually worth.

sections.heading: What IB maths support costs in Dubai, and what sits inside each figure
paragraphs: Start at the top of the range and work down, because the interesting question is not what the cheapest hour costs but what the expensive hour contains that the cheap one does not. At the premium end, BartyED publishes AED 650 an hour. At the budget end, Tutopiya advertises from AED 33 to 52 and EdFlik from AED 45 to 65. That is a spread of more than tenfold for something both ends describe with the same two words, so the spread is the thing worth understanding before any money moves.

What the extra buys, when it buys anything, is route specificity and assessment literacy. A tutor at AED 60 an hour can usually explain how to differentiate. A tutor at AED 300 an hour should be able to say which of the four IB courses your child is on, what Paper 3 looks like, which exploration criterion the draft is weakest against, and why a 'show that' question scores zero without a derivation. Where a high rate buys none of that, it is buying a brand, and a parent is entitled to test it with two specific questions in a trial lesson.

The in-home band is the one to read most carefully. Bestimate's Dubai 2026 table puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to 350, with independent home tutors reaching AED 500, and monthly packages seen in this market run around AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions. A meaningful part of the in-home premium is travel, which is a real cost for the tutor and a cost with no teaching inside it for the family. In Satwa, where the tutor is navigating Satwa Road at 5pm, that share is higher than in a villa community with easy parking.

Every figure on this page belongs to whoever published it and carries the date it was read, October 2026. None of them is an IB Gram price, and no price list is invented here. Market rates in Dubai for IB maths sit roughly between AED 150 and AED 450 an hour for a qualified or specialist tutor, and the honest way to find where in that band a particular arrangement belongs is a free trial lesson and a consultation before anything is paid.
